We observe that execution itself provides a natural but underutilized signal: after each action, the robot directly observes the true next state, revealing the mismatch between predicted and actual outcomes. Building on this insight, we propose feedback world model, an inference-time mechanism that closes the loop between prediction and observation at inference time. Instead of treating the world model as a static open-loop predictor, our method maintains a lightweight feedback state that is updated online to iteratively correct future predictions, compensating for model errors using real-time observations without additional training data or parameter updates. We show that this process can be interpreted as a latent-space observer and admits convergence guarantees under bounded, asymptotically convergent dynamics residuals and a stable feedback gain. We further introduce action-aware guidance to better translate corrected predictions into control by emphasizing action-controllable components while suppressing irrelevant variations. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, Robomimic, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that our method substantially improves both prediction accuracy and policy performance under distribution shift, reducing world model prediction error by up to 76.4%. The same feedback mechanism improves the predictions of the pretrained foundation model Fast-WAM-Joint without updating its parameters, demonstrating its plug-and-play applicability. These results show that incorporating real-time feedback at inference time provides a simple yet powerful alternative to static world modeling.

MMLab@NTU.title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Meng Luo, Zechen Bai, Shanqing Xu, Yanlin Li, Kaixin Li
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper explores recursive self-improvement in physical AI, emphasizing the integration of behavioral and process enhancements through experiential learning and feedback mechanisms.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement, benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also change the improver's knowledge or tools, but the physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way they improve.

MMLab@NTU.title: AirPlayground: Benchmarking Aerial Navigation across Diverse Reconstructed Environments
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Rangya Zhang, Yujing Shang, Zhuoyuan Yu, Mingsheng Li, Qingsong Yan
MMLab@NTU.summary: AirPlayground is a benchmark for aerial navigation, offering 94 photorealistic environments and extensive flight demonstrations to evaluate and train diverse navigation policies.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Large-scale aerial resources provide a foundation for learning navigation across diverse environments. However, existing resources remain limited in providing (1) densely sampled flight demonstrations for learning different policy formulations and (2) broad environment coverage for standardized closed-loop evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for training and evaluating aerial navigation policies across diverse environments. We first construct 94 photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) environments spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation settings, with aligned collision geometry. Building on these environments, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline for automated expert flight collection, yielding 94K demonstrations and 46.5M synchronized observation-state-action samples at 50 Hz. We further provide an extensible API that supports training different policy formulations on this shared corpus and evaluating them under unified protocols in the corresponding environments. We benchmark seven baselines spanning four policy paradigms across three navigation settings in seen and unseen environments, and further examine scaling behavior with ACT. Scaling ACT's training corpus from 5 to 70 scenes raises median success rates on seen and unseen environments from 30.6% and 16.8% to 41.2% and 29.4%, respectively. Through this shared training and evaluation framework, AirPlayground supports analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Our analyses highlight the roles of prediction errors, execution protocols, and scene interactions in closed-loop performance.

MMLab@NTU.title: HEHA: Bounded Suboptimal Planning for Constrained Routing and Its Use in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Exploration of Unknown Environments
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Longrui Yang, Yiyu Wang, Jingfan Tang, Yunpeng Lyu, Shizhe Zhao
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents HEHA, a hierarchical planning approach that optimizes multi-robot exploration in unknown environments by efficiently solving constrained routing problems for heterogeneous robots.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: This paper considers the path planning problem for autonomous exploration of an unknown environment using multiple heterogeneous robots such as drones, wheeled, and legged robots, with different capabilities to traverse complex terrains. A key challenge there is to intelligently allocate the robots to the unknown areas to be explored and determine the visiting order of those areas subject to traversability constraints, which leads to a large-scale constrained multiple hamiltonian path problem (mHPP) that needs to be quickly and iteratively solved every time when new space is explored. To address the hallenge, we propose HEHA (Hierarchical Exploration with Heterogeneous Agents) using a recent hierarchical method that decomposes the exploration into global planning and local planning. The major contribution in HEHA is its global planning, where we propose a new routing algorithm RCH (Routing with Constraints and Heterogeneity) that can quickly find bounded sub-optimal solutions for mHPP to minimize the maximum path length (i.e., makespan) among the agents subject to traversability constraints. Additionally, the local planner in HEHA also considers heterogeneity to avoid repeated and duplicated exploration among the robots. The experimental results show, in the presence of heterogeneous traversability, our RCH can solve mHPP with up to 47% smaller makespan than several baselines, and HEHA can reduce the exploration time by up to 30% compared with existing approaches.

MMLab@NTU.title: SafeDojo: Safe Reinforcement Learning for VLA via Interactive World Model
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Kai Tang, Peidong Jia, Zhong Chu, Jiajun Cao, Jixian Wu
MMLab@NTU.summary: SafeDojo introduces a model-based safe reinforcement learning framework that enhances vision-language-action policies using an interactive world model, achieving improved safety and task success rates in real-world applications.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Safe control is a prerequisite for real-world embodied intelligence, for which safe reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, existing safe reinforcement learning methods either require costly real-world exploration or depend on hand-crafted safety functions. Neither scales to vision-language-action models deployed in open-world physical environments. We propose SafeDojo, a model-based safe reinforcement learning framework that improves vision-language-action policies through world-model imagination. SafeDojo performs online reinforcement learning on top of an interactive video world model. A ResNet success classifier scores predicted future frames, while a lightweight safety head predicts per-step contact probabilities from the current latent context and proposed action chunk, jointly assessing task execution and trajectory safety. These decoupled signals are balanced through Lagrangian-constrained GRPO. On SafeLIBERO Level I, SafeDojo improves average safe-success rate by 8.25 percentage points over the strongest baseline; on the zero-shot Level II setting, it is competitive with the strongest model-free baseline. Real-world Franka deployment further shows the best average task and safe-success rates across five tasks. These results support world-model-based safe reinforcement learning as a promising path toward safer embodied intelligence.

MMLab@NTU.title: Controllable Multi-Object Insertion for Detection Data Augmentation
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jiyang Huang, Tianwei Zhang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
MMLab@NTU.summary: SceneP2F is a novel framework for controllable multi-object insertion that enhances object detection datasets by ensuring category fidelity and visual consistency through coordinated planning and generation.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category--count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is ScenePlan which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is SceneAlign-Fill which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation.

MMLab@NTU.title: DexGraspFlow: Topology-Aware SE(3) Flow Matching for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Bin Zhou, Boyu Ma, Xinyu Zhou, Jiahua Dong, Chuhao Zhou
MMLab@NTU.summary: DexGraspFlow is a novel framework for generating dexterous grasps across different robotic hands, achieving high success rates and efficient performance through advanced kinematic modeling and guidance.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand's kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link--link coordination and link--object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object--hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33\% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49\% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91\% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework's applicability to physical grasp execution.

MMLab@NTU.title: The Show-Up Attack: When Subagents Win Over Their Supervisor
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Maosen Zhang, Jianshuo Dong, Yutong Zhang, Jie Zhang, Tianwei Zhang
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper introduces the "show-up attack," demonstrating how malicious subagents can exploit multi-agent systems, revealing vulnerabilities in six LLMs and highlighting the need for authority boundary enforcement.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed to coordinate multiple large language model (LLM) agents. However, this also creates new attack surfaces: malicious agents may have chances to exploit the coordination. In this paper, we propose and study the \textit{show-up attack}, in which a malicious subagent manipulates the supervisor into involving it in tasks beyond its assigned scope. To evaluate this risk, we propose SUA-Arena, which implements 6 attack strategies and contains 188 test cases. Then, we evaluate 6 frontier LLMs and find that all of them are vulnerable to show-up attacks. For example, GPT-5.6-Sol as a supervisor suffers an ASR of up to 0.93. Mitigation strategies such as prompting and restricted communication fail to reduce the risk consistently. These results show that multi-agent systems need explicit mechanisms for enforcing authority boundaries.

MMLab@NTU.title: Learning Native Reflection in Unified Models with Interleaved Reinforcement Learning
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Yijia Fan, Ziqi Huang, Zhongang Cai, Yan Li, Zimo Wen
MMLab@NTU.summary: UMM-Reflection enhances unified multimodal models' self-repair capabilities through interleaved reinforcement learning, significantly improving performance across multiple benchmarks without requiring external verification.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Unified multimodal models can both look at and render images, so in principle they can repair their own generations: diagnose what an image gets wrong, revise it, observe the result, and diagnose again. Whether a revision helps is known only after it is rendered, so the reflection text and the image generation must be learned jointly, over the whole loop. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on reflection trajectories gives a cold start but does not find the high-success repair paths, and naive RL that optimizes only the renderer or only one head leaves most of the gain untapped. We introduce UMM-Reflection, which applies reinforcement learning (RL) to complete reflection trajectories inside one unified model: sibling trajectories share one initial image, so the group-relative advantage compares reflection strategies, and one trajectory-level advantage updates both the reflection tokens and the flow-based revisions, avoiding the combinatorial blow-up of per-round credit assignment. Unlike single-round editing or pipelines with an external critic, credit flows across rounds and to both roles of the same model, and no verifier is needed at inference. On BAGEL, UMM-Reflection improves GenEval by 12.05 points over SFT, and the gains transfer to WISE (+10.97), OneIG-Bench (+3.48), and T2I-CompBench++ (+4.63), none of which is used in training.

MMLab@NTU.title: AWLS: Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering for One-Step Generative Robotic Manipulation Policies
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jiahong Tang, Jiaju He, Zhiyuan Yang, Ruyang Han, Haiyue Zhu
MMLab@NTU.summary: AWLS enhances one-step generative robotic manipulation policies by using advantage-weighted action reconstruction to improve performance without updating the policy's decoder, minimizing prior drift.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient action segments. While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data, standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes. Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify critic errors and induce prior drift. We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation policies without updating their decoders. AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual correction to the policy's latent noise, and trains it with an advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective. The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates while preserving fast single-step inference. We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise perturbations. Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior. Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/

MMLab@NTU.title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Youwei Zhou, Bohan Hou, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lyu, Yifan Ye
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper evaluates GPT-6 Astra's capabilities in robotic manipulation, revealing strengths in depth perception and learning but significant gaps in execution precision and safety.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.

MMLab@NTU.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Siqi Guo, Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang
MMLab@NTU.summary: PACE is a training-free framework for streaming video understanding that improves response timing by organizing errors and evaluating answers based on stability and completion.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

MMLab@NTU.title: S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Rui Gong, Ruoyu Wang, Yalun Dai, Hao Li, Sidi Yang
MMLab@NTU.summary: S-Agent 2.0 enhances spatial reasoning in general coding agents by integrating a command-line perception toolkit, significantly improving performance on 3D spatial tasks.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.

MMLab@NTU.title: Agentic Ensemble with Vision-Language Models for Visual Anomaly Detection
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Shangquan Sun, Wenjun Luo, Xu He, Yoonsoo Lee, Shijian Lu
MMLab@NTU.summary: AnomalyAgent enhances visual anomaly detection by employing a post-training fusion framework that intelligently reconciles conflicting outputs from multiple pretrained detectors using a constrained vision-language model.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Visual anomaly detection aims to detect abnormal objects, while anomaly samples are often scarce during model training. Assembling multiple pretrained detectors can help by leveraging their transferable image scores and anomaly maps. However, most existing ensemble methods apply fixed fusion rules over saved predictions which struggle when pretrained detectors clearly disagree due to different training objectives, priors, and visual representations. To this end, we design AnomalyAgent, a post-training fusion framework for accurate visual anomaly detection. AnomalyAgent aligns heterogeneous scores and maps, summarizes score- and region-level disagreement, and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. It implements two types of actions: 1) score actions that determine how to fuse image-level detector confidence via consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, or score-map consistency; 2) map actions that fuse dense anomaly responses via consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, or disagreement correction. A constrained vision-language model (VLM) is introduced to inspect high-conflict samples and select valid score action and map action to produce the final prediction. We evaluate AnomalyAgent on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks, together with seven additional public anomaly benchmarks and Real-IAD for large-scale score-level evaluation. Across these benchmarks, AnomalyAgent consistently improves over equal-weight fusion and achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among the compared fusion methods on MVTec AD and VisA, while demonstrating robust transfer across additional anomaly domains.

MMLab@NTU.title: Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits learned barrier certificates to detect inconsistencies with deployed system dynamics, enhancing safety assurance in stochastic systems.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.

MMLab@NTU.title: Detecting Heel Strike and toe off Events Using Kinematic Methods and LSTM Models
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Longbin Zhang, Zhizhang Li, Xinyi Fu, Yi Xie, Zekun Liu
MMLab@NTU.summary: This study compares kinematic methods and an LSTM model for detecting gait events, finding LSTM comparable to the best kinematic method while highlighting the need for further validation.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Accurate gait event detection is crucial for gait analysis, rehabilitation, and assistive technology, particularly in exoskeleton control, where precise identification of stance and swing phases is essential. This study evaluated the performance of seven kinematics-based methods and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model for detecting heel strike and toe-off events across 4363 gait cycles from 588 able-bodied subjects. The results indicated that while the Zeni et al. method achieved the highest accuracy among kinematics-based approaches, other methods exhibited systematic biases or required dataset-specific tuning. The LSTM model performed comparably to Zeni et al., providing a data-driven alternative without systematic bias. These findings highlight the potential of deep learning-based approaches for gait event detection while emphasizing the need for further validation in clinical populations and across diverse gait conditions. Future research will explore the generalizability of these methods in pathological populations, such as individuals with post-stroke conditions and knee osteoarthritis, as well as their robustness across varied gait conditions and data collection settings to enhance their applicability in rehabilitation and exoskeleton control.

MMLab@NTU.title: Refuse the Harm, Complete the Task via Graph-of-Rules Planning for LLM-Enabled Robots
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Ali Taheri, Alireza Taban, Qizhou Wang, Wanhua Li
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents RuleGraph, a multi-agent planning framework that enables LLM-enabled robots to safely complete tasks by refusing harmful instructions while ensuring high task success rates.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, risking either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction's sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents' rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule. In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.

MMLab@NTU.title: Are We Evaluating VLM Token Pruning Right? Looking Beyond Accuracy and Token Count
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Shilin Shan, Jianfei Yang
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper critiques current evaluations of visual token pruning in VLMs, proposing PAA-Bench and new metrics to better assess meaningful token selection and efficiency.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.

MMLab@NTU.title: When Better Policies Leave Harder Failures: Coverage Shift in VLM Success Monitoring
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Isabel Guan, Dingyuan Zhang, Shipeng Lyu, I-Ming Chen
MMLab@NTU.summary: The study reveals that improved robot policies can obscure monitoring of residual failures, termed coverage shift, highlighting a disconnect between task success and failure detectability.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift: learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.

MMLab@NTU.title: Holo4D: Holistic 4D Reconstruction as Geometric Control for Video Diffusion
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Yushi Lan, Zeren Jiang, Koichi Namekata, Xingang Pan, Chuanxia Zheng
MMLab@NTU.summary: Holo4D is a video reshooting framework that integrates 3D trajectory reconstruction with video diffusion models for enhanced novel-view synthesis and camera control.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.

MMLab@NTU.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jize Wang, Yongcheng Jing, Xinyi Le, Cailian Chen, Xinping Guan
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper advocates for a four-stage research agenda to enhance interpretability in Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures by focusing on the dynamics and causal interactions of latent variables.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

MMLab@NTU.title: ActionRoPE: action as coordinates for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game world models
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zhiyang Deng, Yuzhe Wu, Zijun Lin, Yeying Jin
MMLab@NTU.summary: ActionRoPE introduces a parameter-free action interface for spatially consistent control in planar-camera game worlds, enhancing motion fidelity and reducing revisit drift significantly.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Game world models have made rapid progress toward real-time interactive generation. Yet action control is still predominantly implemented as feature conditioning, leaving the model to learn from training data how each action should move the visual world. This formulation is poorly matched to a broad class of planar-camera worlds, such as top-down and isometric games. In these worlds, player motion induces a geometrically well-defined planar camera displacement. We observe that the key to spatially consistent control in such worlds is to represent the effect of each action directly in world coordinates. To this end, we introduce ActionRoPE, a parameter-free action interface that converts action-driven camera displacement into world-coordinate rotary positions. As a result, tokens corresponding to the same world location retain the same positional address across time. These world coordinates further expose a spatial asymmetry in generation: regions covered by the initial observation are geometrically known, while newly revealed regions remain to be synthesized. We therefore propose Coordinate-Conditioned Noise Scheduling (CNS), which assigns token-wise denoising schedules according to this known-new structure. It allows observed regions to stabilize earlier, while new content is generated with reference to them. Compared with four representative action-conditioning mechanisms, our approach follows the commanded motion more faithfully and reduces the revisit drift by 66% over the strongest baseline. The same interface transfers across video backbones from 1.3B to 33B parameters and to out-of-distribution scenes. Project Page: https://teawhite.cn/ActionRoPE/

MMLab@NTU.title: FR-VLA: Implicit Force Reasoning VLA for Contact-Rich Manipulation
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jiaju He, Zhiyuan Yang, Ruyang Han, Jiahong Tang, Zhiping Lin
MMLab@NTU.summary: FR-VLA introduces a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that dynamically integrates force relevance into robot action generation for improved performance in contact-rich manipulation tasks.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation. Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action. This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway. FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation. In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.

MMLab@NTU.title: Procedural Memory for Language Agents: A Neurosymbolic Perspective on Explicit Goal Structure
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jonathan Leung, Zhiqi Shen, Deheng Ye
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper proposes Goal-Oriented Graphs as a solution to enhance procedural memory in language agents, improving their performance on long-horizon tasks through symbolic representation.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Large language models remain unreliable on long-horizon tasks requiring procedural reasoning. We argue that a key cause is the absence of explicit procedural memory: accessible, modifiable knowledge of how tasks are accomplished, distinct from semantic and episodic memory. Goal-Oriented Graphs offer such a representation, encoding goals and prerequisite dependencies as inspectable symbolic structure. We examine their construction, the challenges they pose, and principles for integrating them with neural reasoning.

MMLab@NTU.title: Reward Objectives for Robust (PO)MDPs: A Law-Preserving Equivalence with (Partially Observable) Games
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Durgam Latha, Dion Reji, Dorde Zikelic, Shankaranarayanan Krishna
MMLab@NTU.summary: This paper establishes a unified framework for solving robust partially observable Markov decision processes using law-invariant risk measures, demonstrating their equivalence to partially observable stochastic games.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Robust partially observable Markov decision processes model agents that act under partial observability while adversarial environment resolves uncertainty in the transition probabilities. Reward objectives such as discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward under finite and infinite horizons allow quantifying the utility of an agent. We consider the problem of solving RPOMDPs under all four reward objectives, where the goal is to decide whether the value of a risk measure with respect to a reward objective exceeds a given threshold. We consider different risk measures, such as (1)~expected value, (2)~mean-variance (MV), (3)~conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and (4)~entropic risk (ERisk). Our results can be summarized as follows. First, we formalize the class of law-invariant risk measures, that subsume all four risk measures above. Second, we propose a unified framework for solving RPOMDPs with discounted-sum, long-run average and cumulative reward objectives under any law-invariant risk measure, by reducing the problem to solving partially observable stochastic games (POSGs). Our unified framework applies to (s,a)-rectangular RPOMDPs with polytopic uncertainty sets, which we show to be {\em equivalent} to POSGs, for each of the four reward objectives and any law-invariant risk measure. We prove equivalence by designing logspace reductions between the RPOMDP and POSG models, that map strategies to strategies and preserve the distribution of the reward objective, up to a constant rescaling factor. Third, as a corollary, we derive new computational complexity results for R(PO)MDPs and POSGs. In particular, we show that solving (s,a)-rectangular RMDPs is as hard as solving simple stochastic games.

MMLab@NTU.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Xinhao Ji, Hui En Pang, Hao Li, Kairui Hu, Jiner Wang
MMLab@NTU.summary: EgoXperience introduces a comprehensive framework for learning coherent egocentric representations from video, achieving significant improvements in joint reconstruction and object pose estimation.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

MMLab@NTU.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Tianqi Liu, Hanfei Zhao, Qifeng Liang, Hui En Pang, Jiarui Xu
MMLab@NTU.summary: Ropedia W0 introduces a unified loco-manipulation world model leveraging extensive egocentric data to enhance performance across diverse human and robotic embodiments in real-time interactions.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $Ψ_0$, $ω$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

MMLab@NTU.title: Shape Distribution Matters: Shape-Specific Mixture-of-Experts for Amodal Segmentation Under Diverse Occlusions
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zhixuan Li, Yujia Liu, Chen Hui, Jeonghaeng Lee, Sanghoon Lee
MMLab@NTU.summary: ShapeMoE introduces a shape-specific mixture-of-experts framework for amodal segmentation, enhancing performance in occluded scenes by dynamically routing objects to specialized experts based on their geometric characteristics.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Amodal segmentation aims to predict complete object masks covering both visible and occluded regions, serving as a critical foundation for robust multimedia scene understanding and interactive media editing. This task poses significant challenges in complex visual media due to severe occlusions and extreme shape variation, ranging from rigid furniture to highly deformable clothing. Existing one-size-fits-all approaches struggle to reason about diverse amodal shapes in multimedia content due to limited representation capacity. While a mixture-of-experts framework is a natural solution, naively applying it without considering the underlying shape distribution leads to mismatched routing and redundant experts. To address these issues, we introduce ShapeMoE, a shape-specific sparse mixture-of-experts framework designed for complex visual scene parsing. The key idea is to learn a latent shape distribution space and dynamically route each object to a lightweight expert tailored to its geometric characteristics. Specifically, ShapeMoE encodes each object into a compact Gaussian embedding that captures key shape features. A Shape-Aware Sparse Router then maps the object to the most suitable expert, enabling precise shape-aware routing. Each expert is lightweight and specializes in recovering occluded regions for specific shape patterns. ShapeMoE is designed for shape-specific expert specialization while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate that ShapeMoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Beyond advancing fundamental visual reasoning, ShapeMoE provides a robust and efficient visual prior for downstream multimedia applications, particularly in occlusion-heavy immersive environments.

MMLab@NTU.title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Haoxuan Jia, Yang Liu, Bin Chong, Yingguang Yang, Yancheng Chen
MMLab@NTU.summary: The study reveals that LLM agents' responses to prompt injections are influenced by reasoning processes post-read, challenging assumptions about hijack detection and necessitating repeated task evaluations.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

MMLab@NTU.title: PACE-Mem: Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence for Multimodal Agents
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Shidu Ren, Rong-cheng Tu, Hang Zhou, Xiao Luo
MMLab@NTU.summary: PACE-Mem enhances multimodal agents' memory retrieval by optimizing evidence selection and length, improving question-answering accuracy by 1.6% over existing methods.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate experience, their long-term memories contain many similar observations of recurring scenes, actions, and entities. Answer quality depends on the evidence retrieved from these memories into the model's context. However, query-relevant memories may contain overlapping information, and a fixed retrieval depth may return too little or too much evidence for a given question. To address these challenges, we propose PACE-Mem, Prefix-Aware Complementary Evidence, which constructs a complementary evidence sequence and determines its length from the same selection trajectory. For structured memories, query-guided pooling combines records within each clip to obtain relevance scores and representations. Using these relevance scores and representations, maximal marginal relevance (MMR) selection balances query relevance against overlap with previously selected evidence. From the resulting score trajectory, a prefix-length selection algorithm determines retrieval depth by comparing length-normalized adjacent declines, accounting for both score changes and the amount of evidence accumulated. PACE-Mem is a training-free, plug-in retrieval method for clip-based agent memory systems, leaving memory construction and answer generation unchanged. Across three long-video benchmarks and two agent frameworks, PACE-Mem improves question-answering accuracy by an average of 1.6% over Adaptive-k, the strongest baseline at comparable mean retrieval depths. Further analysis reveals that jointly adding and removing evidence is associated with larger net accuracy gains than either change alone.

MMLab@NTU.title: Continually Evolving Skill Knowledge in Vision Language Action Model
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Yuxuan Wu, Guangming Wang, Zhiheng Yang, Tianchen Deng, Maoqing Yao
MMLab@NTU.summary: The Stellar VLA framework enables scalable continual imitation learning in vision-language-action models without parameter growth, optimizing task representations and knowledge retention for improved performance.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show promising knowledge accumulation ability through pretraining, yet continual learning remains challenging. Existing continual imitation learning (CIL) methods often require additional parameters or modules, limiting scalability for large VLA models. We propose Stellar VLA, a knowledge-driven CIL framework without parameter growth, featuring two variants: T-Stellar for task-centric modeling and TS-Stellar for hierarchical modeling of reusable skills across tasks. Stellar VLA jointly optimizes task representations and a self-evolving knowledge space, with knowledge-posterior-guided expert routing using knowledge relations and Top-K semantic embeddings for task specialization. Experiments on LIBERO demonstrate strong performance against VLA and CIL baselines with only 1% replay. Dual-arm real-world experiments validate knowledge transfer across embodiments and scenes. TS-Stellar excels in hierarchical manipulation, while visualizations demonstrate knowledge retention and task discovery. Project Website: https://stellarvla.github.io/

MMLab@NTU.title: Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a robust 3D manipulation policy that enhances performance under depth corruption while maintaining effectiveness with clean depth data.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.

MMLab@NTU.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Models Understand Movies?
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Emmanouil Zaranis, António Farinhas, Saul Santos, Beatriz Canaverde, Miguel Moura Ramos
MMLab@NTU.summary: The study introduces the MF² benchmark to evaluate vision-language models' narrative understanding of movies, revealing significant gaps compared to human performance and highlighting challenges in processing multimodal contexts.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can increasingly handle extended contexts and answer questions about long videos--but can they understand the narrative structure of movies as humans do? To investigate this question, we introduce MF$^2$ (Movie Facts and Fibs), a fully manually curated benchmark designed to evaluate whether models can identify, recall, and comprehend information central to the movie's storyline, using both the visual and textual modalities. MF$^2$ includes over 50 open-licensed movies, each paired with manually constructed sets of claim pairs: one true claim (fact) and one plausible but false (fib), totaling over 850 pairs. Our analysis across 20 open-source and 2 proprietary models reveals a substantial gap relative to human performance. While subtitles provide a strong signal for narrative understanding, other textual sources (e.g., synopses) are less informative. In contrast, when visual information is distributed across the entire movie and jointly embedded with subtitles, models struggle to identify and effectively use the relevant content. However, when the visual input is restricted to claim-relevant visual content, models improve significantly, indicating substantial room for improvement in processing large multimodal contexts and distinguishing relevant from irrelevant information. Overall, our findings highlight persistent challenges in multimodal narrative understanding for current VLMs. We release our data and code to support further research in this direction.

MMLab@NTU.title: LDDR: Linear-DPP Dynamic-Resolution Frame Sampling for Video MLLMs
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Jingfeng Chen, Jiawen Qian, Wendi Deng, Yinuo Guo, Jiaqi Yu
MMLab@NTU.summary: LDDR is a computationally efficient frame sampling framework for video MLLMs that enhances relevance and reduces redundancy by dynamically allocating token budgets based on frame importance.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models, when used for long video understanding, require selecting an informative frame set from massive and redundant candidates. Limited by the model's visual-token budget and reasoning ability, frame selection is therefore essential to reduce input size while preserving the most relevant information for accurate video reasoning. Existing frame-sampling methods like uniform sampling or relevance/diversity-sampling often miss important events or retain redundant frames. On the other hand, agentic frame selection methods incur very high computational costs. Further, these methods allocate equal tokens to all selected frames, regardless of their importance. We therefore propose LDDR (Linear DPP Dynamic Resolution), which is a training-free and budget-aware video frame sampling framework. It is computationally efficient and allows non-uniform token budget allocation within the candidate frame set. Specifically, LDDR performs query-aware Determinantal Point Process (DPP) frame selection in a task-conditioned feature space, achieving a 3x runtime speedup over standard DPP baselines. It further introduces a Group DPP importance score to guide frame retention and dynamic resolution allocation: assigning more tokens to informative and non-redundant frames while downscaling or pruning less useful ones. We test LDDR on four popular video benchmarks spanning short, medium, and long-range videos. LDDR achieves a 2.5-point gain in low-budget settings and a 1.6-point gain in high-budget scenarios. These improvements are consistently observed across multiple MLLM families and sizes. Further manual qualitative analyses are included to prove the method's effectiveness.

MMLab@NTU.title: Paint Outside the Box: Synthesizing and Selecting Training Data for Visual Grounding
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zilin Du, Haoxin Li, Jianfei Yu, Boyang Li
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents POBF, a novel framework that synthesizes training data for visual grounding by inpainting and selectively filtering data, improving performance in data-scarce settings.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Visual grounding aims to localize the image regions based on a textual query. Given the difficulty of large-scale data curation, we investigate how to effectively learn visual grounding under data-scarce settings in this paper. To address the data scarcity, we propose a novel framework, POBF (Paint Outside the Box and Filter). POBF synthesizes images by inpainting outside the box, tackling a label misalignment issue encountered in previous works. Furthermore, POBF leverages an innovative filtering scheme to select the most effective training data. This scheme combines a hardness score and an overfitting score, balanced by a penalty term. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that POBF consistently improves performance, achieving an average gain of 5.83\% over the real-data-only method and outperforming leading baselines by 2.29\%-3.85\% in accuracy. Additionally, we validate the robustness and generalizability of POBF across various generative models, training data sizes, and model architectures.

MMLab@NTU.title: Scalable Adaptation of 3D Geometric Foundation Models via Weak Supervision from Internet Video
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zihui Gao, Ke Liu, Donny Y. Chen, Duochao Shi, Guosheng Lin
MMLab@NTU.summary: The SAGE framework effectively utilizes static-scene Internet videos for scalable adaptation of 3D geometric foundation models, improving reconstruction accuracy significantly while addressing annotation scarcity.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Geometric foundation models show promise in 3D reconstruction. However, their progress is severely constrained by the scarcity of diverse, large-scale 3D annotations. While static-scene Internet videos are abundant and diverse, utilizing them as a scaling source for geometric learning is challenging due to the absence of ground-truth geometry and the presence of observational noise. To address this, we propose SAGE, a framework for Scalable Adaptation of GEometric foundation models from raw video streams. SAGE leverages a hierarchical mining pipeline to transform videos into training trajectories and hybrid supervisions: (1) Informative training trajectory selection; (2) Sparse Geometric Anchoring via SfM point clouds for global structural guidance; and (3) Dense Differentiable Consistency via 3D Gaussian rendering for multi-view constraints. Besides, we also introduce a regularization strategy that replays a small fraction of supervised data to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Applied to two architecturally distinct backbones, SAGE reduces Chamfer Distance on unseen benchmarks (7Scenes, TUM-RGBD, Matterport3D) by 20-42% with MV-DUSt3R and consistently improves VGGT. SAGE establishes Internet video as a viable and scalable adaptation source for geometric foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/SAGE.

MMLab@NTU.title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Heng Zhang, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou, Weisi Lin, Yan Wu
MMLab@NTU.summary: MANGO-Grasp introduces an anisotropic interaction framework using geometry-oriented 3D Gaussians for effective cross-embodiment dexterous grasping, outperforming existing methods in simulations and real-world tests.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials will be made available upon publication at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.

MMLab@NTU.title: RealtimeWAM: One-Step Asynchronous World Action Models
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Chengtao Lv, Jinyang Du, Shuyi Feng, Yang Yong, Shiqiao Gu
MMLab@NTU.summary: RealtimeWAM enhances World Action Models by enabling one-step action generation and asynchronous inference, achieving significant speedup while maintaining near-lossless performance across various benchmarks.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate visual representations from video generation backbones to guide action prediction. Recent efficient WAMs adopt Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures and compute video representations once for reuse by the action expert. However, intra-expert iteration (\ie, multi-step action denoising) and inter-expert waiting (\ie, sequential execution of the video and action experts) still limit inference efficiency. To this end, we present RealtimeWAM, an extremely efficient WAM variant with one-step action generation and asynchronous inference, addressing these two bottlenecks. To reduce intra-expert iteration, we propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD) to address a local-global error gap: low local consistency error alone does not guarantee accurate final actions. TACD supplements local consistency with explicit supervision from the frozen teacher's multi-step rollout endpoint, enabling accurate one-step action generation. Additionally, we propose Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP) to eliminate unnecessary expert-level waiting. It overlaps the two experts through block-wise sharing of the video KV cache, synchronizing only immediately before the corresponding action attention consumes it. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks (\eg, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin) and model variants (\eg, Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM) demonstrate the superiority of RealtimeWAM. Notably, RealtimeWAM maintains near-lossless performance (\ie, $<1\%$ drop) across these benchmarks while delivering significant end-to-end speedup (\eg, $\sim25\times$ on H100). Our code and checkpoints are available via this \href{https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/scripts/realtimewam}{link}.

MMLab@NTU.title: SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Lingyi Hong, Weiren Cai, Jiayu Chen, Xinyu Zhou, Bailin He
MMLab@NTU.summary: SimpleVLN is a novel framework that enhances Vision-and-Language Navigation by leveraging native multimodal large language models without task-specific architectures, achieving superior success rates.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

MMLab@NTU.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Tanush Kalhan, Anupam Chattopadhyay, Sriram Ranga, Amritendu Mukherjee
MMLab@NTU.summary: This study explores how information density in chain-of-thought reasoning affects answer correctness in large language models, revealing significant insights on model behavior and accuracy improvement techniques.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

MMLab@NTU.title: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Tinghao Wang, Yichen Guo, Rui Huang, Junchi Yao, Qizhe Zhang
MMLab@NTU.summary: The paper presents TOPS, a novel visual token pruning method for multimodal large language models that optimally preserves task-relevant tokens while enhancing efficiency and performance.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design. Our code is available at https://github.com/MAX-7237/TOPS.

MMLab@NTU.title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Yao Long Teng, Jianguo Huang, Yanchen Deng, Jiayi Cai, Bo An
MMLab@NTU.summary: Prism-1 introduces a scoring method for System One models that maintains decision independence from option order and additions, outperforming traditional approaches in accuracy and consistency.
MMLab@NTU.debug_abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. We implement this as Prism-1 (Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models): every option is read in its own block at shared positions, with the model's usual left-to-right attention, in one forward pass. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle, and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions. Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only answers that survive a reordering are counted, while no shuffle changes any of its answers and no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others.

MMLab@NTU.title: MOSS: Mode-Oriented Source Shaping for Robot Flow Matching Policies
MMLab@NTU.authors_text: Zirun Ma, Jindou Jia, Tuo An, Jiaqi Bai, Jiahua Dong
