In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Mixture of Frames Policy: Multi-Frame Action Denoising for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Dian Wang, Jisang Park, Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Shuran Song
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF) enhances bimanual mobile manipulation by synchronizing action denoising across multiple coordinate frames, improving performance over traditional methods.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently multi-frame: local actions may be simple in an end-effector frame, while transport, upright-object handling, and whole-body coordination are better represented in a base-aligned frame. However, modern diffusion-based visuomotor policies typically commit to a single predefined action frame, forcing one denoiser to model action distributions that are often unnecessarily complex in that frame. We propose Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF), a diffusion policy that performs synchronized action denoising across multiple coordinate frames. MoF maintains a single canonical diffusion state, re-expresses it in several task-relevant frames, applies frame-specialized denoisers, and fuses their noise predictions back in the canonical frame. To make this possible for intermediate noisy diffusion states, we adopt a column-based 6D rotation representation within an SE(3) action parameterization that supports exact, differentiable frame transformations without requiring noisy rotations to lie on the SO(3) manifold. Across nine simulated bimanual manipulation tasks, we show that the best action frame is task-dependent and that MoF improves over oracle frame selection and standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) baselines. We further evaluate MoF on two real-world bimanual mobile manipulation tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms all constituent single-frame baselines.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: BEHAVIOR-Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The BEHAVIOR-Spatial benchmark evaluates spatial understanding in robotics through spatial question answering and action performance across various tasks, revealing significant gaps in instruction adherence.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT) enhances robot manipulation by enabling preference adaptation across tasks using self-labeled demonstrations, achieving high accuracy and task success without manual annotations.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Alex Brandes, Haig Conti Georges Sajelian, Manthan Patel, Dominik Hollidt, Chenhao Li
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The EgoHTR dataset enhances humanoid robot training by providing 4D human motion sequences in complex terrains, enabling improved locomotion policies and context-aware navigation.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents a framework for transferring robot data across diverse controllers and embodiments, enhancing adaptability and success in varied tasks by leveraging behavioral interaction context.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: StreamVibe introduces a proactive video agent model that effectively infers and adapts to evolving user intents through a new benchmark and hierarchical memory system.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while overlooking implicit user intents (e.g., "where should I click next?" when a user is navigating a website) and fail to continuously update their understanding as user intents evolve. These limitations make them less suitable for intent-aware interaction in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark that serves as a testbed for user intent understanding and interaction, comprising 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with flexible lifecycles through hierarchical memory, enabling it to track the latest user intents and environmental states. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding capabilities while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over existing baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intents and determining when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation during sustained interactions, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction performance.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Gradient-Free Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Scalable Safety-Critical Control
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Zeyuan Feng, Ali Fuat Sahin, Santiago Thorup, Somil Bansal
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents a gradient-free neural framework for Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, enabling scalable safety-critical control in high-dimensional robotic systems through efficient value propagation and supervised policy learning.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides a principled framework for synthesizing safety certificates and robust controllers for safety-critical robotic systems. However, applying reachability analysis to high-dimensional nonlinear systems remains challenging: classical grid-based solvers suffer from the curse of dimensionality, continuous-time neural solvers require accurate spatial value gradients, and reinforcement-learning-based approaches often suffer from weak boundary anchoring and non-stationary adversarial policy optimization. We propose a discrete-time neural reachability framework for control-disturbance-affine systems that learns backward reachable tubes (BRTs) and backward reach-avoid tubes (BRATs) through Bellman-Isaacs value propagation. Our key idea is to combine equation-driven self-supervision with structured policy learning: rather than computing explicit PDE-gradients, we exploit the bang-bang structure of optimal safety interventions to construct approximate teacher actions from gradient-free value probes, converting adversarial actor learning into supervised policy learning. To stabilize long-horizon value propagation, we leverage the learned actor to train the value function backward from the terminal boundary using a windowed temporal curriculum, where each window is used as the boundary condition for the next window. Across benchmark problems up to 80 dimensions, our method learns accurate reachability value functions while improving stability over existing learning-based solvers. We further demonstrate observation-space scalability on F1-tenth racing with over 16,000-dimensional egocentric inputs. The learned safety filter generalizes zero-shot to unseen tracks and transfers to a physical RC car, achieving real-time robust collision avoidance.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces SCRIM, a method for quantifying state criticality in imitation learning to enhance performance by reweighting losses and optimizing data selection.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Suozhi Huang, Kelsey Fu, Binxu Li, Luna Lyu, Kaize Wu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: LabWorld is a Real2Sim framework that reconstructs interactive 4D laboratory environments from monocular RGB videos, enhancing scientific experimentation through improved asset and event modeling.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) communicate visually, revealing a gap between their intuitive visual cues and human interpretations, affecting task performance.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Deep Learning Warm Starts for Trajectory Optimization on the International Space Station
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Somrita Banerjee, Abhishek Cauligi, Marco Pavone
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper demonstrates the first in-space application of machine learning warm starts to accelerate trajectory optimization for the Astrobee robot on the ISS, significantly improving efficiency.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Trajectory optimization is a cornerstone of modern robot autonomy, enabling systems to compute trajectories and controls in real-time while respecting safety and physical constraints. However, it has seen limited usage in spaceflight applications due to its heavy computational demands that exceed the capability of most flight computers. In this work, we provide results on the first in-space demonstration of using machine learning-based warm starts for accelerating trajectory optimization for the Astrobee free-flying robot onboard the International Space Station (ISS). We formulate a data-driven optimal control approach that trains a neural network to learn the structure of the trajectory generation problem being solved using sequential convex programming (SCP). Onboard, this trained neural network predicts solutions for the trajectory generation problem and relies on using the SCP solver to enforce safety constraints for the system. Our trained network reduces the number of solver iterations required for convergence in cases including rotational dynamics by 60% and in cases with obstacles drawn from the training distribution of the warm start model by 50%. This work represents a significant milestone in the use of learning-based control for spaceflight applications and a stepping stone for future advances in the use of machine learning for autonomous guidance, navigation, & control.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: World from Motion: Generative Dynamic Gaussian Reconstruction from Monocular Video
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Amrita Mazumdar, Tianye Li, Zan Gojcic
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces World from Motion, a method for creating dynamic 3D Gaussian representations from monocular videos, enhancing reconstruction quality and generalization to diverse scenes.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: We present World from Motion, a method for generating freely renderable dynamic 3D Gaussian representations from monocular videos. Our approach conditions a video model on dense, pixel-aligned renderings that encode appearance, geometry, and 3D scene motion along both input and target camera trajectories to correct rendering artifacts and fill in missing regions from an initial reconstruction. To train this model, we construct a dataset of aligned multiview video pairs and dynamic 3DGS representations, with simulated artifacts characteristic of monocular reconstruction. At test time, we distill the model's generations, including newly observed regions and motions, back into a single consistent, high-quality dynamic 3DGS, improving both novel-view synthesis and the underlying 3D motion. Our method sets a new state of the art in 4D reconstruction and seamlessly generalizes to in-the-wild videos with large viewpoint changes and dynamic motions.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: StackGen3D: Stable 3D Block Stack Generation from Multiview Silhouettes
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Xiaopeng Zhang, Luzhe Sun, Yiqing Xu, Matthew R. Walter
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: StackGen3D is a framework that generates stable 3D block structures from silhouettes using a physics-informed graph neural network and conditional flow-matching model.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow-matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI-GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter-matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best-of-10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly. Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/)

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: $Ψ$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: $Ψ$-0.6 is a unified vision-language model that adaptively integrates perception, language, and geometry for enhanced reasoning and counterfactual simulation in AI.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $Ψ$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $Ψ$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $Ψ$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Thomas Landeg, Thierry Tambe
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents Backtrack, a lightweight recovery mechanism for frozen Vision-Language-Action models that enhances failure detection and reduces failure rates by 19-48% without retraining.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: DexPort is a portable interface that simplifies dexterous robot hand data collection by allowing operators to control wrist motion and finger coordination, enhancing task success rates significantly.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: UniAction presents a unified framework for action conditioning in world models, enabling heterogeneous actions to share a model and outperform specialized counterparts through joint training.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: UniMem: Unifying Visual and Textual Memory in VLAs for Non-Markovian Tasks
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Lars Osterberg, Maggie Wang, Mac Schwager
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: UniMem integrates visual and textual memory in a unified framework, enhancing performance on non-Markovian tasks while simplifying training and inference processes.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory. Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline. Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level visual and textual memory and low-level control under one backbone. UniMem employs an event classifier to initiate textual and visual memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense visual memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts. We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical VLM-VLA baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption. Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Guillem Casadesus Vila, Grace Gao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper benchmarks eleven feature matching methods for lunar visual SLAM, revealing SuperPoint's superiority in low-texture environments, while highlighting the limitations of synthetic data comparisons.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Ava Pun, Kevin Dai, Sally Chen, Maxwell Jones, Ruixuan Liu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: BrickWright is a framework that enables agents to generate 100% physically feasible LEGO builds from prompts by using a specialized assembly API and validator.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: EBV-CAN integrates vision-language grounding for endoscope navigation, achieving high localization accuracy and successful task completion through a novel dataset and policy framework.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents Dual Exam, a framework for evaluating the interaction between Multimodal Agents and World Models across various domains, revealing performance inconsistencies and challenges in reciprocal learning.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R) transforms a single human RGB video into thousands of robot demonstrations by semantically aligning objects, enhancing robot learning efficiency.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yash Rampuria, Rohan Garg, Daniele Gammelli, Marco Pavone
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: GGraph is a GPU-accelerated library that enhances graph-based robot deployment and learning, enabling efficient training across hundreds of parallel environments.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Do Earth-Trained Humanoid Controllers Walk on the Moon? Gravity, Terrain, and Soil Transfer
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Guillem Casadesus Vila, Sri Aditya Deevi, Grace X. Gao
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This study evaluates the transferability of Earth-trained humanoid locomotion controllers to lunar conditions, revealing asymmetric survival rates and the impact of terrain and gravity on performance.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo Sánchez
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: ProactEgoMem introduces a benchmark for evaluating proactive memory in streaming egocentric video, focusing on tasks like information capture, state tracking, and location tracking.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: This paper presents a method for force-aware manipulation using visual force prediction from a compliant gripper, eliminating the need for specialized force sensors during deployment.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Adam Lee, Shobhit Agarwal, June Pyo Suh
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Beckmann World Models introduce a novel approach for efficient one-step action-conditioned video prediction, achieving significant accuracy and performance improvements without relying on pretrained generative models.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: MMedAgent-Plus: Scaling Multimodal Medical Agents across Modalities, Tasks and Workflows
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Ruoxin Wang, Yuanting Pan, Binxu Li, Ruiyang Ji, Yaqian Chen
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: MMedAgent-Plus is a multimodal medical AI that effectively orchestrates 18 specialist models across various tasks, achieving high accuracy and synthesis in complex workflows.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Medical workflows often require multiple interdependent analyses, but existing specialist and generalist AI models are not designed to coordinate them. We introduce MMedAgent-Plus, a multimodal medical tool-use agent that combines a vision-language planner with 18 leading specialist models spanning 12 tasks and 8 modalities. Through a unified tool interface, the planner selects specialists, executes them in sequence, and synthesizes responses grounded in their outputs. The planner is instruction-tuned on 208,928 samples from 32 public medical benchmarks, covering single- and multi-tool interactions across single and multiple rounds. We separately evaluate tool orchestration, response synthesis, and end-to-end execution on held-out samples. MMedAgent-Plus achieves tool-call accuracies of 91.0%, 98.1%, and 80.7% in single-tool multi-round, multi-tool multi-round, and multi-tool single-round settings, respectively. Given correct tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus achieves scores of 14.4-14.8 out of 15 for faithfulness, completeness, and conciseness across 600 evaluation samples. In end-to-end execution without pre-supplied tool outputs, MMedAgent-Plus correctly invokes the required specialist in 90.6% of 350 evaluation cases spanning seven tasks. Its final-answer accuracy reaches 0.98, matching the dedicated leading specialist and exceeding the strongest baseline (0.28).

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Hyunji Alex Nam, Michael Dennis, Natasha Jaques, Minsuk Chang
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces TURTLE, an unsupervised method for evolving self-tuning benchmarks that enhance AI tool-use capabilities across diverse applications by generating scalable, adaptable tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (**T**ool **U**se **R**elated **T**asks with **L**ong-Horizon **E**volution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $τ$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165\% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Decoupling Action from Egocentric Observation for World Simulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: EgoACT decouples semantic actions from egocentric observations using a novel video diffusion approach, enhancing action realism and coherence in world simulations.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Matteo Cercola, Katie Z Luo, Milan Ganai, John Alora, Simone Formentin
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces Generative Plan Latents (GPL) for Vision-Language-Action models, enabling flexible reasoning by representing plans as a conditional distribution, enhancing plan selection and adaptation.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $π_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Perceives but Doesn't Brake: A Perception-Action Binding Gap in Reasoning Driving VLAs
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Matteo Cercola, Katie Z Luo, Simone Formentin, Marco Pavone
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper identifies a perception-action binding gap in driving VLAs, where hazard awareness fails to translate into safe actions, proposing a method to enhance braking response.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Taskonomy: Disentangling Task Transfer Learning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Amir Zamir, Alexander Sax, William Shen, Leonidas Guibas, Jitendra Malik
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper presents a computational framework for modeling relationships among visual tasks, enabling efficient transfer learning and reducing labeled data requirements by two-thirds.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Do visual tasks have a relationship, or are they unrelated? For instance, could having surface normals simplify estimating the depth of an image? Intuition answers these questions positively, implying existence of a structure among visual tasks. Knowing this structure has notable values; it is the concept underlying transfer learning and provides a principled way for identifying redundancies across tasks, e.g., to seamlessly reuse supervision among related tasks or solve many tasks in one system without piling up the complexity. We proposes a fully computational approach for modeling the structure of space of visual tasks. This is done via finding (first and higher-order) transfer learning dependencies across a dictionary of twenty six 2D, 2.5D, 3D, and semantic tasks in a latent space. The product is a computational taxonomic map for task transfer learning. We study the consequences of this structure, e.g. nontrivial emerged relationships, and exploit them to reduce the demand for labeled data. For example, we show that the total number of labeled datapoints needed for solving a set of 10 tasks can be reduced by roughly 2/3 (compared to training independently) while keeping the performance nearly the same. We provide a set of tools for computing and probing this taxonomical structure including a solver that users can employ to devise efficient supervision policies for their use cases.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Gibson Env: Real-World Perception for Embodied Agents
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Fei Xia, Amir Zamir, Zhi-Yang He, Alexander Sax, Jitendra Malik
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces the Gibson Virtual Environment, a realistic simulation platform for training perception models in active agents, enhancing real-world applicability without additional adaptation.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Developing visual perception models for active agents and sensorimotor control are cumbersome to be done in the physical world, as existing algorithms are too slow to efficiently learn in real-time and robots are fragile and costly. This has given rise to learning-in-simulation which consequently casts a question on whether the results transfer to real-world. In this paper, we are concerned with the problem of developing real-world perception for active agents, propose Gibson Virtual Environment for this purpose, and showcase sample perceptual tasks learned therein. Gibson is based on virtualizing real spaces, rather than using artificially designed ones, and currently includes over 1400 floor spaces from 572 full buildings. The main characteristics of Gibson are: I. being from the real-world and reflecting its semantic complexity, II. having an internal synthesis mechanism, "Goggles", enabling deploying the trained models in real-world without needing further domain adaptation, III. embodiment of agents and making them subject to constraints of physics and space.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Feng Chen, Pei Zhou, Lixuan He, Yunchao Yao, Li Sun
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The Embodied Playground benchmark evaluates foundation-model agents' ability to perform long-horizon tasks requiring coherent physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning across diverse environments.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: ContactBench 1.0 is an open-source benchmark for evaluating contact-rich robotic manipulation through 36 tasks and 40+ object assets, highlighting challenges in policy performance.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Forecast-PEFT: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Pre-trained Motion Forecasting Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Jifeng Wang, Kaouther Messaoud, Yuejiang Liu, Juergen Gall, Alexandre Alahi
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: Forecast-PEFT introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for motion forecasting that significantly reduces retraining needs while enhancing accuracy compared to traditional approaches.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Recent advancements in motion forecasting have been significantly accelerated by self-supervised pre-training techniques. However, current methods typically rely on extensive fine-tuning of pre-trained models for downstream tasks like trajectory prediction, a process that can be inefficient. This inefficiency primarily arises because traditional fine-tuning strategies fail to fully exploit the close alignment between motion prediction tasks and masked reconstruction objectives used during pre-training. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Forecast-PEFT, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework specifically designed for motion forecasting. Forecast-PEFT preserves most of the pre-trained model's parameters, introducing minimal yet effective adjustments through novel prompts and adapters. By doing so, Forecast-PEFT significantly reduces the number of parameters needing retraining while preserving essential pre-trained knowledge. Our method demonstrates robust generalization across multiple datasets, achieving higher accuracy with only about 17% of the parameters required by traditional full fine-tuning approaches. Additionally, our fully fine-tuned variant, Forecast-FT, further enhances prediction performance, achieving improvements of up to 9.6% over conventional baseline methods. These findings highlight Forecast-PEFT as a scalable, efficient, and effective alternative for fine-tuning pre-trained motion forecasting models. Code is available at https://github.com/csjfwang/Forecast-PEFT.

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: Can LLM Agents Respond to Disasters? Benchmarking Heterogeneous Geospatial Reasoning in Emergency Operations
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Junjue Wang, Weihao Xuan, Heli Qi, Pengyu Dai, Kunyi Liu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The paper introduces DORA, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in end-to-end disaster response, highlighting challenges in grounding, tool selection, and compositional fragility.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Operational disaster response goes beyond damage assessment, requiring responders to integrate multi-sensor signals, reason over road networks, populations and key facilities, plan evacuations, and produce actionable reports.
