We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Elena Wittemyer, Graco Gao
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: This paper presents an autonomous motion planning framework for lunar drones that ensures safe, fuel-efficient hops using vision-guided control and obstacle detection.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Anikait Singh, Teresa Zhang, Yoonho Lee, Roshen Sanjay Nair, Aviral Kumar
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: Librarian Agents enhance LLMs by proactively organizing unstructured data into tailored workspaces, improving query response accuracy and efficiency through reinforcement learning.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Chenyuan Zhou, Yining Hong, Huang Huang, Yunfan Jiang, Wenlong Huang
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: T2-Z optimizes environment latents at test time, enhancing robotic world models to improve predictions and action success in diverse settings without prior environmental knowledge.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Aalap D. Shah, Basil Saeed, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tobias Gerstenberg, Hyowon Gweon
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: GenEA is a novel computational framework that enhances embodied AI's understanding of multi-step plans by integrating biomechanics and intuitive physics, outperforming existing models in reasoning tasks.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: How Many Demonstrations Does a VLA Need? On the Sample Efficiency of VLA Finetuning
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Rahul Chand, Miguel Villa Floran
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: This study evaluates the sample efficiency of six vision language action models, revealing significant differences in adaptation efficiency and demonstration requirements across various settings.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Pretrained vision language action (VLA) models show strong zero-shot performance but they are rarely deployed directly and are often first post-trained on demonstrations from the target setting. Yet VLAs are typically compared by zero-shot or full-data fine-tuned success which reveals little about the data and compute required for downstream adaptation. We study adaptation efficiency for six VLAs ($π_0$, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T N1-N1.7) on four LIBERO suites, varying both demonstrations and training steps. This reveals differences hidden by full-data fine-tuning: models which are within two points on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset differ by up to 3$\times$ in success with 50 demonstrations. $π_{0.5}$ needs 2-5$\times$ fewer demonstrations than $π_0$ and is the most sample-efficient model at every budget, with the largest gap on the long-horizon suite. Within GR00T, N1.5 adapts more efficiently than N1.6 and N1.7 on three of four suites, despite their stronger zero-shot performance. We also study one pretraining factor behind these differences by freezing the VLM during finetuning: this severely degrades the $π$ models whose VLM is jointly trained with the action expert during pretraining, but barely affects GR00T models.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: $A^2$: Smaller Self-Supervised ViTs Localize Better than Larger Ones
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Sreehari Rammohan, Huy Ha, Carl Vondrick
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper introduces $A^2$, a method combining small self-supervised ViTs for localization with large ViTs for richer representations, outperforming traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Robust visual classification often depends on localizing the main foreground objects in an image while ignoring contextual distractors. Surprisingly, we find that the last layer attention maps of smaller self-supervised ViTs localize foreground objects better than those of larger ViTs. However, we still need large ViTs, because they extract richer representations from each patch. To get the best of both worlds, good localization and rich representations, we propose $A^2$, a simple method that leverages this inverse scaling finding by decoupling where to look (a small attention model) from what to extract (a large embedding model): we crop around the attention peaks of a small model and embed the crops with a larger model. $A^2$ uses entirely pretrained features, requires no group labels, and does not require per-dataset attention or backbone training. Across 5 benchmarks, $A^2$ is competitive with backbone-matched loss-level methods like DFR, and outperforms end-to-end attention training under stronger distribution shifts.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: Seeing What Execution Needs: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Yina Jian, Mingkun Xu
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper presents a benchmark for evaluating task-conditioned spatial belief in robotic manipulation, demonstrating high success rates in actionable observation selection across various domains.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Execution Needs, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Its aligned three-domain track contains 1,080 frozen cases (360 each for coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance). The primary coffee protocols -- closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization -- produce over 115,000 evaluator episodes across evaluated methods, budgets, and inference repeats. Each case pairs candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, directly measuring whether selected observations support execution. A metadata-assisted diagnostic reference pipeline maintains spatial-functional beliefs and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, it reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; removing functional fields or command binding reduces functional-OOD success to 0.0% and 19.7%, respectively. Under a separate full-preview contract, seven vision-language models reach 26-43%. Replacing coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores retains 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling these scores reduces success to 15%/11%, supporting dependence on image content. Separately, the aligned three-domain evaluation at H=3 supports portability of the benchmark interface under frozen domain-specific schemas. These results suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated by whether acquired evidence meets the current command's execution requirements.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: Large Language Model Explainability for Planning Lunar Rover Trajectories under Uncertainty
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Michelle Ho, Maximilian Adang, Zachary Booth, David E. Astle, Margaret Hansen
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper presents an LLM-based interactive assistant that enhances explainability and traceability of lunar rover trajectory planning under uncertainty, significantly improving response fidelity.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Planning planetary rover trajectories under probabilistic uncertainty is a multi-objective optimization problem that science teams currently iteratively solve and verify by hand. This process becomes impractical when timelines and constraints frequently shift throughout the mission planning phase. Sampling-based planners such as Monte Carlo tree search can speed up this process, but their outputs do not preserve traceability to the science objectives that justify each plan, which the science team needs to verify. We propose an interactive assistant based on a large language model (LLM) that can explain planner trajectories using domain vocabulary and re-run the planner under user-specified conditions to compare alternatives. Previous work has used LLMs inside planner decision-making loops, but we explore using them for post-planning explanation, where they are more likely to be trusted since they do not directly influence planner decisions. Our framework pairs a simulator inspired by the NASA Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) mission with a ReAct queryable interface that calls curated action tools and retrieval functions. We evaluate the assistant on a query bank consisting of plan comparisons, feasibility, and lookup queries. Experiments show that 90.9% of the assistant's responses are faithful to the planner's outputs, a nearly 65% improvement over zero-shot prompting of the same LLM without tool access, demonstrating the potential for trustworthy explainability of uncertainty-aware traverses with an LLM-based system.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Chunru Lin, Hongxin Zhang, Fenghao Yu, Zhehuan Chen, Thomas L. Griffiths
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: RoboWits introduces a benchmark for evaluating robotic cognitive reasoning and creative problem-solving under unexpected challenges, revealing significant performance gaps in existing models.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable construction of high-quality reasoning-centric unexpected scenarios, we propose an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework, comprising agents for seed task generation and verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation. Using the pipeline, we curated 30 diverse seed tasks and 200 tasks with mutations and graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning. We benchmark popular robot policies, pre-trained VLAs, a zero-shot policy built on a frontier VLM, and oracle-state planners. Our results reveal a significant performance gap: while pre-trained VLAs exhibit preliminary success on seed tasks after fine-tuning, they struggle to perform on mutated tasks, implying their brittleness in manipulation tasks requiring reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments. A zero-shot policy built on GPT-6 Astra outperforms all fine-tuned VLAs, yet still loses about a fifth of its success on mutated tasks, showing that stronger foundation models alone do not close the robustness gap. See our project page https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/RoboWits/ for videos.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: Imperfect World Models are Exploitable
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Logan Mondal Bhamidipaty, Esmeralda S. Whitammer, David Abel, Mykel J. Kochenderfer, Subramanian Ramamoorthy
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper defines model exploitation in reinforcement learning, showing its inevitability in large policy sets and linking it to reward hacking, while proposing a safe planning horizon.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: We propose a novel definition of model exploitation in reinforcement learning. Informally, a world model is exploitable if it implies that one policy should be strictly preferred over another while the environment's true transition model implies the reverse. We analogize our definition with a prior characterization of reward hacking but show that the associated proof of inevitability does not transfer to exploitation. To overcome this obstruction, we develop a general theory of reward hacking and model exploitation that proves that exploitation is essentially unavoidable on large policy sets and yields the corresponding claim for hacking as a special case. Unfortunately, we also find that the conditions that guarantee unhackability in finite policy sets have no counterpart that precludes exploitation. Consequently, we introduce a relaxed notion of exploitation and derive a safe horizon within which it can be avoided. Taken together, our results establish a formal bridge between reward hacking and model exploitation and elucidate the limits of safe planning in world models.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: A Unified Inertial Encoder for Human and Humanoid Motion
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Yutian Chen, Shibo Zhao, Rocky Duan, Karen Liu, Carmelo Sferrazza
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper presents a unified inertial encoder that enables effective transfer of human motion knowledge to humanoid robots, achieving superior velocity estimation and motion understanding without prior fine-tuning.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Learning humanoid state estimation and language-grounded motion understanding from robot recordings ties training coverage to the robot's motion repertoire. Human motion datasets offer broader coverage, yet transferring this knowledge requires overcoming differences in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances. To enable this transfer, we propose a unified inertial encoder whose shared inertial interface uses kinematic IMU synthesis to represent human and humanoid motion at corresponding body sites. Within this common input space, joint training on human and kinematically retargeted humanoid motion combines velocity estimation and motion--text alignment with continuous-time encoding and sensor and motion randomization. The resulting model transfers zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation, real-robot training trajectories, or fine-tuning, achieving the lowest velocity error among evaluated methods across five datasets, including 0.099m/s on real G1. Its motion-description retrieval also extends to retargeted G1 motion categories observed only in human training, demonstrating how human motion knowledge can support the generalization of humanoid inertial odometry and language-grounded motion understanding.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: BATCH is a cross-embodiment learning framework that enhances robot manipulation by aligning human behaviors through self-supervised learning and style transfer, improving generalization in unseen tasks.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and hand control, yet specifying such coordination manually is challenging and often task-specific. In this work, we explore whether complex bimanual dexterity can emerge from a simple object-centric learning objective. We train reinforcement learning policies under a shared object-centric reward, varying their training environments rather than tuning separate rewards for each behavior. These results suggest that this objective provides a simple and scalable interface for learning general bimanual dexterity, shifting the burden from manually designing robot coordination to specifying what should happen to the object.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper critiques LLM agents' stochastic exploration, proposing a curiosity framework that requires predictive modeling and intrinsic motivation for effective investigation in open-ended tasks.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The study quantifies the relative effectiveness of demonstration data in behavior cloning, revealing that lower-quality demonstrations require significantly more samples to achieve comparable success rates.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: UniLatent is a framework that enables effective cross-embodiment transfer of robotic skills by aligning latent observations, achieving high success rates without pixel-level translation.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Robot datasets are costly to collect and are usually tied to a specific embodiment, making it difficult to reuse demonstrations across robots with different geometry, appearance, and kinematics. UniLatent renders paired source-target robot observations in simulation and aligns a source visual encoder to a frozen target encoder. Code, videos and data are available at https://selina2023.github.io/unilatent/.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Jing Liang, Zhenyu Hou, Senthurbavan Kirubaharan, Md Safwan Mondal, Ashok Gudivada
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: MOSU2 enhances long-range robot navigation by integrating two-stage contextual reasoning and multi-modal analysis, significantly improving success rates and condition detection in complex outdoor environments.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Lei Shu, Zizhou Huang, Yunuo Chen, Yifei Li, Tao Du
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: This paper categorizes differentiable physics simulation methods, clarifying derivative sources, implementation impacts on accuracy, and explores gradient utility across various applications and challenges.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Changhe Chen, Pingyue Zhang, Chi Gui
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The Embodied First Exam introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework for coding agents controlling diverse robots, assessing their performance across 1,156 tasks and various settings.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Haoran Yuan, Weigang Yi, Zhenyu Zhang, Wendi Chen, Yuchen Mo
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: VTAM is an efficient visuo-tactile world-action model for contact-rich manipulation that eliminates the need for tactile pretraining while achieving superior performance and reduced inference latency.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Tactile vision-language-action models (VLAs) and tactile world-action models (WAMs) are a promising new paradigm for contact-rich manipulation, but existing models either underutilize touch, rely on large-scale tactile pretraining, or incur high inference latency due to iterative video generation. Trained only on task demonstrations, VTAM outperforms all baselines on four real-robot tasks across two platforms with different tactile sensors, outperforms all baselines without tactile pretraining in average success on eight UniVTAC simulation tasks, and is comparable to tactile VLAs and WAMs pretrained on over 30K hours of largely visuo-tactile robot data (83.4% vs. 84.5% for N0-TWAM). 斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Jinsu Yoo, Zanming Huang, Katie Z Luo, Zheda Mai, Qiyuan Wu
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The paper advocates for a collaborative, community-driven data paradigm in autonomous driving research to enhance dataset integration and accessibility, addressing current limitations in diversity and usage.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Autonomous driving has made remarkable progress, with recent AI advances enabling commercial deployments that are reshaping urban mobility. Yet the field remains far from its universal social promise: autonomous systems that can operate robustly anywhere, anytime, for anyone. We posit that this gap is not merely a modeling problem, but a problem of the prevailing data paradigm. Current research relies heavily on a few benchmark datasets with limited spatial and scenario coverage, even though the community has collectively produced over 600 autonomous driving datasets across nearly 50 countries. However, this abundance has not translated into broad research impact: most datasets remain significantly underused due to fragmentation, limited visibility, incompatible protocols, and benchmark incentives that concentrate attention on a few dominant datasets. We therefore argue that autonomous driving research requires a collaborative, community-driven data paradigm. Such a paradigm would improve the discovery, reuse, integration, and evaluation of diverse datasets; make underexplored data easier and more rewarding to study; and lower the barrier for new contributors. We outline its key principles, illustrate an early realization, and call for collaboration across academia and industry to transform fragmented datasets into shared community infrastructure for anytime-anywhere autonomy.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Kenneth Llontop, Cherie Ho, Dylan Zhou, Anuva Banwasi, Priya Sundaresan
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: MessyNav introduces a zero-shot navigation framework using vision-language models for robots to manipulate obstacles in messy environments, achieving significant performance improvements without task-specific training.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Hao Wang, Max Cohen, Zeyuan Feng, Donggeon David Oh, Oswin So
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: This paper offers a comprehensive tutorial on synthesizing safety certificates using Hamilton-Jacobi reachability and control barrier functions, providing benchmarks for method comparison and practical guidance.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Safety is a central concern in modern autonomous systems. Safety certificates---functions whose existence guarantees that a system meets its safety specification---have long been used as a principled tool for rigorously reasoning about safety. Methods for synthesizing such certificates are scattered across research areas, with little guidance on when to use a particular approach. This tutorial provides a holistic treatment of safety certificate synthesis centered on two widely used families: Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis and control barrier functions (CBFs). For each family of methods, we first introduce its general formulation, along with classical and learning-based tools for certificate synthesis. Next, we introduce two benchmark problems consisting of vehicle systems of differing complexity to assess the certificate quality of different synthesis methods and their effectiveness in safety-critical control. We use these benchmarks to compare various methods and provide practical guidance for selecting an approach.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Jingnan Gao, Jiahui Huang, Sven Elflein, Jianhao Zheng, Bingxin Ke

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: We present MetricTrail, a streaming system for accurate camera motion estimation and dense reconstruction from long monocular videos. To keep inference efficient over long sequences, we revisit DPVO's sparse local estimator. The correspondence estimator and adapters are trained on diverse short clips without additional long-sequence training.
