斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models often combines several rewards by normalizing each one and adding them with fixed weights. When the rewards are correlated, the variation they share is counted once for every reward that carries it. In terms of the ZCA-decorrelated components of the reward signal, the weighted sum applies weights $Σ^{1/2} w$ rather than the chosen weights $w$, where $Σ$ is the reward correlation matrix. We study WAS-PO, which whitens the normalized advantages with $Σ^{-1/2}$ before adding them, so that the chosen weights apply to those components. We derive the scalarized objective whose gradient it follows when normalization statistics are held fixed, show that its weights on the raw rewards can be negative, give an exact two-reward condition under which the lighter-weighted reward is reversed, and give a loose bound on the error from estimating $Σ$ during training. On tool calling with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, WAS-PO reached a higher mean training reward than GDPO in all seven seeds with three rewards (3.8% higher) and all three seeds with four (3.9% higher). WAS-PO also replaces GDPO's per-prompt normalization with batch-level normalization, and we did not separate the two changes with three or four rewards. The training-reward gains did not carry over to held-out accuracy, which was slightly lower than GDPO's with three rewards (not significant) and 0.03 lower in absolute terms with four (two seeds evaluated). With two rewards, WAS-PO trailed GDPO in training reward, and a three-seed control weakly suggests that the gap comes from batch-level normalization rather than whitening. In a math setting where the two rewards were nearly identical by construction, WAS-PO drove down the lighter-weighted reward, as the sign condition predicts.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Sean Wu, Aneesh Pappu, Jiaru Zou, Yubin Kim, Yuncong Mao
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark evaluates AI agents' teamwork across 240 tasks, revealing significant weaknesses in collaborative capabilities despite individual model proficiency.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Progress in AI is often measured by what a single model can do on its own. Yet teams of AI agents are starting to make breakthroughs and discoveries in science, medicine, mathematics and software engineering. As AI begins to work in teams of agents and people, the ability to collaborate becomes a core part of their intelligence. Research on human teams has measured this ability for decades. Inspired by this, we introduce the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark, which measures how well an AI agent works as a teammate. It contains 240 tasks across 8 dimensions of teamwork, from refusing an unsafe shortcut to checking the work that a weaker model leaves behind. Each task comes from a real record or an existing benchmark, from aviation accident reports and clinical cases to coding tasks and negotiations, and has a programmatically verifiable outcome. To isolate teamwork from individual capability, models are scored only on tasks that they can solve by themselves when they have full information. We evaluate 18 closed- and open-weight models and find that every model, across sizes and families, has clear weaknesses as a teammate, with the best model scoring only 82.2 out of 100. Frontier models almost always refuse unsafe shortcuts and report misconduct, yet they cave under interpersonal pressure, reaching the best overall deal in only 14% of conflicts, and their pass rate drops from 97% to 81% when they take over a task in which a weaker model has cheated. Crucially, general capability does not guarantee good teamwork, as models with nearly the same capability score differ by up to 11 points as teammates. The benchmark includes 160 public tasks with code and data, along with 80 held-out tasks for evaluation. As AI agents increasingly work alongside other agents and people, the ability to collaborate effectively is becoming a crucial capability to measure and develop.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Xilun Zhang, Liam Achenbach, Luis Pabon, Matthew Foutter, Marco Pavone
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: CUE is an agentic system that autonomously interacts with its environment to accurately identify physical parameters, significantly reducing simulation errors in contact-rich dynamics.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: SurgPace: Complexity-Aware Progressive Distillation for Surgical Multimodal Large Language Models
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Zhicheng He, Xiaohan Xing, Hongqiu Wang, Kun Yuan, Guankun Wang
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: SurgPace introduces a complexity-aware framework for progressive distillation of surgical multimodal large language models, enhancing efficiency and stability in training through tailored supervision strategies.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: VLALagBench: Understanding When and Why VLA Inference Latency Matters
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Qi Wen, Borui Xu, Hussein Amro, Hongshi Tan, Hanmin Lin
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: VLALagBench benchmarks VLA inference latency's impact on task success, revealing significant sensitivity to latency and guiding algorithm configurations for optimal performance in robotics.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward general-purpose robot manipulation. While inference latency can affect task success in a constantly evolving physical world, the relationship between latency and task success rate remains poorly understood. In this paper, we introduce VLALagBench, a comprehensive benchmark for studying VLA inference latency sensitivity across task types, object speeds, execution modes (synchronous and asynchronous), and VLA policies. Using VLALagBench, we find that even a modest inference latency of 100 ms can nearly halve task success on moving targets, with sensitivity varying substantially across tasks and policies. These differences reflect task-specific requirements for precision and continuous motion. By overlapping inference with action execution, asynchronous execution can recover some of the lost success at the cost of more frequent inference requests. Building on these findings, we develop an empirical model that predicts task success from limited calibration data, achieving root-mean-square prediction errors of only 5.7-7.8% across various VLA policies. Given an inference system's latency and per-robot throughput, these predictions guide the selection of system-specific VLA algorithm configurations to maximize task success. We believe VLALagBench and these findings provide a solid foundation for future robotics algorithm-system co-design.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: I3L: Iterative Interactive Imitation Learning for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Wensi Ai, Christopher Luey, Karthik Dharmarajan, Evans Han, Yunfan Jiang
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: I3L is an innovative system that enhances whole-body mobile manipulation by integrating iterative policy refinement and hardware corrections, significantly improving task success rates and reducing intervention time.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates: A Hidden Training-Inference Mismatch and an Unbiased One-Line Fix
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Andrew Gao, William Gao
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper introduces Fair Cast, a one-line fix using unbiased rounding to address the significant policy update loss in reinforcement learning due to bf16 conversion mismatches.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of language models keeps fp32 master weights in the optimizer and serves rollouts from a bf16 copy produced by round-to-nearest conversion. At the learning rates in common use, most per-step updates are smaller than half a bf16 spacing and the conversion discards them: on Qwen3-1.7B only 0.4-0.5% of served weights change per step, and the policy that generates the training data lags the optimizer by 50-150 steps. Existing mismatch corrections cannot see this lag because they compare two copies downstream of the same rounding. We propose Fair Cast: export the master with an unbiased rounding rule (stochastic rounding or error feedback) and compute the training loss on the served copy. The change is one line at the export call, adds no hyperparameters and costs 22-38 ms per export of 1.7B parameters. Across 25 matched seed-pairs on Qwen3-0.6B to 4B with AdamW and Muon, Fair Cast is ahead on 18, tied on 6 and behind on 1, with a mean gain of 6.1 points; on zebra puzzles it reaches 0.57 +/- 0.16 over four runs where round-to-nearest collapses to 0.33 +/- 0.10. It also makes the saved fp32 checkpoint agree with the served model, and it exposes the implicit lag of round-to-nearest as a regularizer that can be restored explicitly when a task needs it.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Rome Wasn't Built in One Turn: Replay-Grounded Reward Signals for Long-Horizon Freeciv Agents
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Yanchen Liu, Xinyu Che, Brihi Joshi, Renzo Fukuda, Junhua Liu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper introduces CivHarness and CivMarshmallow, enhancing long-horizon strategy game training by using replay-grounded reward signals to overcome scoreboard traps in Freeciv.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Training language-model agents to play long-horizon strategy games is hard because deterministic feedback is sparse and often arrives only at the end of a game. In-game scores can offer dense signals, but they do not reliably predict future outcomes: in 8-68% of position pairs across eight strategy games, the higher-scoring position leads to the worse outcome. We term this phenomenon scoreboard traps. In Freeciv, an open-source turn-based empire-building game where several players manage units, cities, and diplomacy over hundreds of turns, we look into better reward signals for gameplay agents. To facilitate this, we build CivHarness, an open system that saves current game states, branches on different decisions, and replays the game to future turns to provide measurable long-horizon feedback from saved positions. We use CivHarness to train CivTelescope, an LLM Judge that predicts which one of two game positions will yield the better outcome. On scoreboard-trap pairs, CivTelescope is 1.3-2.0 times more accurate than off-the-shelf language models, and it generalizes to new game starts, later turns, and unseen rules. We then train a Freeciv gameplay agent with CivTelescope as a dense reward, and call this recipe CivMarshmallow. When used in the middle stage of the game where scoreboard traps are common, CivMarshmallow reaches an average training phase gain of 8.94 points, 77% more than the best baseline, the end-of-game reward. Over the full 120-turn game, CivMarshmallow uses a hybrid reward that starts from the scoreboard or the end-of-game reward and shifts to CivTelescope as the game advances; this hybrid reward scores highest among the rewards we compare.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper audits test-time scaling in world-action models, revealing limited candidate selection benefits and efficiency gains, emphasizing the need for comprehensive evaluation beyond success rates.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Shengguang Wu, Suning Huang, Cherie Ho, Ria Doshi, Hao Zhu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: RoboArchitect automates the design of robotic agent harnesses, significantly improving performance on unseen tasks and scenes without modifying model weights.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: DyCraft: An Agentic System for Long-Horizon 4D Scene Generation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Jeff Tan, Hang Dai, Zeqian Long, Yanzhe Lyu, R. Kenny Jones
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: DyCraft enhances long-horizon 4D scene generation by decomposing animations into manageable steps, improving coherence and reducing physical violations compared to existing coding agents.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: While frontier coding agents can generate high-quality 3D scenes and articulated assets, they struggle to create coherent long-horizon animations. When equipped with general-purpose harnesses, they frequently produce physically implausible outputs, generating objects that interpenetrate, lack physical support, or move unnaturally. Such bare agents struggle to repair these errors because they default to scripting the full animation in one pass, making it difficult to verify their work and disentangle complex spatiotemporal constraints. Drawing on the practice of human animators, we introduce DyCraft, a system for animated 3D scene generation that breaks animation into steps that coding agents can more reliably solve. DyCraft first expands the user's prompt into a detailed plan and builds a static scene. It then creates a 3D storyboard of key animation poses, where each frame is a static 3D scene that the agent can build and debug in isolation. Storyboarding decomposes the problem into pairs of verified start and end states, allowing the agent to author local motion between them with a collection of motion authoring tools. We evaluate DyCraft on 24 long-horizon, multi-shot animation tasks covering humanoid robots, human and animal characters, and physical mechanisms. Compared with a native GPT-6 agent in Codex and prior agentic baselines, DyCraft substantially reduces physical violations and generates higher-quality animated 3D scenes that are more often preferred by human raters.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Design and Validation of a Robotic Knee Exoskeleton with Musculoskeletal Simulation-Derived Biological Torque Control
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Rajiv V. Joshi, Jimin An, Ilseung Park, Dawit Lee, Inseung Kang
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper presents an open-source knee exoskeleton utilizing a simulation-derived biological torque controller, enabling effective assistance without requiring device-specific data collection.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Data-driven controllers have enabled lower-limb robotic exoskeletons to adapt assistance to the user across many tasks. A leading example is biological torque control, which estimates the user's own joint moment from onboard sensors and assists in proportion to that estimate. However, its estimators are trained on data recorded with the target device, so deploying the controller on new hardware requires collecting new data. Existing open-source efforts release hardware, software, or controllers separately, so this data collection must still be repeated on the assembled device. Here, we present an open-source knee exoskeleton, built from off-the-shelf components and widely available fabrication tools, with a biological torque controller derived entirely from simulation. A muscle-driven imitation policy reproduces squatting motions from an open biomechanics dataset, and the resulting knee moments are distilled into an estimator that uses only onboard sensors, so no training data are recorded on the device. In seven able-bodied participants, assistance reduced peak biological knee extension moment by 21.5% and peak vastus medialis activation by 26.7% during squatting, relative to squatting without the exoskeleton (p<0.05). Our results demonstrate that a biological torque controller derived from simulation can transfer to physical hardware without device-specific data collection. Because the hardware and training pipeline are released together, research groups can train and compare knee exoskeleton controllers on shared hardware without additional data collection overhead.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: Training language models in simulated environments significantly enhances their performance in psychiatric intake interviews, improving diagnostic accuracy and patient communication while highlighting the need for clinician oversight.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Mixture of Frames Policy: Multi-Frame Action Denoising for Bimanual Mobile Manipulation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Dian Wang, Jisang Park, Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Shuran Song
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF) enhances bimanual mobile manipulation by synchronizing action denoising across multiple coordinate frames, improving performance over traditional methods.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently multi-frame: local actions may be simple in an end-effector frame, while transport, upright-object handling, and whole-body coordination are better represented in a base-aligned frame. However, modern diffusion-based visuomotor policies typically commit to a single predefined action frame, forcing one denoiser to model action distributions that are often unnecessarily complex in that frame. We propose Mixture of Frames Policy (MoF), a diffusion policy that performs synchronized action denoising across multiple coordinate frames. MoF maintains a single canonical diffusion state, re-expresses it in several task-relevant frames, applies frame-specialized denoisers, and fuses their noise predictions back in the canonical frame. To make this possible for intermediate noisy diffusion states, we adopt a column-based 6D rotation representation within an SE(3) action parameterization that supports exact, differentiable frame transformations without requiring noisy rotations to lie on the SO(3) manifold. Across nine simulated bimanual manipulation tasks, we show that the best action frame is task-dependent and that MoF improves over oracle frame selection and standard Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) baselines. We further evaluate MoF on two real-world bimanual mobile manipulation tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms all constituent single-frame baselines.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: BEHAVIOR-Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The BEHAVIOR-Spatial benchmark evaluates spatial understanding in robotics through spatial question answering and action performance across various tasks, revealing significant gaps in instruction adherence.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT) enhances robot manipulation by enabling preference adaptation across tasks using self-labeled demonstrations, achieving high accuracy and task success without manual annotations.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Alex Brandes, Haig Conti Georges Sajelian, Manthan Patel, Dominik Hollidt, Chenhao Li
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The EgoHTR dataset enhances humanoid robot training by providing 4D human motion sequences in complex terrains, enabling improved locomotion policies and context-aware navigation.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Cross-Controller Transfer via In-Context Behavior Adaptation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper presents a framework for transferring robot data across diverse controllers and embodiments, enhancing adaptability and success in varied tasks by leveraging behavioral interaction context.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: StreamVibe: Proactive Video Agents for Evolving User Intent
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: StreamVibe introduces a proactive video agent model that effectively infers and adapts to evolving user intents through a new benchmark and hierarchical memory system.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while overlooking implicit user intents (e.g., "where should I click next?" when a user is navigating a website) and fail to continuously update their understanding as user intents evolve. These limitations make them less suitable for intent-aware interaction in real-world scenarios. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark that serves as a testbed for user intent understanding and interaction, comprising 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically adapts its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with flexible lifecycles through hierarchical memory, enabling it to track the latest user intents and environmental states. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding capabilities while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over existing baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intents and determining when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation during sustained interactions, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction performance.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Gradient-Free Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Scalable Safety-Critical Control
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Zeyuan Feng, Ali Fuat Sahin, Santiago Thorup, Somil Bansal
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper presents a gradient-free neural framework for Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, enabling scalable safety-critical control in high-dimensional robotic systems through efficient value propagation and supervised policy learning.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides a principled framework for synthesizing safety certificates and robust controllers for safety-critical robotic systems. However, applying reachability analysis to high-dimensional nonlinear systems remains challenging: classical grid-based solvers suffer from the curse of dimensionality, continuous-time neural solvers require accurate spatial value gradients, and reinforcement-learning-based approaches often suffer from weak boundary anchoring and non-stationary adversarial policy optimization. We propose a discrete-time neural reachability framework for control-disturbance-affine systems that learns backward reachable tubes (BRTs) and backward reach-avoid tubes (BRATs) through Bellman-Isaacs value propagation. Our key idea is to combine equation-driven self-supervision with structured policy learning: rather than computing explicit PDE-gradients, we exploit the bang-bang structure of optimal safety interventions to construct approximate teacher actions from gradient-free value probes, converting adversarial actor learning into supervised policy learning. To stabilize long-horizon value propagation, we leverage the learned actor to train the value function backward from the terminal boundary using a windowed temporal curriculum, where each window is used as the boundary condition for the next window. Across benchmark problems up to 80 dimensions, our method learns accurate reachability value functions while improving stability over existing learning-based solvers. We further demonstrate observation-space scalability on F1-tenth racing with over 16,000-dimensional egocentric inputs. The learned safety filter generalizes zero-shot to unseen tracks and transfers to a physical RC car, achieving real-time robust collision avoidance.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Where Small Mistakes Matter: Quantifying State Criticality for Imitation Learning
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper introduces SCRIM, a method for quantifying state criticality in imitation learning to enhance performance by reweighting losses and optimizing data selection.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: LabWorld: Learning Interactive 4D Worlds for Scientific Experimentation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Suozhi Huang, Kelsey Fu, Binxu Li, Luna Lyu, Kaize Wu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: LabWorld is a Real2Sim framework that reconstructs interactive 4D laboratory environments from monocular RGB videos, enhancing scientific experimentation through improved asset and event modeling.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Autonomous scientific agents must not only reason about experiments but also interact with the physical environments in which they are executed. Existing laboratory simulators typically rely on manually constructed assets and predefined procedures, while laboratory videos capture real equipment, layouts, and interactions but leave this information implicit in pixels. We introduce LabWorld, an agent-driven Real2Sim framework for reconstructing interactive 4D laboratory worlds from monocular RGB video. LabWorld recovers reusable 3D assets, a metric scene, time-varying object states, and procedure events. Multi-frame observations provide complementary evidence for asset and scene reconstruction, while motion reconstruction combines visual and geometric observations with event constraints encoding the spatial and temporal requirements of laboratory interactions. We evaluate LabWorld on real pipetting and vortexing videos collected in our laboratory against general-purpose agentic and dedicated reconstruction baselines. For pipetting, LabWorld achieves a mean Mask IoU of 0.501, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.033. For vortexing, it achieves a mean Tube-Length-Normalized PCK-AUC of 0.638, exceeding the strongest baseline by 0.035. On five pipetting videos, event-conditioned reconstruction increases the fraction of modeled physical constraints satisfied from 14.3% (5/35) to 100% (35/35). The resulting worlds expose geometry, motion, articulation, and events as explicit, editable state for replay, inspection, and future embodied scientific systems.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Alexa R. Tartaglini, Zhengxuan Wu, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Martin Wattenberg, Been Kim
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) communicate visually, revealing a gap between their intuitive visual cues and human interpretations, affecting task performance.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Deep Learning Warm Starts for Trajectory Optimization on the International Space Station
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Somrita Banerjee, Abhishek Cauligi, Marco Pavone
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper demonstrates the first in-space application of machine learning warm starts to accelerate trajectory optimization for the Astrobee robot on the ISS, significantly improving efficiency.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Trajectory optimization is a cornerstone of modern robot autonomy, enabling systems to compute trajectories and controls in real-time while respecting safety and physical constraints. However, it has seen limited usage in spaceflight applications due to its heavy computational demands that exceed the capability of most flight computers. In this work, we provide results on the first in-space demonstration of using machine learning-based warm starts for accelerating trajectory optimization for the Astrobee free-flying robot onboard the International Space Station (ISS). We formulate a data-driven optimal control approach that trains a neural network to learn the structure of the trajectory generation problem being solved using sequential convex programming (SCP). Onboard, this trained neural network predicts solutions for the trajectory generation problem and relies on using the SCP solver to enforce safety constraints for the system. Our trained network reduces the number of solver iterations required for convergence in cases including rotational dynamics by 60% and in cases with obstacles drawn from the training distribution of the warm start model by 50%. This work represents a significant milestone in the use of learning-based control for spaceflight applications and a stepping stone for future advances in the use of machine learning for autonomous guidance, navigation, & control.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: World from Motion: Generative Dynamic Gaussian Reconstruction from Monocular Video
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Liyuan Zhu, Shengyu Huang, Amrita Mazumdar, Tianye Li, Zan Gojcic
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper introduces World from Motion, a method for creating dynamic 3D Gaussian representations from monocular videos, enhancing reconstruction quality and generalization to diverse scenes.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: We present World from Motion, a method for generating freely renderable dynamic 3D Gaussian representations from monocular videos. Our approach conditions a video model on dense, pixel-aligned renderings that encode appearance, geometry, and 3D scene motion along both input and target camera trajectories to correct rendering artifacts and fill in missing regions from an initial reconstruction. To train this model, we construct a dataset of aligned multiview video pairs and dynamic 3DGS representations, with simulated artifacts characteristic of monocular reconstruction. At test time, we distill the model's generations, including newly observed regions and motions, back into a single consistent, high-quality dynamic 3DGS, improving both novel-view synthesis and the underlying 3D motion. Our method sets a new state of the art in 4D reconstruction and seamlessly generalizes to in-the-wild videos with large viewpoint changes and dynamic motions.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: StackGen3D: Stable 3D Block Stack Generation from Multiview Silhouettes
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Xiaopeng Zhang, Luzhe Sun, Yiqing Xu, Matthew R. Walter
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: StackGen3D is a framework that generates stable 3D block structures from silhouettes using a physics-informed graph neural network and conditional flow-matching model.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow-matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI-GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter-matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best-of-10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly. Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/)

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: $Ψ$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Khai Loong Aw, Klemen Kotar, Baihan Zhang, Yifan Liu, Lilian Chen
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: $Ψ$-0.6 is a unified vision-language model that adaptively integrates perception, language, and geometry for enhanced reasoning and counterfactual simulation in AI.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $Ψ$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $Ψ$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $Ψ$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Thomas Landeg, Thierry Tambe
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper presents Backtrack, a lightweight recovery mechanism for frozen Vision-Language-Action models that enhances failure detection and reduces failure rates by 19-48% without retraining.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: DexPort is a portable interface that simplifies dexterous robot hand data collection by allowing operators to control wrist motion and finger coordination, enhancing task success rates significantly.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: UniAction presents a unified framework for action conditioning in world models, enabling heterogeneous actions to share a model and outperform specialized counterparts through joint training.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: UniMem: Unifying Visual and Textual Memory in VLAs for Non-Markovian Tasks
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Lars Osterberg, Maggie Wang, Mac Schwager
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: UniMem integrates visual and textual memory in a unified framework, enhancing performance on non-Markovian tasks while simplifying training and inference processes.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory. Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline. Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level visual and textual memory and low-level control under one backbone. UniMem employs an event classifier to initiate textual and visual memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense visual memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts. We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical VLM-VLA baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption. Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Guillem Casadesus Vila, Grace Gao
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper benchmarks eleven feature matching methods for lunar visual SLAM, revealing SuperPoint's superiority in low-texture environments, while highlighting the limitations of synthetic data comparisons.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Ava Pun, Kevin Dai, Sally Chen, Maxwell Jones, Ruixuan Liu
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: BrickWright is a framework that enables agents to generate 100% physically feasible LEGO builds from prompts by using a specialized assembly API and validator.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Chi Kit Ng, Shuchang Liu, Jinsong Lin, Yidong Zhang, Xizi Wang
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: EBV-CAN integrates vision-language grounding for endoscope navigation, achieving high localization accuracy and successful task completion through a novel dataset and policy framework.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper presents Dual Exam, a framework for evaluating the interaction between Multimodal Agents and World Models across various domains, revealing performance inconsistencies and challenges in reciprocal learning.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R) transforms a single human RGB video into thousands of robot demonstrations by semantically aligning objects, enhancing robot learning efficiency.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Yash Rampuria, Rohan Garg, Daniele Gammelli, Marco Pavone
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: GGraph is a GPU-accelerated library that enhances graph-based robot deployment and learning, enabling efficient training across hundreds of parallel environments.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Do Earth-Trained Humanoid Controllers Walk on the Moon? Gravity, Terrain, and Soil Transfer
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Guillem Casadesus Vila, Sri Aditya Deevi, Grace X. Gao
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This study evaluates the transferability of Earth-trained humanoid locomotion controllers to lunar conditions, revealing asymmetric survival rates and the impact of terrain and gravity on performance.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: ProactEgoMem: Benchmarking Proactive Memory in Streaming Egocentric Video
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo Sánchez
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: ProactEgoMem introduces a benchmark for evaluating proactive memory in streaming egocentric video, focusing on tasks like information capture, state tracking, and location tracking.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: This paper presents a method for force-aware manipulation using visual force prediction from a compliant gripper, eliminating the need for specialized force sensors during deployment.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Adam Lee, Shobhit Agarwal, June Pyo Suh
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: Beckmann World Models introduce a novel approach for efficient one-step action-conditioned video prediction, achieving significant accuracy and performance improvements without relying on pretrained generative models.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.
