Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: We study how trajectory-shape diversity in demonstrations affects imitation learning (IL) performance across models, tasks, and data scales. We introduce Geometric Entropy (H_G), a task-agnostic metric that quantifies the intrinsic diversity of transit trajectories after normalizing away extrinsic variation, such as goal pose and workspace scale, via target-frame alignment. Across multiple IL architectures and both simulated and real-robot contact-rich manipulation tasks, we observe a consistent inverted-U relationship between success and H_G: increasing geometric diversity improves robustness in low-diversity regimes but degrades performance once diversity induces strategy ambiguity. Moreover, the optimal entropy shifts toward lower values as task mastery increases through more data, easier tasks, or stronger priors, and for a pretrained vision-language-action model the trend becomes effectively monotonic decreasing. Practically, H_G enables fast pre-training auditing of demonstration datasets and offers a simple guideline for calibrating demonstrations toward the learnable regime.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: RoboLineage: Agent-Native Data Lifecycle Governance Across Robot Policy Iterations
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Qian Luo, Wentao Guo, Zhennan Qin, Nanchun Guo, Yunhan Zhao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: RoboLineage is an open-source governance system that enhances robot policy iteration by explicitly managing data lifecycle artifacts, improving efficiency and auditability in real-robot workflows.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: We present RoboLineage, an agent-native data lifecycle governance system for robot policy iteration. Modern robot policies improve through repeated data collection, review, retraining, evaluation, and release decisions, but the evidence connecting these steps is often scattered across local tools, scripts, and expert memory. RoboLineage makes this lifecycle explicit by representing rollouts, reviews, dataset decisions, training runs, policy metadata, evaluations, deployment recommendations, and next-collection plans as typed lineage artifacts. Agents interpret embodied rollout evidence, adapt accepted data to existing training stacks, maintain data health, and summarize cross-iteration state under explicit artifact boundaries. In real-robot manipulation workflows, RoboLineage makes routine policy iteration faster and more auditable while maintaining downstream policy performance. We open source RoboLineage as a lightweight lifecycle layer for different robot embodiments and training families. Project page: https://robolineage.github.io/

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Zheng Sun, Zhihao Li, Zhuo Li, Wenrui Liu, Xin Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: ReSkill is a selective self-improvement framework that enhances robot manipulation by identifying and revising capability gaps, leading to significant performance improvements in task execution.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Online Geometric Consistency Assessment of LiDAR Measurements via Recursive Bayesian Comparison
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Mingqiao Han, Qigeng Duan, Xuchen Liu, Jinqiang Cui, Xi Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper presents a recursive Bayesian method for online geometric consistency assessment of LiDAR measurements, effectively detecting registration errors in real-time navigation systems.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: LiDAR-based localization and mapping systems produce registered point clouds that serve as geometric measurements for downstream estimation and navigation. Registration errors introduce duplicated surfaces and structural deformation into these measurements. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment relies on geometry accumulated from earlier measurements. Such assessment requires tolerance to sampling variation and an accumulation process in which observations enter the history only after evaluation. We therefore formulate a recursive Bayesian comparison that couples geometric assessment with history maintenance. A Normal-Inverse-Wishart model represents historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, while a weak isotropic reference adapts to current sampling. Comparing the marginal predictive support of the same current points under both models yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE). Assessment precedes assimilation: positive NDE triggers an alarm and preserves the preceding historical state; otherwise, the current observations update the history. Across 14 real-world sequences totaling approximately 73 min from four platform types, alarms identified all nine corrupted sequences and were absent from all five consistent sequences. In four representative scenarios with event references, first alarms occurred within 0.9 s of the reference times, with no preceding alarms. Cross-backend evaluation demonstrates consistent responses to reconstructed geometry. Ablation and controlled perturbation results establish the roles of uncertainty modeling, recursive history, displacement, and geometric support. Mean processing time is 4.2--6.1 ms per update at 1 Hz. In ten UAV trials, alarms initiated odometry isolation, landing, relocalization, and mission continuation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Bias-Eliminated PnP for Stereo Visual Odometry: Provably Consistent and Large-Scale Localization
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Guangyang Zeng, Yuan Shen, Ziyang Hong, Yuze Hong, Viorela Ila
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper introduces a bias-eliminated PnP estimator for stereo visual odometry, enhancing pose estimation accuracy and reliability in large-scale environments through improved triangulation and error suppression.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: In this paper, we first present a bias-eliminated weighted (Bias-Eli-W) perspective-n-point (PnP) estimator for stereo visual odometry (VO) with provable consistency. Specifically, leveraging statistical theory, we develop an asymptotically unbiased and $\sqrt {n}$-consistent PnP estimator that accounts for varying 3D triangulation uncertainties, ensuring that the relative pose estimate converges to the ground truth as the number of features increases. Next, on the stereo VO pipeline side, we propose a framework that continuously triangulates contemporary features for tracking new frames, effectively decoupling temporal dependencies between pose and 3D point errors. We integrate the Bias-Eli-W PnP estimator into the proposed stereo VO pipeline, creating a synergistic effect that enhances the suppression of pose estimation errors. We validate the performance of our method on the KITTI and Oxford RobotCar datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method: 1) achieves significant improvements in both relative pose error and absolute trajectory error in large-scale environments; 2) provides reliable localization under erratic and unpredictable robot motions. The successful implementation of the Bias-Eli-W PnP in stereo VO indicates the importance of information screening in robotic estimation tasks with high-uncertainty measurements, shedding light on diverse applications where PnP is a key ingredient.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xudong Wu, Guangchen Lan, Mingqi Yuan, Jiayu Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: JoMoHa is a novel reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes model weights and harnesses, significantly enhancing performance in language agents through recursive self-improvement.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Reaching Is Not Finding: Map-Anchored Visual Prompting for the Last Mile of Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ningbo Li, Kebin Liu, Jingcan Chen, Weichen Zhang, Rong Ding
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces MAP-VP, a module that enhances aerial vision-language navigation by improving object identification relative to landmarks, significantly boosting success rates without retraining.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) asks a drone to find an object described in natural language. The description usually locates the object relative to named landmarks, such as streets and buildings. We observe that current navigators often bring the drone close to the target and then stop at the wrong place: they reach the target without finding it. This gap is shared by navigators of very different designs, from imitation learners to a fine-tuned 7B vision-language model. A simple test reveals the cause. When we replace the target object in the instruction with another one next to the same landmarks, no navigator goes to it, and most stop where they did before. Navigators learn to reach the landmarks, not to identify the described object. We therefore propose MAP-VP, a plug-and-play module for the last step. After any navigator stops, MAP-VP draws the landmarks named in the instruction onto the drone's current view, using the landmark outlines that the benchmark provides on a map. A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model then locates the target relative to these landmarks. The training data are generated automatically from the benchmark annotations. Neither drawing the landmarks nor fine-tuning helps much alone, but together they are highly effective. Without retraining any navigator, MAP-VP significantly improves all six navigators we test on CityNav. It roughly doubles the success rate of the two strongest trained navigators, raising HETT from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%, whereas CityNav's official detector-based last step adds less than two points to HETT.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: The Relative Value of Demonstration Data: Execution Time Limits and Operator Mixtures in Behavior Cloning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Youran Sun, Jingxin Yang, Kejia Zhang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The study quantifies the relative effectiveness of demonstration data in behavior cloning, revealing that lower-quality demonstrations require significantly more samples to achieve comparable success rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: FUSE-PnPL: Flexible, Unified, Statistically Consistent, and Asymptotically Efficient Camera Pose Estimation from Points and Lines
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Guangyang Zeng, Yuan Shen, Yiguo Peng, Guodong Shi, Biqiang Mu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: FUSE-PnPL is a unified, efficient camera pose estimator leveraging point and line features, ensuring statistical consistency and real-time applicability for robotics.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Camera pose estimation from 3D-2D correspondences is fundamental to robotics. Three practical considerations motivate this work. First, point and line features provide complementary geometric information, motivating a unified estimator. Second, the number and composition of available features vary across scenarios, requiring support for minimal and arbitrary non-minimal configurations. Third, modern visual front ends extract abundant features from individual images, enabling highly accurate pose estimation. We propose FUSE-PnPL, a flexible and unified camera pose estimator that is statistically consistent and asymptotically efficient. Specifically, we represent each line using two distinct points and adopt a unified image-space noise model for point and line measurements. By employing Plücker coordinates for line parameterization, we explicitly characterize the propagation of image endpoint noise into line residuals and formulate a joint maximum likelihood (ML) estimation problem for combined point and line measurements. To efficiently solve this problem, FUSE-PnPL employs a two-stage estimation scheme. First, noise variance estimation and bias elimination yield a consistent initial pose estimate. A single Gauss-Newton iteration then refines this estimate, achieving asymptotic efficiency as its mean squared error asymptotically attains the Cramér-Rao lower bound. Moreover, the proposed estimator has linear computational complexity with respect to the number of correspondences, making it suitable for high-precision and real-time robot pose estimation. Extensive experiments on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks validate the theoretical properties of FUSE-PnPL and demonstrate its advantages in both static global localization and dynamic SLAM systems.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LLM-as-Code: Agentic Programming for Agent Harness
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Junjia Qi, Zichuan Fu, Jingtong Gao, Wenlin Zhang, Hanyu Yan
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces Agentic Programming, where LLMs are integrated as adaptive components within a controlled program flow, enhancing stability in complex task execution.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Every major LLM agent framework gives the LLM the role of orchestrator; the model decides what to do next, when to call tools, and when to stop. We argue that token explosion, control-flow hallucination, and unreliable completion are not implementation bugs but architectural consequences of assigning the deterministic work of looping, branching, and sequencing to a probabilistic system. A better prompt or a stronger model cannot guarantee the reliability of the LLM agent. We therefore propose Agentic Programming, in which the program governs all control flow, and the LLM is itself part of it, an adaptive component we call LLM-as-Code and invoke only where a task calls for reasoning or generation. Within each call the model keeps full flexibility, but it cannot alter the program's execution path. With control in the program, the LLM's context is built from the execution history's call tree and forms a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each call's context length is then determined by its call depth rather than by accumulation over steps. A case study of computer-use agents shows that the design is practical, not just a theoretical stance, substantially improving the stability of long visual operation sequences.Code is available at https://github.com/FuzzyKuji/OpenProgram.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Chenhao Zhang, Zhongan Wang, Mingxuan Li, Hehe Fan, Zheng Zhu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces ECOS, an environment-calibrated self-distillation method for language agents that enhances performance by optimizing guidance based on environmental outcomes.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: From Reflection to Co-Evolution: Self-Evolving Agents with Locally Verified Memory
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xinxiang Yin, Xinglang Zhang, Haodong Chen, Zhiqing Cui, Weidong Tang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents Anchor, a self-evolving agent that optimizes memory retention through source decision testing, enhancing performance in long-horizon tasks while reducing redundancy.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: LLM agents have made impressive progress in coding and mathematical reasoning, motivating growing interest in learning from long-horizon interaction. Memory supports this process, but plausible lessons can be redundant or reinforce inappropriate actions. Can a memory's source decision provide a practical test for whether to retain it? We localize consequential trajectory steps, extract candidate memories, and replay each source decision with and without its candidate under the same context. This reveals two properties: most candidates barely shift the probed distribution, and both successful and failed source actions can be reinforced or suppressed. These observations motivate Anchor, which tests shift magnitude and source-role alignment before retention. Admitted memories guide later trajectories, enabling experience-driven improvement under a frozen policy. On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, Anchor improves success rate and mean score by up to 19.9% and 17.2%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline for each backbone. With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld cards than unfiltered retention and outperforms all four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Group of Skills: Group-Structured Skill Retrieval for Agent Skill Libraries
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Siyu Zhang, Haoyue Liu, Yuecheng Zhuo
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: GoSkills enhances agent skill retrieval by organizing skills into role-labeled groups, improving execution context and performance across multiple benchmarks compared to existing methods.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Skill-augmented agents increasingly rely on large reusable skill libraries, but retrieving relevant skills is not the same as presenting usable context. Existing methods typically return atomic skills or dependency-aware bundles whose internal roles remain implicit, leaving the agent to infer the execution entry point, support skills, visible requirements, and failure-avoidance guidance. We introduce Group of Skills (GoSkills), an inference-time group-structured retrieval method that changes the agent-facing retrieval object from a flat skill list to a compact, role-labeled execution context. GoSkills builds anchor-centered skill groups from a typed skill graph, expands support groups through a group graph, bottlenecks the selected group plan into a bounded set of atomic skill payloads, and renders a fixed execution contract with Start, Support, Check, and Avoid fields, without changing the downstream agent, skill payloads, or execution environment. Across SkillsBench, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench 2 with six backbones, GoSkills attains the highest mean reward or accuracy among the evaluated methods in every benchmark-backbone setting, and matched controls show higher reward and fewer agent turns with group selection than with fixed-contract or post-hoc role-annotation alternatives.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Beyond Action Residuals: Real-World Robot Policy Steering via Bottleneck Latent Reinforcement Learning
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Dongjie Yu, Kun Lei, Zhennan Jiang, Jia Pan, Huazhe Xu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents Z-Perturbation Reinforcement Learning (ZPRL), which enhances pretrained robot policies through a compact bottleneck latent interface, improving adaptation and performance in real-world tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Pretrained imitation policies have become a strong foundation for robot manipulation, but online adaptation can further improve policy performance within their pretrained behavioral support. A central question is therefore how reinforcement learning (RL) should adapt policies after offline pretraining. Existing lightweight methods commonly apply residual corrections directly in action space. We investigate how the steering interface affects online RL. In this work, we propose Z-Perturbation Reinforcement Learning (ZPRL), an approach that steers pretrained policies through a compact bottleneck latent rather than through policy weights or output actions. Building on an offline-learned bottleneck policy interface introduced by previous work, ZPRL turns this representation into an online RL control space through reward-driven residual perturbations while freezing the pretrained policy. We instantiate ZPRL on flow-matching policies and evaluate it on eight simulation tasks and four real-world tasks. Across diverse manipulation settings, ZPRL improves sample efficiency with competitive or better final performance. In the real world, ZPRL improves the average success rate on four tasks by 33.7 percentage points over imitation base policies. Our qualitative and quantitative results also indicate that ZPRL combines task success with smooth actions without explicit temporal filtering or smoothness regularization. These results suggest that a compact, task-aligned bottleneck latent provides an effective interface for online RL adaptation. Videos and code can be found at https://manutdmoon.github.io/ZPRL/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Frequency-Aware Flow Matching for Continuous and Consistent Robotic Action Generation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jianing Guo, Fangzheng Chen, Zihao Mao, Wong Lik Hang Kenny, Zhenhong Wu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Frequency-Aware Flow Matching (FAFM) enhances robotic action generation by enabling continuous, consistent actions from heterogeneous frequency inputs, improving performance across various benchmarks and real-world applications.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a standard paradigm for robotic manipulation owing to its strong expressive power for modelling complex, multimodal action distributions, alongside similar approaches like diffusion policy. However, existing methods rely on discretized action chunks, making them brittle to demonstrations collected at heterogeneous control frequencies and prone to temporally inconsistent actions that degrade control stability. In this paper, we propose Frequency-Aware Flow Matching (FAFM), which outputs continuous, temporally consistent actions. To handle heterogeneous frequency input, we transform discrete action sequences into the frequency domain with the discrete cosine transform (DCT), perform flow matching over the resulting coefficients, and reconstruct continuous actions via cosine basis expansion. To generate temporally consistent actions, we regularize the first-order temporal derivative to promote smooth actions. This corresponds to a Sobolev-type constraint that suppresses high-frequency errors and discourages abrupt action changes. Our FAFM is simple, introduces no additional network parameters and applies to standalone flow-matching policies and vision-language action models. Across synthetic toy benchmark, obstacle avoidance, LapGym, and LIBERO, FAFM improves success rates, multimodal expressivity, motion smoothness, convergence speed, robustness to mechanical bias and mixed-frequency input. These gains are consistent when deployed on a real-world Franka robot. Code available at https://github.com/gakakulicc/FAFM.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SurgTAP-3D: A Large-Scale Cross-Surgery Video Dataset with Contact-Aware 3D Motion Tracking
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jiaxin Guo, Wenzhen Dong, Taoyu Wu, Haomin Kuang, Mengya Xu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SurgTAP-3D is a comprehensive dataset for 3D motion tracking in minimally invasive surgery, addressing tool-tissue interactions and enhancing autonomous surgical system development.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LHNav: Long-Horizon Humanoid Navigation via Multirate Coordination and Physics-Grounded Action Data
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xueyang Wang, Zehong Shen, Dingkun Wei, Huaijin Pi, Changpeng Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: LHNav enables long-horizon humanoid navigation through a multirate coordination system, enhancing task execution and motion fidelity across multiple destinations using physics-grounded data.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Chengcheng Wang, Wei He, Wenhao Li, Hongguang Li, Kai Han
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Concertina presents an Embodied Vision-Language Model that integrates manipulation and cognition into a single diffusion framework, achieving high performance on various benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)--either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5%-35.1% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit, we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC-D. Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Concertina Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/Traly/concertina

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Semantics-to-Contact: A Stagewise Framework for Robust Contact-Rich Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Guanren Qiao, Ruixiang Ouyang, Sheng Xu, Yueci Deng, Yunxin Tai
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The Semantics-to-Contact framework enhances robust contact-rich manipulation by combining semantic localization and fine-tuned reinforcement learning, improving performance across diverse visual conditions.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires precise control under complex contact dynamics while remaining robust to diverse visual conditions. However, real-world reinforcement learning often overfits to the visual appearance of training scenes. We propose Semantics-to-Contact (S2C), a stagewise framework for visually robust contact-rich manipulation. The insight is to decompose the problem into two stages: semantic focusing and contact refinement. In the first stage, a vision-language model localizes task-relevant regions across visually diverse scenes, providing coarse spatial guidance and reducing the burden of exploration. In the second stage, a real-world human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning policy learns fine-grained contact behaviors within the localized region using force feedback. To further improve visual robustness, we introduce an object-centric visual augmentation strategy that randomizes background appearance while preserving the robot and task-relevant objects. Experiments on six contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks exhibit that S2C consistently improves success rates over strong baselines and maintains reliable performance under significant visual and positional variations. These results demonstrate that stagewise semantic focusing and contact refinement provide a practical path toward visually robust real-world contact-rich manipulation. Our demos can be seen in https://edem-ai.github.io/S2C/.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: A Unified Fractal Impedance Control Framework
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Adnan Takriti, Mahmoud Sadeq, Quentin Rouxel, Daniele Cafolla, Michael Mistry
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper presents the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm, an advanced Fractal Impedance Controller for safe human-robot interaction, validated through experiments on a Kinova Gen3 arm.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Physical human--robot interaction requires controllers capable of maintaining intrinsically bounded interactions with the environment. The Fractal Impedance Controller (FIC) has been proven to guarantee these safety characteristics by design. This paper introduces the robotic implementation and experimental validation of its most advanced architecture: the Harmonic-Passive Motion Paradigm (H-PMP), an evolution of the Passive Motion Paradigm designed to mimic human-like interaction. Furthermore, we present a unified framework for FIC deployment, supported by an open-source software suite featuring ROS2, MuJoCo, and physical hardware integrations. Through three experiments conducted on a Kinova Gen3 arm (trajectory tracking, a wall press with sudden loss of contact, and learning-by-demonstration) we compare the H-PMP against earlier FIC architectures. The results demonstrate that the H-PMP achieves a seamless trade-off between admittance and impedance behaviours. This makes it ideal for deployment in unstructured environments, enabling the robot to transition between interaction modes with no computational overhead.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PlayGen2: Learning Real-Time Playable Worlds with Explicit 3D State
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Jihai Zhang, Yuhan Zhou, Junyou Li, Deheng Ye, Qi Dou
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PlayGen2 is a real-time interactive world model that separates 3D state evolution from rendering, enabling consistent gameplay dynamics and efficient simulation in complex environments.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Reverse to Advance: Teleoperation-Cost Effective Hard Policy Learning from Reversed Easy Tasks
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Qiyuan Qiao, Ge Yuan, Can Wang, Dong Xu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents a framework that leverages reversed easy-task trajectories to efficiently train hard-task policies in teleoperation, enhancing data efficiency and training stability.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: High-quality teleoperation datasets are costly to collect, particularly for hard tasks. We observe that many tasks exhibit directional asymmetry: completing the forward hard task is difficult, whereas reversing it by relaxing or disrupting the environment is comparatively easy. This suggests that reversed easy-task trajectories can serve as a scalable supervision signal for the hard task, reducing the cost of manual demonstration collection. However, reversed data can be noisy, and directly training on it may yield suboptimal policies. To enable largely automated acquisition and effective use of reversed data, we propose a teleoperation-cost effective framework for hard policy learning via temporal reversal of easy tasks, consisting of three key components: a closed-loop data collection pipeline that alternates between hard-task and easy-task policies to autonomously reset the environment and generate diverse trajectories; a hierarchical data refinement pipeline that temporally inverts easy-task rollouts and filters low-quality motion using kinematic priors and a critic-guided advantage filter; and an iterative policy learning method that trains the hard-task policy using both initial reversed easy-task demonstrations and the filtered reversed data in a continuous online learning loop. By combining automated collection, hierarchical refinement, and iterative learning, our method enables scalable, reliable training of complex, high-precision manipulation tasks. Across two simulated benchmarks and real-robot experiments, we demonstrate that our method improves hard-task success rates with higher data efficiency and more stable training compared to reversal-based and reinforcement-learning baselines, without requiring extensive hard-task teleoperation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: RoboCasa-Mem introduces a benchmark for evaluating memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation through nine tasks requiring environment and process memory, supported by a Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy baseline.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao, Hongrui Wu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: TurnWise introduces a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video RL, enhancing decision-making by aligning learning with individual interactions and reducing redundant responses.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Riemannian Optimization-based Whole-body Obstacle Avoidance for Mobile Continuum Robots in Cluttered Environments
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Duo Tang, Ping Deng, Sophie Armanini, Yajing Shen, Toshio Fukuda
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper presents a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots that enhances obstacle avoidance and motion coordination in cluttered environments through Riemannian optimization.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Inspired by the coordination of global motion and local shape adaptation in snakes, elephant trunks, and octopus arms, we propose a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots in cluttered and confined environments. Existing approaches often address high-level path planning and local motion control separately, limiting coordinated base-arm motion, kinematic consistency, and collision avoidance. Our framework integrates long-horizon trajectory planning with real-time geometric refinement under kinematic and environmental constraints. The global layer combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning to generate smooth reference trajectories. The local layer uses a geometry-consistent inverse kinematics solver and Riemannian optimization to coordinate mobile-base motion and continuum deformation while avoiding obstacles. We evaluate the framework through simulated pipe-traversal tasks with multiple baseline planners and real-world experiments involving navigation among dense obstacles and manipulation in confined spaces. Results demonstrate improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability, supporting coordinated whole-body motion of mobile continuum robots in constrained environments.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Traffic-VL: Reinforced Vision-Language Models for Generalizable End-to-End Traffic Signal Control
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xingchen Zou, Maonan Wang, Kemou Jiang, Jie Li, Yiqi Chen
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: Traffic-VL is a vision-language model that enhances traffic signal control by directly linking multi-view images and natural language to decisions, outperforming traditional methods and demonstrating robust generalization.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: IntentNav: Learning Spatial-Visual Object Navigation from Human Demonstrations
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yuxin Cai, Zongtai Li, Maonan Wang, Muyi Bao, Haokun Zhu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: IntentNav is a spatial-visual imitation framework that learns human-like object navigation policies from demonstrations, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Object navigation requires a robot to search for an unobserved target in an unknown environment by deciding where to explore next under partial observability. Effective search resembles human-like exploration: selectively probing visually promising frontiers while relying on spatial memory to avoid redundant revisits. We propose IntentNav, a spatial-visual imitation framework that learns human-like ObjectNav policies from human demonstrations. To infer high-level search intent from low-level human actions, we introduce Frontier-based Human-Intent Labeling, which looks ahead in human demonstrations and labels the frontier that best explains the demonstrator's future search direction. We construct a spatial-visual candidate space, where BEV memory tracks explored regions, unexplored frontiers, and trajectory history, while egocentric visual memory provides semantic cues for each candidate. A VLM policy is trained to select among these grounded candidates, using Intent-Aligned Objective to encourage consistent and human-like exploration. IntentNav achieves state-of-the-art performance among learning-based methods on the MP3D, HM3D-v1, and HM3D-v2 ObjectNav benchmarks, attaining the best success rate among all compared methods. The proposed candidate-level navigation interface transfers zero-shot to wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots without further VLM fine-tuning. \href{https://wmn7.github.io/IntentNav/}{Project page}.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Physical Diffusion Policy via MPM-Guided 3D Gaussian Simulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Can Wang, Qiyuan Qiao, Lei Liu, Ge Yuan, Xinhui Liu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents a physics-aware diffusion policy that enhances manipulation learning by integrating visual imitation with material property estimation and adaptive behavior generation for diverse objects.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PrimeSim is a robust action-conditioned multiview world model simulator that enhances long-horizon rollouts and action fidelity through advanced training techniques and cross-embodiment representations.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: RoboMemory: A Brain-inspired Multi-memory Agentic Framework for Interactive Environmental Learning in Physical Embodied Systems
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Mingcong Lei, Honghao Cai, Yuyuan Yang, Yimou Wu, Jinke Ren
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: RoboMemory is a brain-inspired framework that enhances long-horizon learning in embodied agents by integrating diverse memory types and utilizing a dynamic spatial knowledge graph.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to learn, reason, and generalize robustly across complex real-world environments. However, existing approaches often struggle with partial observability, fragmented spatial reasoning, and inefficient integration of heterogeneous memories, limiting their capacity for long-horizon adaptation. To address this, we introduce RoboMemory, a brain-inspired framework that unifies Temporal, Spatial, Semantic, and Episodic memory for efficient long-horizon planning and interactive learning. Its core innovations are a comprehensive memory system designed for embodied tasks, and a dynamic spatial knowledge graph for scalable, consistent memory updates. Extensive experiments on EmbodiedBench show that RoboMemory improves the average success rate of Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Ins by 26.5 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to strong closed-source VLM agents. Real-world trials further suggest RoboMemory's potential for interactive environmental learning by reusing accumulated experience across repeated task attempts. These results demonstrate RoboMemory as a scalable memory-augmented framework for embodied agents, improving long-horizon planning and cumulative learning in complex interactive environments.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: LLM4Robot-Bench: How Far Can GPT-6 Astra Go in Robotic Manipulation? A Hierarchical, Paired Sim-Real Benchmark
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Haibao Yu, Jiaqi Meng, Zijian Zhang, Bowen Jing, Lei Yang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The LLM4Robot-Bench evaluates GPT-6 Astra's robotic manipulation across 16 tasks, revealing significant performance declines with increasing interaction complexity in both simulated and real environments.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: We introduce LLM4Robot-Bench, a hierarchical, paired Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper introduces an action-conditioned latent foresight model that enhances humanoid loco-manipulation by evaluating command sequences for improved execution success rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Xinge Peng, Zhen Fang, Ruibing Wang, Yongxuan Lv, Haodong Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: ExeWorldBench is a novel benchmark for evaluating code-based 3D world modeling, integrating world understanding and executable realization across three progressively challenging tasks.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3D Gaussian World State
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Sicheng Yu, Liu Liu, Xinjie Wang, Xinjiang Wang, Taojun Ding
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: GSExplorer introduces a persistent 3D Gaussian world state for interactive world generation, enhancing scene consistency and camera control through a novel generation-reconstruction framework.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging as target-view guidance becomes incomplete and inconsistencies accumulate across repeated scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a condition-driven video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where inconsistency filtering prevents conflicting content from corrupting the scene and cross-chunk bundle adjustment improves spatial alignment across generation steps. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, with strong camera control and consistency across both settings, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency, demonstrating the value of maintaining a reliable 3D world state for continued exploration.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: UA-Depth: Uncertainty-Aware Depth Restoration for Material-Agnostic Object Manipulation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Rui Cao, Jia-Hui Pan, Yin Zhang, Qiwei Meng, Jiapeng Li
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: UA-Depth is an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that enhances robotic manipulation by improving depth accuracy for non-Lambertian objects through iterative co-refinement and uncertainty-gated features.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Robotic manipulation requires accurate metric depth, yet commodity RGB-D cameras often fail on non-Lambertian objects such as transparent, reflective, and translucent materials, producing holes, structured noise, and biased depth. Most restoration methods produce only a single depth map, treating noisy and reliable regions uniformly for downstream tasks while ignoring regional uncertainty. We present UA-Depth, an uncertainty-aware depth restoration framework that iteratively co-refines depth and pixel-wise uncertainty, and uses uncertainty-gated features to suppress unreliable cues for stable updates. To strengthen zero-shot behavior, UA-Depth leverages a frozen depth foundation model as a prior to initialize missing or unreliable depth, and applies two-stage MAD-weighted log-depth scale normalization to reduce outlier bias in relative-to-metric alignment. We introduce an eight-dataset zero-shot benchmark across diverse scenes, materials, and sensors. Across these benchmarks, UA-Depth achieves the best mean rank among representative baselines, with particularly strong gains on datasets dominated by transparent and reflective objects. Beyond depth metrics, we demonstrate downstream improvements in category-level 6D pose estimation and 6D grasp synthesis by exploiting the predicted uncertainty. \emph{Code, models, and data for training and evaluation will be released upon publication.}

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Peter Bell
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: This paper demonstrates that a compact omni-modal agent for audio-visual question answering can achieve similar or improved accuracy while reducing inference costs by 70% compared to specialized agents.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows via Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Zichuan Fu, Junjia Qi, Xian Wu, Wenlin Zhang, Yimin Deng
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows that optimizes complex task execution through semantic decomposition and iterative refinement based on execution feedback.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: PointPilot: Unified Robotic Manipulation via Object-Centric 3D Point Flow Prediction
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yihan Fang, Yuxin Tian, Ruixiang Wang, Zhanqi Zhang, Xing Hu
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: PointPilot is a unified robotic manipulation framework that predicts 3D point flow for task-focused objects, enabling zero-shot generalization across diverse embodiments and manipulation modes.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in robotics, calling for policies that address domain variations from multiple dimensions such as diverse embodiments, camera poses, and/or scene layouts. In order to approach this problem, we introduce PointPilot, a task-focused and 3D aligned manipulation framework built on a 3D space point-flow prediction. Rather than modeling the global scene, PointPilot only represents task-focused objects (robot grippers treated as objects), avoiding the prediction of potentially redundant scene parts unrelated to the manipulation tasks. Moreover, PointPilot aligns 3D spatial representation in one unified coordinate and supports closed-loop and fully automatic action execution across different manipulation modes from object point flow without a separately trained action expert, while existing works typically need an extra action head or are (semi-)automatic and single-arm mode specific. Given sensor observations and language instructions, our model jointly learns subtask planning, task-relevant object grounding, and 3D point flow prediction in an end-to-end way. By processing heterogeneous data in a shared 3D point flow space, PointPilot is able to absorb demonstrations from different embodiments. Extensive simulative and real world experiments validate our method. Notably, we demonstrate zero-shot embodiment generalization with PointPilot. A single trained policy can be deployed on previously unseen embodiments and successfully complete manipulation tasks without any additional fine-tuning.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: Positive Safety Margins from Artificial Potential Field Reward Augmentation for Size-Robust Obstacle Avoidance under Partial Observability
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Ziyi Hao
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper demonstrates that augmenting reinforcement learning rewards with an artificial potential field can significantly enhance obstacle avoidance safety margins under partial observability, achieving high success rates.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: SurgPace: Complexity-Aware Progressive Distillation for Surgical Multimodal Large Language Models
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Zhicheng He, Xiaohan Xing, Hongqiu Wang, Kun Yuan, Guankun Wang
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: SurgPace introduces a complexity-aware framework for progressive distillation of surgical multimodal large language models, enhancing efficiency and stability in training through tailored supervision strategies.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential in robotic surgery for question answering, scene understanding, and grounded assistance, but their high computational cost limits real clinical deployment. Knowledge distillation provides a practical way to build compact surgical MLLMs, yet direct distillation is not well suited to surgical data because surgical samples vary greatly in difficulty, visual ambiguity, and required clinical context, making uniform teacher-student transfer unstable. In addition, the role of supervision changes during training: early stages require stronger teacher guidance for multimodal alignment, while later stages rely more on task supervision for effective optimization. To address these challenges, we propose SurgPace, a complexity-aware continuous curriculum framework for progressive distillation of surgical vision-language models. SurgPace estimates sample complexity using predictive confidence and Lorentz geometric consistency, and uses the fused score to guide a continuous easy-to-hard training process. We further introduce hierarchical representation alignment, which aligns the student with the teacher at the feature, logit, and probability levels, while gradually shifting the training focus from teacher imitation to task supervision. This design separates sample-level curriculum from objective-level scheduling, leading to more stable and effective distillation. We evaluate SurgPace on Surg-396K, a benchmark built from four public surgical datasets and covering five dialogue paradigms. SurgPace consistently outperforms strong MLLM distillation baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness for building compact, memory-efficient surgical MLLMs with faster decoding under controlled benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hezhicheng2002/SurgPace.

Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.title: ROOF: Learning Humanoid Fall Recovery under Overhead Constraints
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.authors_text: Yidan Lu, Jiayuan Yu, Zongrui Cai, Jingwen Sun, Jinrui Han
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.summary: The paper presents a reinforcement learning approach for humanoid fall recovery under overhead constraints, achieving significant success in both simulation and real-world scenarios.
Language and Vision (LaVi) Lab.debug_abstract: A fallen humanoid beneath an overhead obstacle faces a coupled recovery problem. It must create clearance while organizing support for a stable rise, since attempting to stand before making room can further increase obstruction. We introduce a reinforcement learning method with contact-supported geometric escape guidance, which rewards incremental reduction of robot-obstacle overlap without prescribing an escape path.
