SG-CoR combines dynamics-aware multi-robot frame sampling, spectral- and geometric-guided view fusion, and geometry- and motion-informed prompt distillation, enabling the model to benefit from privileged robot-pose supervision during training while requiring only egocentric videos at test time. Across 22 MLLM baselines, SG-CoR consistently improves cooperative reasoning, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned baseline by +3.87% on Habitat and +7.12% on iGibson. It also shows stronger generalization to unseen team sizes and real-world robot tests. Code can be found at https://github.com/KPeng9510/seeing-together.git.

机器人系统实验室 (RSL).title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).authors_text: Zirui Wu, Chen Guo, Tianjian Jiang, Zeren Jiang, Zeming Li
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).summary: The P$^{3}$-WAM model integrates 3D perception, action prediction, and planning for egocentric dexterous manipulation, outperforming specialized methods in various tasks through unified training.
机器人系统实验室 (RSL).debug_abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Project Page: https://p3-wam.pages.dev/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learn-To-Propagate: Distributionally Robust Motion Planning for Nonlinear Uncertain Systems
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper introduces L2P-DR-Forest, a distributionally-robust motion planning algorithm for nonlinear stochastic systems that ensures safety and correctness despite uncertain distributions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Swim2Real: Vision-Language Models for Simulator Calibration of a Soft Robotic Fish
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Kevin Qiu, Kyle Liam Walker, Mike Yan Michelis, Marek Cygan, Josie Hughes
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: Swim2Real employs a vision-language model to effectively calibrate a soft robotic fish simulator, significantly reducing error in swimming simulations compared to random and permuted directions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Calibrating a soft aquatic robot simulator requires matching coupled deformation and propulsion from limited pool recordings. Swim2Real uses a vision-language model (VLM) to compare real and simulated swimming videos and propose updates to 16 simulator parameters. A backtracking line search tests each direction and accepts updates that reduce marker error. To test whether the proposals carry useful directions, we compare them with random and signed-permuted directions under the same line search and simulator budget. In an independent, preregistered fifty-seed replication, Swim2Real reduces the mean best-so-far error over 40 simulator evaluations by 63.4 mm against random directions and 53.2 mm against permuted directions. Both paired comparisons pass Holm correction ($p<10^{-5}$), conditional on run completion. A 24-seed experiment with a second VLM supports the same direction effect. Backtracking averages 16.1 VLM proposals per run versus 39 for Vid2Sid, which attains lower error at the same simulator budget. Ten hardware trials demonstrate open-loop execution of simulator-generated motor commands. Project page and videos: https://swim2real.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Benchmarking Real-World Robotic Manipulation through Stochastic Challenges
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Elias Gläßer, Gülhan Şikaroğlu, Pavlo Kupyn, Marc Pollefeys, Zuria Bauer
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper introduces stochastic challenges for benchmarking robotic manipulation, enabling reproducible comparisons across platforms in real-world environments through randomized task samples.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Soft Robotic Dynamics with Active Exploration
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Hehui Zheng, Bhavya Sukhija, Chenhao Li, Klemens Iten, Andreas Krause
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents an uncertainty-aware active exploration framework that enhances dynamics modeling of soft robots, achieving superior performance in diverse tasks and conditions.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Soft robots offer adaptability and safety in unstructured environments, yet their compliant, high-dimensional, and nonlinear dynamics make modeling for control difficult. Existing data-driven approaches often fail to generalize, constrained by narrowly focused task demonstrations or inefficient random exploration. We introduce an uncertainty-aware active exploration framework that autonomously learns task-agnostic and generalizable dynamics models of soft robotic systems. We evaluate this framework on three simulated platforms---a continuum arm, an articulated fish in fluid, and a musculoskeletal leg---and on a real-world pneumatically actuated continuum arm. Compared with random exploration and task-specific baseline, our method achieves higher modeling accuracy by actively collecting informative data. This improved model quality yields higher returns in zero-shot control on unseen tasks and robust performance under sensing noise, actuation delays, and material nonlinearities. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-driven active exploration enables data-efficient dynamics learning across soft robotic morphologies, supporting autonomous and adaptable control for compliant robots.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Dynamic Shape Control of Soft Trunk Robots
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Hehui Zheng, Marc Stampanoni, Roshan S. Kaundinya, Ronan Hinchet, George Haller
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents an aSSM-based model predictive control method for dynamic shape regulation in soft trunk robots, significantly outperforming linear approaches in practical tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Controlling the shape profile of soft trunk robots extends their reach into complex regions of the workspace and enhances their use in practical applications. Recent advances in soft robot design have enabled soft trunk robots to achieve greater flexibility in conforming to complex shapes. Specifically, trunk robots whose geometries are designed as helicoids have been shown to enable extreme shape-changing capabilities. Their compliance makes them highly nonlinear, which in turn makes shape control difficult. On similar tendon-driven trunk robots, model-based controllers based on the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) have achieved high accuracy in closed-loop end-effector tracking. We extend this approach by learning an aSSM model of the full body of a trimmed-helicoid soft trunk robot from data and use this in a model predictive control (MPC) scheme to demonstrate a range of shape control tasks on hardware. On closed-loop dynamic shape regulation, our method outperforms the available linear baselines by a factor of 10. In human-in-the-loop interactive demos, our method completes section-by-section shaping and balances a tennis ball for over 25 seconds, while the linear baselines fall short. A model-free reinforcement learning policy trained for 12 hours on hardware fails on the same balancing task. These results establish aSSM-based MPC as a practical route to full-body shape control on real soft hardware.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf Römer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This study demonstrates that reinforcement learning can enhance generalist robot policies for simultaneous multi-task performance, improving adaptability and generalization beyond initial training tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: SNAP: Semantic Navigation Among Pedestrians
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jakob Wolfram, Pascal Roth, Fan Yang, Cesar Cadena, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents an RL navigation policy that integrates semantic terrain and dynamic obstacle avoidance for robots in crowded urban settings, outperforming existing methods.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Sparse Anchors for Visual Multi-Session Registration in Changing Environments
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yunus Talha Erzurumlu, Niklas Trekel, Saurabh Gupta, Nico Koltermann, Olga Vysotska
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a method for visual multi-session registration using sparse absolute pose anchors to achieve accurate trajectory alignment in changing environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Repeated robotic monitoring requires localization across visits to the same environment, even if the environment changes. Such changes can substantially reduce persistent visual content, and repetitive structures can lead to incorrect cross-session correspondences. In this paper, we address visual multi-session registration of a new data recording (the query session) to a previously reconstructed reference map. Under substantial visual and structural changes, cross-session localization may be possible only for parts of the trajectory. In our approach, we therefore rely on a sparse set of reliable absolute pose constraints and combine them with within-session relative-pose information to register the complete trajectory to the reference map. We first estimate absolute alignment hypotheses through visual place recognition, local feature matching, and geometric verification. We then use sequence consensus to reject hypotheses that are inconsistent with a common query-to-reference alignment and retain the remaining poses as absolute anchors. These anchors are refined through featuremetric alignment against a Gaussian feature field and combined with within-session relative-pose constraints in a robust pose-graph optimization. We evaluate our approach on 15 cross-session experiments from the challenging HILTI26 construction-site dataset, covering substantial scene changes and difficult-to-match environments. Our method achieves 94.4% recall within 1m and 100.0% within 5m, outperforming independent image localization, which peaks at 65.3% and 70.7%, respectively, as well as direct registration of independently reconstructed Structure-from-Motion geometry. Our results show that sparse, reliable absolute anchors can provide accurate and complete trajectory registration even when reliable cross-session correspondences are available only for part of the query session.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: WayTrace is a hierarchical navigation system that translates web-map directions into actionable commands for robots, enabling robust urban navigation despite GNSS inaccuracies.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: LocalNav: Distilling Frontier VLMs and Embodied RL for On-Device Object Goal Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Nicolas Baumann, Liam Boyle, Pu Deng, Edoardo Ghignone, Boyang Sun
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: LocalNav introduces a distillation strategy for lightweight Vision Language Models, enhancing on-device object goal navigation while significantly reducing latency and maintaining performance.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have emerged in the robotic domain as a powerful tool that enables environmental perception with language context, serving as a catalyst for open- vocabulary tasks like Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav). Yet, their computational footprint typically confines them to cloud execution, hindering low-latency inference with local deployment on resource-constrained robots. To address this challenge, we present a distillation strategy that aligns a lightweight, 4B- parameter local VLM to our spatial-semantic navigation interface via frontier model traces for edge execution on embedded GPU devices (e.g., Jetson Orin). While cloud models establish a baseline achieving 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on the HM3D OVON benchmark, zero-shot deployment of our proposed architecture with Qwen3.5-4B reaches only 25.97% SR. We demonstrate that distilling frontier reasoning traces and subsequent finetuning with Embodied Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (E- RLVR) obtains a 37.36% SR, substantially narrowing the gap to large cloud models. However, while deployable on memory- constrained devices, the model cannot compete with round-trip cloud inference time: we identify Token Generation (TG) as the main driver of latency and reduce it with Token Generation (TG)- regularized E-RLVR. The combined method reduces latency by 69.29% and retains a SR of 35.53%. Combined with quantization, this joint strategy yields a cumulative 80.21% reduction in overall inference latency without significantly sacrificing performance, presenting a viable paradigm for local, low-latency VLM execu- tion on mobile robots.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Agile Humanoid Dodgeball with Onboard Monocular Vision
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Feng Tian, Yulin An, Chenhao Li, Matthias Heyrman, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents an integrated system for humanoid robots to effectively dodge balls using onboard monocular vision, achieving high success rates in dynamic environments.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Humanoid robots operating in shared, dynamic environments must respond to rapidly approaching objects while maintaining balance. We study dodgeball as a controlled test of this capability, coupling visual threat assessment with whole-body evasion, recovery, and target reacquisition. We develop a system that integrates onboard monocular perception, temporal ball-state and threat-flag estimation, and learned whole-body control. A ball detector supplies bounding-box histories, and a temporal estimator predicts relative ball position and a binary threat flag. Separate dodge/recovery and search/track policies share this interface and are composed to support repeated encounters. A three-stage curriculum first trains control with privileged ball states, then starts estimator supervision from stable policy rollouts, and finally replaces the actor's privileged inputs with estimator outputs. Analytic projection and perception randomization provide detector-like training observations without image rendering. Across approach-angle bins in controlled simulation, dodge success ranges from 97.8--100.0% for 5.0 m launches at 6 m/s to 33.2--40.8% for 2.5 m launches at 10 m/s, with 1000 throws per speed--distance condition. On a physical Unitree G1, controlled single-throw success exceeds 85% over more than 15 trials. A hardware sequence demonstrates full-azimuth target reacquisition followed by another dodge. These results demonstrate an integrated onboard-monocular-vision system under highly dynamic motions.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: GoalDex: Learning Image-Goal-Conditioned Policies for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Arjun Bhardwaj, Mayank Mittal, Maximum Wilder-Smith, Vaishakh Patil, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: GoalDex introduces an end-to-end framework for dexterous in-hand manipulation that learns policies from RGB inputs without pose estimation, outperforming traditional methods.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation is commonly formulated around explicit object pose estimation, yet reliable pose tracking is challenging under severe hand-object occlusions and often requires object-specific supervision. This dependence creates a bottleneck between perception and control that can limit robustness and scalability. We present an end-to-end visuomotor framework for dexterous in-hand reorientation that operates on RGB observations and proprioception without intermediate pose estimation. Our approach jointly learns visual representations and control policies through behavior distillation from privileged state teachers and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. Furthermore, we introduce image-goal-conditioned reorientation, allowing desired object configurations to be specified directly through images rather than canonical pose representations. We evaluate our approach across a diverse set of object geometries and instances in simulation, where it consistently outperforms pose-based methods and policies built on pretrained visual encoders. Finally, we demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer of a single image-goal-conditioned policy across five real-world objects, showing that accurate dexterous reorientation can be achieved without explicit pose estimation. For videos and code release, please refer to the project website: https://rffr.leggedrobotics.com/works/goaldex/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Closing the Dynamics Gap through Self-Directed Robotic Interaction
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Xilun Zhang, Liam Achenbach, Luis Pabon, Matthew Foutter, Marco Pavone
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: CUE is an agentic system that autonomously interacts with its environment to accurately identify physical parameters, significantly reducing simulation errors in contact-rich dynamics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Agentic Real2Sim2Real systems can reconstruct a scene in simulation from camera observations, but contact-rich dynamics such as friction and restitution cannot be observed without interaction. We call this the dynamics gap and present CUE, an agentic system that closes it by interacting with the environment itself. Given only a high-level instruction and no resets, the agent builds its own perception, identifies physical parameters, and targets interactions where its simulation is least accurate. On billiards, CUE reduces held-out ball-position error by 72% relative to the strongest baseline across 25 hidden-physics conditions in simulation, and we further deploy it on a real pool table. More details can be found on the project website: https://cue-dynamics.github.io/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jiaheng Xiao, Jiangtao Han, Jiachen Wang, Honghai Li, Lijun Sun
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: AgenticMobility is an open-source platform enabling the study of multi-AI-agent interactions in urban mobility dynamics, facilitating experiments on adaptation and policy impacts.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback. In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes. The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning to Build: Autonomous Robotic Assembly of Stable Structures Without Predefined Plans
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jingwen Wang, Johannes Kirschner, Paul Rolland, Luis Salamanca, Stefana Parascho
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework enabling autonomous robots to construct stable structures adaptively, without predefined plans, using targets and obstacles.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: This paper presents a novel autonomous robotic assembly framework for constructing stable structures without relying on predefined architectural blueprints. Instead of following fixed plans, construction tasks are defined through targets and obstacles, allowing the system to adapt more flexibly to environmental uncertainty and variations during the building process. A reinforcement learning (RL) policy, trained using deep Q-learning with successor features, serves as the decision-making component. As a proof of concept, we evaluate the approach on a benchmark of 15 2D robotic assembly tasks of discrete block construction. Experiments using a real-world closed-loop robotic setup demonstrate the feasibility of the method and its ability to handle construction noise. The results suggest that our framework offers a promising direction for more adaptable and robust robotic construction in real-world environments.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Antonio Terpin, Francesco Banelli, Alan Bonomi, Raffaello D'Andrea
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The ART of PIV automates the particle image velocimetry pipeline selection, enhancing accuracy and speed for real-time flow control by reducing errors and improving performance.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Contact-based optimization for collision-free motion planning for a million robots
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Jan Kamm, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents a contact-based optimization algorithm, SCI, enabling efficient collision-free motion planning for up to one million robots by leveraging contact dynamics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Multi-agent robotic systems have attracted growing interest in recent years, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. At the planning level, robot motion is often modeled using double-integrator dynamics (with low-level controllers handling the physical dynamics during execution) with a minimum-energy objective subject to collision-avoidance constraints and limits on position, velocity, and acceleration. The complexity of the problem resides in the constraints, which couple the trajectories and make the optimization problem nonconvex. Existing numerical approaches typically discretize and optimize entire trajectories, which becomes expensive for large fleets. We exploit the structure of optimal trajectories by organizing optimization around contacts, at which robots reach the minimum allowed separation. We formulate a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstruct trajectories analytically between contacts. Our algorithm, sequential contact insertion (SCI), starts from unconstrained trajectories, inserts contacts at separation violations, and jointly adjusts their times and states. Numerical experiments demonstrate planning for one million robots in minutes and thousands of robots in fractions of a second. On problems feasible for a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline, SCI achieves median speedups of several orders of magnitude at matching solution accuracy.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Rethinking Asymmetry in Self-Supervised 3D Geometry Learning
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Gyeongjin Kang, Freeman Cheng, Botao Ye, Weijie Lyu, Ming-Hsuan Yang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper proposes a novel self-supervised 3D geometry learning approach that enhances depth and pose estimation by imposing asymmetry in the 3D representation space rather than the input space.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Self-supervised learning relies on asymmetry between what a model observes and what it must explain. Recent methods learn 3D geometry from unposed images by predicting cameras and scene structure, then rendering held-out views. To avoid trivial solutions, they impose this asymmetry in the input space, restricting how views interact through separate branches or masked attention. We revisit this design with geometric accuracy, rather than rendering quality, as the main objective. When a held-out view lies between context views, the context already constrains the geometry it observes. We therefore impose the asymmetry in the 3D representation space, excluding held-out views only from the reconstructed scene while a shared backbone uses all views for correspondence. This improves depth and pose estimation over input-space designs. We further exploit view density: sparse and dense observations depict the same scene but provide different amounts of correspondence. Aligning sparse-context features with dense-context features supplies a geometric training signal alongside rendering, without a pretrained geometric teacher. We additionally align features with a frozen vision foundation model, which brings further gains. None of these signals requires geometric annotation, and the resulting model improves geometry estimation over prior self-supervised methods. Controlled experiments isolate the contribution of each component, and self-supervised pretraining also improves subsequent supervised training.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Rapid co-design of Buoyancy-assisted robots for Challenging Locomotion using Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Ankit Sinha, Nitish Sontakke, Dennis Hong, Yusuke Tanaka, Sehoon Ha
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists (GES), a framework that optimizes buoyancy-assisted robot designs and control, significantly improving performance and reducing co-design time.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Designing high-performance legged robots requires jointly optimizing morphology and control. Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) enables learning complex controllers during co-design, but repeatedly training policies across candidate morphologies makes design optimization computationally expensive. Existing approaches can amortize policy learning across morphologies, but a single shared policy tends to converge toward one control strategy regardless of morphology, which we refer to as behavioral diversity collapse. We introduce Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists (GES), an RL-based co-design framework that maintains a population of specialist policies whose design-space territories evolve according to their relative control performance. We evaluate GES on the Buoyancy-Assisted Light Legged Unit (BALLU) robot for obstacle traversal and ramp walking over design spaces of up to four dimensions. GES achieves higher best design performance than Monolithic and Mixture-of-Experts baselines, with gains of 5.0-9.0 cm in obstacle height and 10.0-12.7 points in ramp grade. For the same 200 design-optimization evaluations, GES reduces wall-clock co-design time by 67.4% compared with retraining a policy for every candidate. Finally, teleoperated hardware experiments evaluate the optimized BALLU morphology, which traverses obstacles of up to 24 cm, compared with 8 cm on the original design.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Adam Deryło, Alexey Gavryushin, Daniel Cremers, Marc Pollefeys, Xi Wang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: EgoContact is a large-scale egocentric dataset that evaluates manipulation priors by predicting contact points, revealing current methods' limitations and improving grasp success in robotics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: EgoHTR: Egocentric 4D Demonstrations of Human Terrain Traversal
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Alex Brandes, Haig Conti Georges Sajelian, Manthan Patel, Dominik Hollidt, Chenhao Li
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The EgoHTR dataset enhances humanoid robot training by providing 4D human motion sequences in complex terrains, enabling improved locomotion policies and context-aware navigation.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Deploying humanoid robots in unstructured terrain remains an open problem. While classic reinforcement learning struggles with the sheer complexity of real-world interactions, more promising methods leveraging human priors remain limited to models lacking contextual awareness. The restricted motion synthesis is a direct consequence of existing dataset pipelines failing to capture human-scene sequences in challenging environments. To bridge this gap between humanoid learning and scene reconstruction, we introduce the Egocentric Human-Terrain Reconstruction (EgoHTR) dataset. We develop and open-source a reconstruction pipeline capturing 55 scene-aligned 4D human motion sequences in diverse, complex environments using a multi-sensor setup of egocentric wearables and a portable 3D scanner. The resulting dataset comprises over 150k frames, which we evaluate against motion-capture ground truth, demonstrating state-of-the-art accuracy and establishing a rigorous benchmark for human motion analysis and synthesis. Further, we leverage this data to train perceptive locomotion policies, demonstrating hardware deployment on a Unitree G1 for reconstructed reference motions. Our pipeline enables community-driven dataset extensions and factors the problem to help researchers build foundational, context-aware robots that reliably traverse uneven terrain.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschläger, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a phase-conditioned policy optimization method for training robots in complex loco-manipulation tasks across diverse hardware, enhancing efficiency and adaptability.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Compatibility and future-proof testing for multi-agent systems
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yueshan Li, Lorenzo Fiaschi, Andrea Censi, Emilio Frazzoli
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper proposes a bi-level structure for ensuring compatibility and future-proofness in independently developed autonomous agents through seed agents and independent testing, avoiding centralized design constraints.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Independently developed autonomous agents, such as autonomous vehicles, must guarantee joint compatibility, such as safety and task-completion requirements, when they operate in a shared environment. Existing methods require a centrally designed specification, or interaction mechanism before any agent is deployed. However, such centralized design is unrealistic when agent designs are confidential to their developers, and it is not flexible enough to accommodate future agent designs. We study a bi-level structure in which a regulator coordinates developers by publishing seed agents, and each developer independently tests its agent to ensure that it is compatible with every seed-compatible agent, a property we call future-proofness. Under this structure, joint compatibility is guaranteed for any agents that are designed and tested independently, without any coordination with each other. In this work, we first formulate compatibility for general multi-agent systems and show why it is not trivially implied by seed-compatibility. We then characterize the future-proof agents as the closure of the seed and show that this closure is monotone in the seed. Finally, we study a class of executable tests that involve interaction with the seed alone, and we ask to what extent such tests can distinguish the future-proof agents.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: FTP-1: A Generalist Foundation Tactile Policy Across Tactile Sensors for Contact-Rich Manipulation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Chengbo Yuan, Zicheng Zhang, Mingjie Zhou, Wendi Chen, Yi Wang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: FTP-1 is a pioneering generalist tactile policy that enables transferable manipulation skills across diverse sensors, improving performance in contact-rich tasks by significant margins.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Despite the success of vision-based generalist robotic policies, existing tactile-based policies remain tied to fixed embodiments and sensor setups. This is because tactile signals are highly heterogeneous across hardware, making cross-sensor generalization difficult. We present FTP-1,the first generalist foundation tactile policy pretrained to acquire transferable tactile manipulation abilities across diverse sensors and embodiments. FTP-1 supports varied tactile inputs, including image-, array-, and state-based signals, by using heterogeneous encoders to project them into unified morphology-aware latent tokens that are jointly modeled by a shared tactile Transformer expert. Pretrained on around 3,000 hours of tactile manipulation data aggregated from 26 data sources, spanning human and robot demonstrations across 21 sensors, FTP-1 learns tactile skills that transfer beyond the sensors seen during pretraining. Across downstream finetuning experiments spanning 5 hardware configurations, FTP-1 improves contact-rich manipulation on seen sensor setups by +17.2% and, surprisingly, transfers to two previously unseen tactile-sensor setups, achieving a +31% gain in success rate. FTP-1 establishes the first unified foundation baseline for tactile manipulation, providing future tactile policies with a shared model-level starting point. Pretrained models, datasets, training code and more visualization at https://ftp1-policy.github.io.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: From Frames to Temporal Graphs: In-Context Egocentric Action Recognition with Vision-Language Models
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Bessie Dominguez-Dager, Francisco Gomez-Donoso, Miguel Cazorla, Marc Pollefeys, Daniel Barath
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a method for egocentric action recognition by transforming videos into Temporal Action Graphs, enhancing performance of Vision-Language Models through symbolic reasoning.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Action reasoning in egocentric video requires capturing fine-grained transitions of hand-object interactions, a task where general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) often struggle when operating directly on raw pixels. We propose to decouple visual perception from symbolic reasoning by converting videos into Temporal Action Graphs. In a multi-stage prompting pipeline, we first generate dense natural language narratives over short temporal windows as a semantic bottleneck, then formalize them into structured, open-vocabulary graph representations. On the EGTEA and Epic-Kitchens-100 datasets, the symbolic representation unlocks efficient in-context learning: few-shot graph demonstrations yield substantial accuracy gains over zero-shot frame-based inference. Even in the zero-shot setting, graph-based reasoning remains competitive with pixel-based inference despite potential pretraining contamination favoring the latter. Across 11 open-weight VLMs from 6 model families ranging from 2B to 235B parameters, our findings indicate that current VLMs are more effective as symbolic reasoners than as direct visual observers. By projecting video into the language domain, we provide a scalable, fine-tuning-free alternative to end-to-end approaches that better leverages these models' latent reasoning strengths. The code will be made public.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Thomas Landeg, Thierry Tambe
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper presents Backtrack, a lightweight recovery mechanism for frozen Vision-Language-Action models that enhances failure detection and reduces failure rates by 19-48% without retraining.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Philipp Lindenberger, Paul-Edouard Sarlin, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: FlexGlue is a neural network that efficiently performs asymmetric sparse-to-dense feature matching and disambiguation, enhancing accuracy and speed in visual correspondence tasks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Junzhe He, Kehan Wen, Chong Zhang, Clemens Schwarke, Zewei Zhang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a novel framework combining attention-based contact planning and reinforcement learning to enhance humanoid mobility over complex terrains through adaptive whole-body coordination.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body-environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: MeSS: City Mesh-Guided Outdoor Scene Generation with Cross-View Consistent Diffusion
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Xuyang Chen, Zhijun Zhai, Kaixuan Zhou, Zengmao Wang, Jianan He
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: MeSS introduces a method for generating high-quality outdoor scenes using city mesh models and enhanced image diffusion techniques to ensure geometric consistency and style transfer.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Mesh models have become increasingly accessible for numerous cities; however, the lack of realistic textures restricts their application in virtual urban navigation and autonomous driving. To address this, this paper proposes MeSS (Meshbased Scene Synthesis) for generating high-quality, styleconsistent outdoor scenes with city mesh models serving as the geometric prior. While image and video diffusion models can leverage spatial layouts (such as depth maps or HD maps) as control conditions to generate street-level perspective views, they are not directly applicable to 3D scene generation. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing consistent view sequences that depict scenes but often struggle to adhere to predefined camera paths or align accurately with rendered control videos. In contrast, image diffusion models, though unable to guarantee cross-view visual consistency, can produce more geometry-aligned results when combined with ControlNet. Building on this insight, our approach enhances image diffusion models by improving cross-view consistency. The pipeline comprises three key stages: first, we generate geometrically consistent sparse views using Cascaded Outpainting ControlNets; second, we propagate denser intermediate views via a component dubbed AGInpaint; and third, we globally eliminate visual inconsistencies (e.g., varying exposure) using the GCAlign module. Concurrently with generation, a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene is reconstructed by initializing Gaussian balls on the mesh surface. Our method outperforms existing approaches in both geometric alignment and generation quality. Once synthesized, the scene can be rendered in diverse styles through relighting and style transfer techniques. project page: https://albertchen98.github.io/mess/

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: No Pose, No Problem in 4D: Feed-Forward Dynamic Gaussians from Unposed Multi-View Videos
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Matteo Balice, Yanik Kunzi, Chenyangguang Zhang, Matteo Matteucci, Marc Pollefeys
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: NoPo4D is a novel feed-forward system for dynamic 3D scene reconstruction from unposed multi-view videos, outperforming existing methods in speed and accuracy.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D gaussian splatting methods have made dramatic progress on individual aspects of 3D scene reconstruction, but no existing method jointly addresses dynamic content, multi-view input, and unknown camera poses in a single feed-forward pass. Methods that handle dynamics either require accurate camera poses or accept only monocular input; pose-free multi-view methods address only static scenes; and per-scene optimization methods bridge some of these gaps but at minutes-to-hours cost per scene. We introduce NoPo4D, the first feed-forward system that addresses this empty quadrant. Building on a pretrained geometry backbone and recent 4D Gaussian frameworks, NoPo4D introduces a velocity decomposition that splits Gaussian motion into per-pixel image-plane shifts and depth changes, allowing direct supervision from pseudo ground-truth optical flow on the 2D component. This sidesteps both the differentiable rendering that couples prior posed methods to pose accuracy and the 3D motion ground truth that prior pose-free methods require. The system is rounded out by a bidirectional motion encoder for cross-view and cross-frame feature aggregation, and view-dependent opacity that mitigates cross-view and cross-timestep Gaussian misalignments. On four multi-view dynamic benchmarks, NoPo4D consistently outperforms prior feed-forward baselines, and with an optional post-optimization stage surpasses per-scene optimization methods, while running orders of magnitude faster.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Can AI Co-Design Structures? An AI Agent for Early-Stage Structural Design
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Ricardo Maia Avelino, Mennatallah El-Assady, Tom Van Mele, Philippe Block
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a proof-of-concept AI agent for early-stage structural design that translates natural language prompts into editable, graph-based structural models via a COMPAS API.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Recent advances in large language models and agentic workflows offer a new paradigm to early-stage structural design translating design intent into structural models. Although text-to-3D approaches have demonstrated that natural language can be used to produce visual, mesh-based geometric models, structural design requires domain-specific geometric arrangements and semantically rich data types. This paper introduces a proof-of-concept workflow for prompt-to-structure generation using an AI agent connected to a COMPAS-based structural modelling API through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Through controlled modelling operations, the agent creates and modifies a graph-based structural data model composed of explicit building elements. The resulting artifacts can be inspected, modified, serialised, and further connected to downstream AEC workflows. The approach is demonstrated through selected prompt-to-structure examples and by progressive and editable design sequences that resemble typical iterative structural design workflows. The results are preliminary, but demonstrate the possibility of combining natural language, agentic workflows, and domain-specific structural data structures as a first step toward AI-assisted structural co-design.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R) transforms a single human RGB video into thousands of robot demonstrations by semantically aligning objects, enhancing robot learning efficiency.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: LitePT: Lighter Yet Stronger Point Transformer
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Yuanwen Yue, Damien Robert, Jianyuan Wang, Sunghwan Hong, Jan Dirk Wegner
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: LitePT optimizes 3D point cloud processing by combining early convolution layers for geometry and deep attention layers for semantics, achieving significant efficiency improvements.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Modern neural architectures for 3D point cloud processing contain both convolutional layers and attention blocks, but the best way to assemble them remains unclear. We analyse the role of different computational blocks in 3D point cloud networks and find an intuitive behaviour: convolution is adequate to extract low-level geometry at high-resolution in early layers, where attention is expensive without bringing any benefits; attention captures high-level semantics and context in low-resolution, deep layers more efficiently, where convolution inflates the parameter count. Guided by this design principle, we propose a new, improved 3D point cloud backbone that employs convolutions in early stages and switches to attention for deeper layers. To avoid the loss of spatial layout information when discarding redundant convolution layers, we introduce a novel, parameter-free 3D positional encoding, PointROPE. The resulting LitePT model has $3.6\times$ fewer parameters, runs $2\times$ faster, and uses $2\times$ less memory than the state-of-the-art Point Transformer V3, but nonetheless matches or outperforms it on a range of tasks and datasets. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/prs-eth/LitePT.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Jumping in Lunar Gravity
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Levin Müller, Oliver Fischer, Marco Trentini, Yusuke Tanaka, Marco Hutter
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper presents a multistage reinforcement learning approach for a legged robot's effective point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity, demonstrating successful simulation and hardware execution.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone. We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible. In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot's body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to \SI{1}{s} during flight. Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot's hardware limits.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Samuel Foo Enze, Manthan Patel, Fan Yang, Linus Kramer, Pascal Roth
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: RangeNav is a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained on synthetic data, enhancing robot navigation in complex environments through improved representation learning and performance metrics.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: BA-T: An Iterative Transformer for Two-View Bundle Adjustment
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Ganlin Zhang, Weirong Chen, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: BA-T is an iterative Transformer that enhances 3D reconstruction accuracy and cross-view consistency using lightweight, BA-inspired structured updates instead of heavy decoder stacks.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Feed-forward models for 3D reconstruction have achieved strong performance using deep cross-view attention to exchange information across images. However, these approaches often depend on heavy decoder stacks and lack a structured mechanism for geometry refinement, resulting in poor multi-view consistency. We address this by drawing inspiration from classical bundle adjustment (BA), which can be viewed as an iterative information propagation process between poses and local geometry. Inspired by BA, we propose BA-T, an iterative Transformer that implements BA-style structured updates as a repeatable layer in implicit token space. Instead of relying on deep attention stacks, BA-T refines predictions based on latent residual by a single lightweight layer. Experiments demonstrate that BA-T progressively improves pose and reconstruction accuracy across iterations, achieves stronger cross-view consistency than conventional decoders, and matches or surpasses substantially larger models while using only 16% of their decoder parameters. BA-T provides a compact, efficient, and structural alternative to depth-heavy attention, enabling accurate 3D reconstruction within a lightweight architecture. Github repository: https://github.com/zhangganlin/BA-T.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Rodrigo Casado Noguerales, Dimitri von Rütte, Bernhard Schölkopf, Thomas Hofmann, Aran Raoufi
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: The paper introduces Binary Discrete Diffusion, enhancing discrete diffusion models for logic and planning tasks by representing uncertainty with candidate sets, outperforming traditional methods in challenging scenarios.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Actron3D: Learning Actionable Neural Functions from Videos for Transferable Robotic Manipulation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Anran Zhang, Hanzhi Chen, Yannick Burkhardt, Yao Zhong, Johannes Betz
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: Actron3D enables robots to learn transferable 6-DoF manipulation skills from uncalibrated RGB videos by utilizing a Neural Affordance Function for efficient knowledge transfer.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: We present Actron3D, a framework that enables robots to acquire transferable 6-DoF manipulation skills from monocular, uncalibrated, RGB-only human demonstration videos. Our key idea is to represent manipulation knowledge within a video as a continuous neural function over object space. At the core of Actron3D lies the Neural Affordance Function, which distills geometry, visual features, contact priors, and action flows from diverse demonstration videos into a compact 3D neural representation. During deployment, we adopt a hierarchical pipeline that retrieves the matched affordance function and transfers encoded manipulation knowledge to novel objects through coarse-to-fine differentiable optimization. Leveraging the continuous nature of Neural Affordance Function, the framework performs spatial queries over multimodal features to align demonstrations with observations and generates precise 6-DoF manipulation policy. Experiments in both simulation and the real-world demonstrate that Actron3D significantly outperforms prior methods, achieving a 14.9 percentage point improvement in the average success rate across 13 tasks while requiring only 2-3 demonstration videos per task.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Boxin Bu, Simon Boche, Haoming Zhang, Jaehyung Jung, Jiaxin Wei
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: GOFusion is a real-time mapping system that enhances autonomous robot navigation by integrating Gaussian primitives with local occupancy maps for improved spatial awareness and path planning.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: In this letter, we present GOFusion, a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial SLAM and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion. We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: MAGS-SLAM: Monocular Multi-Agent Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Geometrically and Photometrically Consistent Reconstruction
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Zhihao Cao, Qi Shao, Shuhao Zhai, Jing Zhang, Anh Nguyen
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: MAGS-SLAM introduces an RGB-only multi-agent 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM framework for collaborative scene reconstruction, achieving competitive performance without relying on depth sensors.
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.debug_abstract: Collaborative photorealistic 3D reconstruction from multiple agents enables rapid large-scale scene capture for virtual production and cooperative multi-robot exploration. While recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) SLAM algorithms can generate high-fidelity real-time mapping, most of the existing multi-agent Gaussian SLAM methods still rely on RGB-D sensors to obtain metric depth and simplify cross-agent alignment, limiting their deployment on low-cost or power-constrained robotic platforms, especially given the wider availability of RGB cameras. To address this challenge, we propose MAGS-SLAM, the first RGB-only multi-agent 3DGS SLAM framework for collaborative scene reconstruction. Each agent independently builds local monocular Gaussian submaps and transmits compact submap summaries rather than raw observations. To facilitate robust collaboration in the presence of monocular scale ambiguity, our framework integrates compact submap communication, geometry- and appearance-aware loop verification, and occupancy-aware Gaussian fusion, enabling coherent global reconstruction without active depth sensors. We further introduce ReplicaMultiagent Plus, a benchmark containing larger robot teams for evaluating collaborative Gaussian SLAM. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that MAGS-SLAM, using RGB images alone, achieves tracking accuracy, rendering quality, and geometric quality that are competitive with or superior to those of state-of-the-art RGB-D collaborative Gaussian SLAM methods.

Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.title: Seeing Together: Multi-Robot Cooperative Egocentric Spatial Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.authors_text: Kunyu Peng, Zhikun Zhou, Kailun Yang, Di Wen, Ruiping Liu
Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab (S.summary: This paper introduces CoopSR and EgoTeam for multi-robot cooperative spatial reasoning, presenting SG-CoR, an MLLM framework that enhances reasoning accuracy using synchronized egocentric videos.
