Supplementary materials, including code and field data, are available at https://sparolab.github.io/research/skid_slam/.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Xu Shen, Lingyong Yan, Shuaiqiang Wang, Jianmin Wu, Zhikai Chen
Quest for Intelligence.summary: The paper proposes Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD) to enhance long-horizon task execution by improving coordination, context management, and goal awareness among agents.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

Quest for Intelligence.title: 4D Reconstruction with Events & RGB
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Dulanga Weerakoon, Darshana Rathnayake, Van Minh Do, Hemanth Sabbella, Kaichen Zhou
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This study demonstrates that augmenting an RGB-only 4D reconstruction model with event camera data significantly enhances robustness against motion artifacts, particularly under high motion conditions.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes over time (4D reconstruction) from a single moving camera is central to robotics and AR/VR applications, yet state-of the-art feed-forward methods rely solely on RGB frames and therefore inherit the failure modes of conventional cameras, including motion blur and temporal aliasing under fast or non-uniform camera and object motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously at microsecond resolution, offering a complementary signal that is largely immune to these artifacts, but whether this modality can be incorporated into existing RGB based 4D reconstruction pipelines without a full architectural redesign remains an open question. In this preliminary study, we investigate a minimal extension: we augment Monst3R, an existing RGB-only 4D reconstruction model, with an additional event-camera input branch, leaving the rest of the architecture unchanged. Across 3 benchmark datasets, this simple RGB-event fusion reduces Abs Rel by 3.4% on average relative to the RGB-only Monst3R baseline, and a sensitivity analysis shows that the improvement grows with the magnitude of camera and object motion, with the largest gains observed under high object motion conditions where RGB-only reconstruction degrades most. These early results suggest that even a lightweight, non-invasive fusion of event data can meaningfully improve 4D reconstruction robustness, motivating a more thorough architectural investigation in future work.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Electric-Field Induction Motor with Discrete Circuit Elements and Improved Rotor Dynamics
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Alex S. Miller, Jeffrey H. Lang
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper presents a novel electric-field induction motor design utilizing discrete circuit elements on the rotor to enhance torque performance across various speeds.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Electric-field-based actuators and machines lead the design space at the nanoscale and in biological systems, while having the potential to be used in favorable macroscale applications which prioritize minimal mass, performance in a vacuum, or performance in high temperatures. Electric-field induction motors consist of a set of stator electrodes which induce opposite charges onto a movable rotor surface. In earlier work, rotor surfaces for electric-field induction motors have been made of single continuum materials, which are limited in possible resistivity, permittivity and circuitry characteristics. To enhance design freedom, we develop a rotor for electric-field-based machines which may be constructed out of discrete circuit components between a finite number of conductive vanes. Magnetic-field induction motors, which are common in machinery, often utilize ``deep bar'' rotors, consisting of conducting bars which decrease the rotor time constant with increasing frequency using the skin depth effect. We propose, analyze, design and demonstrate a macro-scale electric-field induction motor which uses circuitry on the rotor surface to emulate the ``deep bar'' design, providing improved torque over a wide range of speeds.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Perceiving and Predicting Dynamic Sports: Spatiotemporal Intelligence in Vision Models for Egocentric Tennis Video
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Tudor Braicu, Joseph DelPreto, Jared Boyer, Mónika Farsang, Maximilian Stölzle
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This study evaluates vision models' effectiveness in spatiotemporal tasks using an annotated egocentric tennis dataset, revealing insights into dynamic scene interpretation and future event prediction for agile robots.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Vasil Vasilev, Siddharth Nayak
Quest for Intelligence.summary: The study evaluates LeWorldModel's action sensitivity across scales, revealing significant discrepancies in action direction geometry and suggesting the need for scale-specific assessments.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median angles of about $36^\circ$ and $42^\circ$, respectively, at the smallest scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized Gram discrepancy by roughly 70\% on Reacher and 47\% on Cube. Geometry measured in pixels and embeddings varies more across scales than the chosen physical-state geometry. On held-out directions, environment Grams achieve median embedding response errors of 17\% and 28\%, compared with 26\% and 38\% for an isotropic reference with the same trace. LeWM's errors are higher at this scale. These findings support scale-specific evaluation of action sensitivity; its effect on control remains an open question.

Quest for Intelligence.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma
Quest for Intelligence.summary: EgoForesight enhances policy learning by integrating noisy egocentric actions and robot demonstrations, improving performance and scaling through reliability-aware action learning and outcome-informed representation transfer.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.

Quest for Intelligence.title: MixPT: Point Transformer with Interleaved Window and Global Attention
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Minkyun Seo, Hyungtae Lim, Jaesik Park
Quest for Intelligence.summary: MixPT introduces an interleaved attention mechanism combining window and global attention in point cloud transformers, achieving competitive accuracy with reduced latency across various benchmarks.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Point cloud transformers aim to capture detailed local geometry and relationships across a scene at a manageable computational cost. Two common approaches are window attention and global attention. They differ in how they enable scene-wide interaction, which refers to information exchange among tokens across a scene. Window attention reduces computational cost by restricting self-attention to groups of tokens called windows; in serialized designs, each window contains a fixed number of consecutive tokens from a spatially ordered sequence. Because each block only directly connects tokens within the same window, information exchange across windows relies on changes in window membership across blocks and hierarchical pooling. Global attention, in contrast, directly connects all tokens within a scene, but computing attention over all token pairs can be costly when the number of tokens is large. To balance computational cost and scene-wide interaction, we introduce MixPT, a point transformer that uses a mix of window and global attention blocks in an interleaved schedule, while retaining a single fixed serialization pattern for its window blocks. For scenes with a large number of tokens, MixPT applies global attention to spatially pooled tokens and returns residual updates to the original-resolution stream. Across indoor and outdoor benchmarks, MixPT achieves competitive accuracy with lower latency than representative window and global attention baselines. We further demonstrate the feasibility of scaling the attention stage in depth by repeating the interleaved pattern of window and global attention blocks.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Shashank A. Deshpande, Blake T. Edwards, Jonathan P. How
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper presents WarpWeaver, a decentralized real-time planner for multi-robot coordination that achieves near-optimal agreements through asynchronous negotiation, outperforming centralized and decentralized baselines in simulations and hardware tests.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Dual Exam: Controlled Evaluation of Multimodal Agents and World Models
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Zhefan Rao, Meng Chu, Xuan Zhang, Jingfan Chen, Guohao Cai
Quest for Intelligence.summary: The paper presents Dual Exam, a framework for evaluating the interaction between Multimodal Agents and World Models across various domains, revealing performance inconsistencies and challenges in reciprocal learning.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: World Models (WMs) can support Multimodal Agents (MAs) through simulated experience, while Agent trajectories can inform World Model refinement. Evaluating this interaction requires separate evidence about action selection and state evolution. We introduce Dual Exam, which tests Agents under fixed environment response mechanisms and World Models under fixed action interventions across physical, digital, social, and scientific domains. The Agent track compares 10 configurations on 1,088 items in 15 reporting categories. The World Model track contains 400 cases across eight scenarios; 15 configurations have full coverage and one covers six scenarios. GPT 6 Astra leads the case-weighted Agent Index at 31.3, and GPT-Image-2 leads the full-coverage WM Overall at 21.7. These scores use different tasks and metrics and are not directly comparable. A 150-case pilot of one coupled pairing records zero task successes and motivates component-level diagnosis. Results reveal uneven task performance and failures to preserve task-relevant state. Their value for predicting coupled success or sustained reciprocal learning remains to be established.

Quest for Intelligence.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu
Quest for Intelligence.summary: T-WLA integrates visual memory with tactile feedback to enhance contact-rich manipulation, achieving significant improvements in hand-motion prediction and real-world task success rates.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper presents a method for force-aware manipulation using visual force prediction from a compliant gripper, eliminating the need for specialized force sensors during deployment.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

Quest for Intelligence.title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: William Huang, David Li, Xiang 'Anthony' Chen, Xun Qian, Nels Numan
Quest for Intelligence.summary: GenXR-Bench is a pioneering benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive XR development, assessing their performance across diverse tasks and identifying key failure areas.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

Quest for Intelligence.title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Carson Sobolewski, Anjali Parashar, Fei Chen, Yingke Li, Chuchu Fan
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper presents a factorized risk model for vision-language-action systems that estimates the benefits of removing visual corruptions, outperforming existing methods in failure attribution.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution. Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and $π_{0.5}$ in simulation and $π_{0.5}$-DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.

Quest for Intelligence.title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Jiushu Li, Haoran Wang, Yumeng Liu, Zhiyang Dou, Yuan Liu
Quest for Intelligence.summary: World2HOSI is a multi-expert framework that enhances long-horizon human-object-scene interaction generation by orchestrating existing models to produce diverse, high-quality interaction data.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Towards Autonomous Bricklaying Using Boston Dynamics Spot
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Karl-Johan Sorensen, Nico vom Hofe, Frank H. P. Fitzek
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper demonstrates an autonomous bricklaying system using a Boston Dynamics Spot robot, achieving high placement accuracy in varied environments through advanced navigation and localization techniques.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Mobile legged robots offer unique advantages for on-site construction, including the ability to traverse unstructured terrain, climb stairs, and operate independently between spatially separated work zones. This paper presents a proof-of-concept system for autonomous brick stacking using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. The system operates between a supply area and an assembly area, using AprilTag fiducials for localization and autowalk missions for navigation. Target brick positions and orientations are specified in CAD software and exported directly for robotic execution. We evaluate placement accuracy through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall comprising 14 wooden bricks. Results show mean translation errors below 10 mm and mean yaw errors below 1.5 degrees, while the overall RMSE across all runs is 27.72 mm (translation) and 2.06 degrees (rotation). The system was also tested outdoors with stairs between the two areas. The workflow is modular and easily extendable to different wall geometries.

Quest for Intelligence.title: RoboEdit: Turning Human Manipulation Videos into Scalable Robot Experience
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Yaowei Guo, Zeng Tao, Yuxin Jiang, Yunuo Chen, Zhiyang Dou
Quest for Intelligence.summary: RoboEdit transforms human manipulation videos into scalable robot training data, creating a large dataset and enabling high-fidelity supervision for diverse robotic interactions.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Collecting robot hand-object interaction data is costly and embodiment-specific, yet abundant human-object videos remain unusable for robot training. We present RoboEdit, a human-to-robot video editing suite that transforms human manipulation videos into action-consistent, physically plausible robot videos with aligned 3D hand states. To enable scalable supervision, we introduce RoboEdit-ADC, an automatic pipeline that reconstructs and retargets 3D interactions from RGB videos across embodiments. This pipeline generates RoboEdit-14M, a large-scale dataset of 174K aligned video pairs (14M frames) spanning seven robot embodiments, diverse scenes, and interaction types. The core editing engine, RoboEdit-Trans, employs cross-embodiment adaptation modules to preserve temporal coherence while adapting appearance and motion. It further integrates a 3D Robot-State Decoder to recover per-frame hand states for structured motion supervision. Experiments show that RoboEdit achieves state-of-the-art editing quality and supports downstream robot control policies in real-world manipulation tasks. Ultimately, the RoboEdit suite unlocks the vast potential of unlabeled human videos, providing scalable, high-fidelity visual and 3D motion supervision for generalizable robot learning. Project webpage: https://roboedit.github.io/

Quest for Intelligence.title: OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Josef Biberstein, Sertac Karaman
Quest for Intelligence.summary: OrTeN introduces a neural inverse rendering approach for constructing digital terrain maps from line-scan satellite images, optimizing camera trajectory and surface reconstruction without structural priors.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Hyunwoo Ryu, Eric Ming Chen, Max Wilcoxson, Vincent Sitzmann
Quest for Intelligence.summary: The paper presents Mirror, a self-supervised model that learns video-to-action mappings through environmental interactions, achieving superior performance without expert data or rewards.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video-to-action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.

Quest for Intelligence.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
Quest for Intelligence.summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.

Quest for Intelligence.title: FracEvent: Event-Camera Simulation via Fractional-Relaxation Pixel Dynamics
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Langyi Chen, Chuanzhi Xu, Haoxian Zhou, Pengfei Ye, Ziyu Luo
Quest for Intelligence.summary: FracEvent is a novel event-camera simulator utilizing fractional-relaxation dynamics to enhance event generation accuracy and performance in vision tasks, outperforming existing methods.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Event cameras asynchronously report brightness changes with microsecond-level temporal resolution, but real event data remain difficult to collect at scale because specialized sensors, careful synchronization, and task-specific annotations are required. Event-camera simulation is therefore important to event-based vision tasks. Most practical simulators build on contrast-threshold event generation, some with additional filtering, stochastic noise, or calibrated sensor parameters. While effective, such formulations can simplify the temporal structure produced by a pixel's recent response history. We introduce FracEvent, a physics-inspired sensor-side simulator with compact fractional-relaxation voltage dynamics. Given a log-intensity trajectory, FracEvent combines fast and slow response modes, emits ON/OFF events by localizing threshold crossings on the continuous voltage trajectory, and updates the event reference while retaining the mode states. This retained state links residual response to later event timing. We evaluate FracEvent through direct event-stream comparison and downstream transfer on image reconstruction and optical flow estimation. Across multiple datasets, FracEvent achieves leading results on multiple metrics in both evaluations, showing its practical value for event-camera simulation. Project page: https://bonaparte233.github.io/FracEvent/

Quest for Intelligence.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Quest for Intelligence.summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

Quest for Intelligence.title: GROW$^2$: Grounding Which and Where for Robot Tool Use
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Yuhong Deng, Yuyao Liu, David Hsu
Quest for Intelligence.summary: GROW$^2$ enables robots to creatively use tools by hierarchically grounding object parts through semantic reasoning and geometric localization, outperforming existing methods in diverse tasks.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Can the robot use a plate to cut a cake if no knife is available? Tool use greatly expands robot capabilities, but to use tools creatively beyond their intended functions, the robot faces the challenge of $\textit{open-world affordance grounding}$: select an open-category object to act as a tool and localize its specific region of action. To this end, we introduce GROW$^2$ (GROunding Which and Where), which leverages object parts as a natural abstraction to split the grounding process hierarchically into semantic and geometric levels, thus bypassing the need for data-heavy, end-to-end training. Semantically, GROW$^2$ harnesses the commonsense reasoning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to parse a natural-language task instruction, select a suitable object as the tool, and identify task-relevant parts on the tool and the target object. Geometrically, vision foundation models then ground the selected parts into precise 3D regions from a single RGB-D image. Experiments on established benchmarks show that GROW$^2$ outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on affordance prediction benchmarks. Further, it achieves zero-shot generalization over open-category objects and outperforms baselines in both simulated and real-world robot tool use experiments.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Antonia Bronars, Younghyo Park, Kushal Kedia, Pulkit Agrawal
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper demonstrates that legged robots can achieve precise assembly tasks using only proprioceptive feedback from joint sensors, successfully transferring learned policies from simulation to real-world applications.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Foundation-Model-Driven 3D Scene Graphs for Mobile Manipulation
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper integrates foundation-model-driven 3D scene graphs into mobile manipulation, demonstrating their effectiveness for object detection, mapping, navigation, and task execution.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Florian Lercher, Karan Mahesh, Yujun Huang, Meshal Alharbi, Runyu Zhang
Quest for Intelligence.summary: The paper presents a framework for multi-agent motion planning using posetal games to ensure compliance with legal guidelines while allowing for private objectives and decentralized coordination.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

Quest for Intelligence.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
Quest for Intelligence.authors_text: Helena Merker, Nick Walker, Andreea Bobu
Quest for Intelligence.summary: This paper introduces a method for robots to ask targeted preference queries, enhancing reward learning by reducing human effort and improving feature focus through informed prior and explanations.
Quest for Intelligence.debug_abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Practical Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits via Fake Data Injection
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Qirun Zeng, Eric He, Richard Hoffmann, Xuchuang Wang, Jinhang Zuo
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: This paper introduces a practical adversarial attack model for stochastic bandits, employing limited fake data injection to mislead algorithms while minimizing attack costs.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Adversarial attacks on stochastic bandits have traditionally relied on some unrealistic assumptions, such as per-round reward manipulation and unbounded perturbations, limiting their relevance to real-world systems. We propose a more practical threat model, Fake Data Injection, which reflects realistic adversarial constraints: the attacker can inject only a limited number of bounded fake feedback samples into the learner's history, simulating legitimate interactions. We design effective attack strategies under this model, explicitly addressing both magnitude constraints (on reward values) and temporal constraints (on when and how often data can be injected). Our theoretical analysis shows that these attacks can mislead a class of bandit algorithms into selecting a target arm in nearly all rounds while incurring only sublinear attack cost. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our strategies, revealing vulnerabilities in stochastic bandit algorithms under practical adversarial scenarios.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Beyond Topology: A Morphological Symmetry Graph Representation for Locomotion Policy Learning
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Sizhe Wei, Xulin Chen, Fengze Xie, Garrett Ethan Katz, Zhenyu Gan
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The paper presents a morphological symmetry graph representation for locomotion policy learning, enhancing performance in articulated robots by integrating topology and symmetry in reinforcement learning.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled impressive locomotion skills on articulated robots, but common policy representations remain only weakly aligned with robot physics. Generic networks ignore kinematic structure, while graph-based policies encode connectivity without specifying how physical quantities transform across symmetric body parts. We introduce a morphological symmetry graph representation for locomotion policy learning, instantiated as MS-PPO with PPO on Go2 and MS-SAC with FastSAC on G1. Starting from the robot's topological graph, our representation explicitly incorporates the permutations and sign changes induced by morphological symmetry on observations and actions, yielding a graph actor with an equivariant action mean and an invariant critic. We evaluate the representation on Unitree Go2 command tracking and asymmetric joint-failure tasks, and on Unitree G1 29-DoF whole-body locomotion, including zero-shot sim-to-real deployment. Our approach achieves the lowest tracking errors in both simulation and hardware, and the highest mean simulation returns across all three joint-failure types on Go2 among the evaluated baselines. On Go2, MS-PPO uses only 34.6% of the parameters of the PPO baseline. These results support the effectiveness of jointly encoding topology and morphological symmetry across robot embodiments and learning frameworks.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: GeoWind2Plan: Mission-Time 3D Urban Wind Prediction for Energy-Efficient UAV Planning
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Shaoxiang Qin, Yucheng Zhao, Fuyuan Lyu, Di Zhou, Jiachen Yao
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: GeoWind2Plan is a rapid framework for 3D urban wind prediction that enhances energy-efficient UAV planning by utilizing localized geometry and neural operators, outperforming traditional CFD methods.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: In urban low-altitude flight, buildings reshape ambient wind into spatially varying 3D flow, making unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) energy depend on local wind exposure as well as path length. However, building-resolved wind is rarely available when a mission must be planned. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) produces high-fidelity urban flow fields, but each simulation is tied to a fixed inflow boundary condition and can take hours to days, which is incompatible with urban UAV missions that typically last minutes to tens of minutes. We present GeoWind2Plan, a geometry-to-wind-to-planning framework for mission-time 3D urban wind prediction and energy-efficient UAV planning. Given only a background wind vector, 3D building geometry, and a start-goal pair, GeoWind2Plan transforms the building geometry into a reference-wind frame, predicts mission-relevant 3D wind patches with a localized geometry-conditioned neural operator, stitches them into a local wind field, and optimizes a feasible 3D path and speed profile using a physically grounded UAV energy model. Rather than pursuing CFD-perfect reconstruction, GeoWind2Plan targets decision-useful wind prediction: trajectories are planned with predicted wind and evaluated under high-fidelity CFD wind. Across held-out urban domains, wind speeds, and mission wind-angle regimes, GeoWind2Plan performs corridor-localized wind inference in about 3 s, compared with roughly 8 h for CFD. Under CFD evaluation, trajectories planned with GeoWind2Plan reduce energy by 6.9%, 12.7%, and 4.5% in tailwind, headwind, and crosswind missions relative to wind-agnostic planning, recovering 87.9%, 85.7%, and 75.0% of CFD-reference savings. These results show that fast, corridor-localized 3D urban wind prediction can make wind-aware UAV energy planning practical at mission time. Code/dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/GeoWind2Plan/ . Demo: https://geowind2plan.com .

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Neural Integral Control Barrier Functions for Agile Collision Avoidance
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Dasari Raj Vamsi, Vrushabh Zinage, Efstathios Bakolas, Rohan Chandra
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: This paper introduces a data-driven approach to learn integral control barrier functions for agile collision avoidance, enhancing safety and performance in dynamic environments.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a standard way to keep a planner inside a safe set, but they assume control affine dynamics, a barrier function given in closed form, and a known nominal controller. Integral control barrier functions (ICBFs) remove the first assumption and absorb input constraints, yet they still assume a given nominal controller and a barrier function. In this work, we present an approach to learn all three from data, using neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the dynamics, imitation for the nominal controller, and supervised regression for the barrier function. The learned dynamics, nominal controller, and the barrier function are used to build the ICBF filter constraint analytically. Furthermore, the barrier is trained on viability rather than geometry, meaning that a state counts as safe only if some emergency maneuver can still avoid the constraint under the actuator limits, a correction that geometric labels miss entirely and that grows with speed. Actuator limits then enter the online program as hard bounds while the learned barrier rows may be relaxed, which keeps the program solvable at every state and the actuator limits exact, and we bound how far the input it returns can drift from the one the true models would give. On agile racing with a 6-D dynamic bicycle, the filter removes all 12 unsafe episodes from 200 held out layouts at an unchanged success rate and above 100 Hz on one CPU core, holds the input constraint on every episode of a benchmark where a jointly trained baseline holds it on 53.38%, and keeps that advantage under large errors in the plant friction.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Alexander Detkov, Dashiel Karish, Matthew Oleynikov, Matt Thomson
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The paper introduces benchmarks to evaluate knowledge integration in large language models, revealing that in-context information significantly enhances reasoning over pretrained knowledge.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: WildOS: Open-Vocabulary Object Search in the Wild
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Hardik Shah, Manthan Patel, Erica Tevere, Deegan Atha, Marcel Kaufmann
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: WildOS integrates safe geometric exploration with semantic visual reasoning for efficient long-range object search in unstructured environments, outperforming traditional navigation methods.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Autonomous navigation in complex, unstructured outdoor environments requires robots to operate over long ranges without prior maps and limited depth sensing. In such settings, relying solely on geometric frontiers for exploration is often insufficient. In such settings, the ability to reason semantically about where to go and what is safe to traverse is crucial for robust, efficient exploration. This work presents WildOS, a unified system for long-range, open-vocabulary object search that combines safe geometric exploration with semantic visual reasoning. WildOS builds a sparse navigation graph to maintain spatial memory, while utilizing a foundation-model-based vision module, ExploRFM, to score frontier nodes of the graph. ExploRFM simultaneously predicts traversability, visual frontiers, and object similarity in image space, enabling real-time, onboard semantic navigation tasks. The resulting vision-scored graph enables the robot to explore semantically meaningful directions while ensuring geometric safety. Furthermore, we introduce a particle-filter-based method for coarse localization of the open-vocabulary target query, that estimates candidate goal positions beyond the robot's immediate depth horizon, enabling effective planning toward distant goals. Extensive closed-loop field experiments across diverse off-road and urban terrains demonstrate that WildOS enables robust navigation, significantly outperforming purely geometric and purely vision-based baselines in both efficiency and autonomy. Our results highlight the potential of vision foundation models to drive open-world robotic behaviors that are both semantically informed and geometrically grounded. Project Page: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/wildos/

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: FORGE: Feasible Online Reduced-Order Reference Generation and Whole-Body Execution for Agile Humanoid Locomotion
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Adrian B. Ghansah, Yujin An, Jeeseop Kim, Soon-Jo Chung
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The paper introduces FORGE, a two-stage framework for agile humanoid locomotion that combines online reduced-order model reference generation with whole-body tracking control, achieving versatile movement capabilities.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: This paper presents a two-stage learning framework for versatile and agile humanoid locomotion that couples online reduced-order model (ROM) reference generation with whole-body tracking control. In the first stage, we train a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator using single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics. In the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. Learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified ROM space enables us to generate references over a broad command space and over multiple locomotion strategies using a single unified framework. We demonstrate the approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, achieving longitudinal velocities from -2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across the commands, all using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Explore Where It Matters: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Jacob Levy, Arthur Bouton, Tristan D. Hassler, Hari Nayar, David Fridovich-Keil
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: TERRA is an online adaptation framework that enhances rover mobility on challenging terrains by efficiently targeting exploration to correct model errors during deployment.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Embodied Learning of Reward for Musculoskeletal Control with Vision Language Models
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Saraswati Soedarmadji, Yunyue Wei, Chen Zhang, Yisong Yue, Yanan Sui
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The MoVLR framework utilizes vision-language models to iteratively explore and refine reward functions for musculoskeletal control, aligning high-level movement goals with effective motor strategies.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Discovering effective reward functions remains a fundamental challenge in motor control of high-dimensional musculoskeletal systems. While humans can describe movement goals explicitly such as "walking forward with an upright posture," the underlying control strategies that realize these goals are largely implicit, making it difficult to directly design rewards from high-level goals and natural language descriptions. We introduce Motion from Vision-Language Representation (MoVLR), a framework that leverages vision-language models (VLMs) to bridge the gap between goal specification and movement control. Rather than relying on handcrafted rewards, MoVLR iteratively explores the reward space through iterative interaction between control optimization and VLM feedback, aligning control policies with physically coordinated behaviors. Our approach transforms language and vision-based assessments into structured guidance for embodied learning, enabling the discovery and refinement of reward functions for high-dimensional musculoskeletal locomotion and manipulation. These results suggest that VLMs can effectively ground abstract motion descriptions in the implicit principles governing physiological motor control.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: OWLS: Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields for Zero-Shot Rover Navigation
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Chahyon Ku, Erica Tevere, Georgios Georgakis, Rudra Mukherjee, Bernadette Bucher
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: OWLS leverages open-vocabulary vision-language models to enable zero-shot rover navigation by scoring terrain traversability from camera images without requiring task-specific training or mapping.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Stella Kombo, Masih Haseli, Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala, Peter I. Renn, Morteza Gharib
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The paper presents a disturbance-aware Koopman Control framework for quadrotors that enhances real-time trajectory tracking by adapting to unmodeled aerodynamic disturbances during flight.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Michael Chen, Hong Chul Nam, Xi Deng, Anima Anandkumar
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The paper presents Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that effectively learns noise-aware value fields for efficient planning in uncertain environments, outperforming existing methods.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: Bio-inspired Thrust-Assisted Trotting on a legged-Aerial Robot via Real-Time QP-MPC
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Shreyansh Pitroda, Eric Sihite, Alireza Ramezani, Morteza Gharib
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: This paper details a QP-MPC controller for the thruster-assisted bipedal robot Harpy, enabling bio-inspired trotting by regulating ground forces and thrust vectoring.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: This paper presents the hardware implementation of a quadratic program-based controller on Harpy: thruster-assisted bipedal robot to perform thruster-assisted trotting. This is inspired by wing-assisted locomotion observed in birds such as the chukar partridge, which employ thrust vectoring to manipulate the ground reaction force. The proposed controller formulates the thruster-assisted spring-loaded inverted pendulum dynamics as a condensed QP-based model predictive control problem, enabling simultaneous regulation of ground contact force and active thrust vectoring at 500 Hz. A decoupled control architecture is used, where the robot's sagittal dynamics are controlled using QP-MPC while the frontal dynamics is regulated using a cascade orientation stabilization controller. Two experiments were conducted with different forward reference velocities of 0 m/s and 0.1 m/s. While the instantaneous velocity oscillates, the mean velocities can track their respective reference. Additionally, joint tracking error remains within 1 deg while tracking the desired leg length given by the leg trajectory controller and desired swing trajectory given by Raibert's heuristic. The QP-MPC problem is consistently solved with 0.18ms, which is well within the 2ms computation budget while satisfying the GRF friction cone constraint.

加州理工-机器人实验室.title: A Paired RGB-Sonar Dataset for Fish Monitoring with Consumer Sonar
加州理工-机器人实验室.authors_text: Mourad Derbedrosian, Michael Hobley, Pietro Perona
加州理工-机器人实验室.summary: The HaCKRS dataset pairs RGB video with consumer sonar recordings to enhance fish monitoring accessibility and support automated detection and tracking methods.
加州理工-机器人实验室.debug_abstract: Imaging sonar enables underwater observation in conditions where optical imaging is ineffective due to darkness and turbid water. However, imaging-sonar systems previously used for ecological monitoring have typically been expensive, limiting their accessibility. Consumer forward-looking sonar has the potential to make fish monitoring more accessible, but its noisy imagery makes annotation and the development of automated methods challenging. We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring.

具身智能多模态大模型中心.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Agent Distillation across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
具身智能多模态大模型中心.authors_text: Ziluowen Luo, Senzhang Wang, Chaozhuo Li, Jun Yin, Hao Yan
具身智能多模态大模型中心.summary: This paper presents a unified survey on Agent Distillation, emphasizing persistent knowledge transfer across models, artifacts, and harnesses to enhance agent capabilities and adaptability.
具身智能多模态大模型中心.debug_abstract: Knowledge distillation provides a teacher-student framework for transferring capabilities at reduced cost and has been widely studied for large language models (LLMs). As LLM-based agents move from response generation to sustained, closed-loop task solving, distillation expands beyond model parameters to knowledge retained in reusable resources and execution workflows. This shift from model-level to agent-level knowledge transfer supports efficient deployment, broader capability access, and continual self-evolution. However, existing surveys largely examine model distillation and agent system design separately, limiting comparison of transfer strategies across agent components. To bridge this gap, we formalize Agent Distillation as persistent knowledge transfer between teacher and student agents and present its first unified survey. Distinguishing experience used for transfer from knowledge retained for reuse, we develop a knowledge-substrate taxonomy based on where knowledge persists: models, artifacts, or harnesses. Building on this taxonomy, we analyze cross-substrate transfer paths and hybrid strategies. To assess the resulting capabilities, we review benchmarks and evaluation protocols for retention, causal attribution, and deployed utility without further teacher support. This survey provides a unified basis for studying agent knowledge transfer and developing efficient, adaptable, and self-evolving agents.

具身智能多模态大模型中心.title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
具身智能多模态大模型中心.authors_text: Fuhao Li, Wenxuan Song, Qizhou Huang, Ziyang Zhou, Jingbo Wang
具身智能多模态大模型中心.summary: The SLA model enhances robotic manipulation by integrating continual pre-training for spatial understanding, optimizing action prediction, and utilizing diverse datasets for improved 3D spatial alignment.
具身智能多模态大模型中心.debug_abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

具身智能多模态大模型中心.title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
具身智能多模态大模型中心.authors_text: Jintao Li, Zhiyong Cao, Baihua Xiao, Yu Bai, Börje F. Karlsson
具身智能多模态大模型中心.summary: EviSeek is a framework that enhances embodied question answering by explicitly linking evidence acquisition objectives to actions, improving accuracy and efficiency in information seeking.
具身智能多模态大模型中心.debug_abstract: Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit.
