These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.

上海科技大学.title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
上海科技大学.authors_text: Haoyang Luo, Junhao Qin, Jingyan Cao, Yi Huang, Guangjie Yang
上海科技大学.summary: InstAgent is a recursively self-improving operating system that enhances heterogeneous robot collaboration by organizing behaviors into agentic trees and utilizing shared memory for improved task execution.
上海科技大学.debug_abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.

上海科技大学.title: SceneReVis: A Self-Reflective Vision-Grounded Framework for 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis via Multi-Turn RL
上海科技大学.authors_text: Yang Zhao, Shizhao Sun, Meisheng Zhang, Yingdong Shi, Xubo Yang
上海科技大学.summary: SceneReVis introduces a self-reflective framework for 3D indoor scene synthesis that utilizes multi-turn reinforcement learning to resolve spatial conflicts and enhance generation fidelity.
上海科技大学.debug_abstract: Current one-pass 3D scene synthesis methods often suffer from spatial hallucinations, such as collisions, due to a lack of deliberative reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce SceneReVis, a vision-grounded self-reflection framework that employs an iterative "diagnose-and-act" loop to explicitly intercept and resolve spatial conflicts using multi-modal feedback. To support this step-wise paradigm, we construct SceneChain-12k, a large-scale dataset of causal construction trajectories derived through a novel reverse engineering pipeline. We further propose a two-stage training recipe that transitions from Supervised Fine-Tuning to Agentic Reinforcement Learning, evolving the model into an active spatial planner. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SceneReVis achieves state-of-the-art performance in high-fidelity generation and goal-oriented optimization, with improved transfer to underrepresented room categories in the dataset and promising potential for extension to out-of-distribution room types.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Rajpurkar Lab.title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Zilin Dai, Lehong Wang, Yi Yang, Xiang Fei
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: WireSeg-32K is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 images for wire instance segmentation, utilizing a co-simulation pipeline for realistic wire deformation and improving model performance in real-world applications.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shuyue Stella Li, Priyanka Kargupta, Haocheng Wang, Jinu Lee, Dean Light
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This paper analyzes cognitive elements in reasoning, revealing differences between human and LLM processes, and proposes a framework to enhance model reasoning accuracy through structured guidance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning and knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and apply it to 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, alongside 1,346 human think-aloud traces on a new, domain-agnostic dataset for human-model comparison. We find that models are able to deploy cognitive elements seen in human reasoning but differ in how they use them. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffolds successful reasoning topologies, improving the accuracy of the strongest models by 9.7 percentage points on ill-structured problems. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements but rarely targets self-awareness, whose use differs between human and model reasoning. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Haoyu Han, Jack Benarroch Jedlicki, Jiahui Lei, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: XM4D presents a certifiably optimal framework for 4D reconstruction, efficiently estimating camera motion and non-rigid deformation through structured QCQP and SDP relaxations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Hindsight Relabeling is All You Need for Reach-Avoid Learning
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kevin Li, Marinka Zitnik
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: RADT introduces a novel decision transformer for offline goal-conditioned reach-avoid learning, utilizing hindsight relabeling to dynamically specify avoid-regions without reward supervision, outperforming existing methods.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning methods have shown promise for reach-avoid tasks, where an agent must reach a target state while avoiding undesirable regions of the state space. Existing approaches typically encode avoid-region information into an augmented state space and cost function, which prevents flexible, dynamic specification of novel avoid-region information at evaluation time. They also rely heavily on meticulously designed reward and cost functions, limiting transferability to novel environments and specifications. We introduce RADT, a decision transformer approach for offline, reward-free, goal-conditioned, avoid-region-conditioned RL. RADT encodes goals and avoid-regions directly as prompt tokens, allowing any number of avoid-regions of arbitrary size to be specified at evaluation time. Using only suboptimal offline trajectories from a random policy, RADT can learn reach-avoid behavior in a completely data-driven manner using our novel avoid-region hindsight relabeling approach, without the need for reward/cost supervision. We benchmark RADT against existing offline goal-conditioned RL models across 17 tasks, environments, and experimental settings. RADT generalizes in a zero-shot manner to out-of-distribution avoid-region sizes and counts, outperforming baselines that require retraining. In one such zero-shot setting, RADT achieves 35.7% improvement in normalized cost over the best retrained baseline while maintaining high goal-reaching success. We also apply RADT to cell reprogramming in biology, demonstrating its versatility.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: GRASP introduces a gradient-guided sampling method for effective physics-based motion retargeting in robots, achieving high success rates in complex tasks without task-specific rewards.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Flow Equivariant World Models: Structured Memory for Dynamic Environments
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Hansen Jin Lillemark, Benhao Huang, Fangneng Zhan, Yilun Du, Thomas Anderson Keller
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that enhances dynamic environment predictions by utilizing time-parameterized symmetries in a structured latent memory.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Embodied systems experience the world as 'a symphony of flows': a combination of many continuous streams of sensory input coupled to self-motion, interwoven with the dynamics of external objects. These sensory streams and the underlying dynamics of the world obey smooth, time-parameterized symmetries which existing world models ignore. Without a memory that respects this structure, partial observability presents a major obstacle to existing methods: each observation reveals only a fraction of the world, while unobserved regions continue to evolve. In this work, we introduce Flow Equivariant World Modeling, a framework that leverages time-parameterized symmetries within a latent memory for stable and accurate dynamics prediction over long horizons. The latent memory shifts and transforms equivariantly with self-motion and inferred external object motion, keeping information about out-of-view regions aligned as time progresses. We demonstrate the advantage of this framework over state-of-the-art diffusion, memory-augmented, and recurrent world model architectures on 2D and 3D partially observed video world modeling benchmarks. More broadly, our results suggest that predictive representations become more powerful when they are organized in line with the temporal and dynamical structure of the world they model. Project page: https://flowequivariantworldmodels.github.io/

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Towards Trustworthy Physical Intelligence: From Theory to Practice Across Life Cycle
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yang Wang, Hongxuan Liu, Xinghui Xu, Arjun Menon, Xiaoran Cai
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper establishes a framework for trustworthy physical intelligence, addressing its unique challenges and operationalizing principles for governance throughout its life cycle.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Physical intelligence refers to intelligence systems that understand, reason about and act in accordance with the physical world and its underlying laws, dynamics, and constraints. Unlike conventional AI systems, physical intelligence interacts continuously with uncertain physical environments, and its actions produce consequences that are physically irreversible. As existing trustworthy AI frameworks have been developed primarily for digital AI systems, they do not fully capture the distinctive challenges of Physical Intelligence, such as physical safety, cyber-physical security, and physical manufacturing process. To address this gap, our paper develop a foundation for understanding, operationalizing, and governing trustworthy physical intelligence. First, we characterize the fundamental capabilities of physical intelligence. Second, we investigate the role of physical laws and principles in AI and analyze the associated challenges of physical intelligence. Third, we provide a unified structure of the end-to-end physical intelligence life cycle across five core stages and introduce the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence Operationalization (T-PAIO) framework. Fourth, we formulate the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence (T-PAI) Principles as a theoretical framework that synthesizes key trustworthiness dimensions and establishes a conceptual foundation for the governance of physical intelligence systems.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: BEACON: Cross-Domain Co-Training of Generative Robot Policies via Best-Effort Adaptation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Antong Zhang, Han Qi, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: BEACON is a framework for training generative robot policies that enhances robustness and data efficiency by using discrepancy-aware co-training across diverse source domains.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: We introduce BEACON--Best-Effort Adaptation for Cross-Domain Co-Training--a theory-guided framework for training generative robot policies with abundant source demonstrations and limited target demonstrations. BEACON casts cross-domain co-training as a discrepancy-aware importance-reweighting problem, jointly learning a diffusion-based visuomotor policy and per-sample source weights through an objective inspired by the Best-Effort Adaptation (BEA) bound. To make this approach practical for high-dimensional sequence policies, we develop scalable instance-level discrepancy proxies, stochastic alternating updates for policy and weights, and a multi-source extension that balances heterogeneous source domains. Across sim-to-sim, sim-to-real, and multi-source manipulation settings, BEACON improves robustness and data efficiency over target-only, fixed-ratio co-training, and feature-alignment baselines. Without an explicit alignment objective, BEACON also brings source and target representations closer together as an implicit result of discrepancy-aware co-training.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Iterative Gumbel Planning for Continuous Control
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shaohuai Liu, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du, Le Xie
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP) aligns continuous control policies with search candidates, enhancing performance and stability in reinforcement learning for robotics.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Search-based planning remains a powerful policy improvement paradigm in reinforcement learning, driving milestone successes in discrete domains. However, extending this paradigm to continuous control exposes a structural mismatch: search evaluates a finite set of action candidates, whereas continuous RL typically relies on Gaussian policies. We show that winner-action distillation into a continuous Gaussian induces a \textit{projection error} and a stepwise variance-expanding gradient tendency when the selected action is sufficiently far from the current mean. Empirically, this tendency is associated with elevated terminal variance and a return gap on the evaluated tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Iterative Gumbel Planning (IGP)}. By adopting a per-dimension factorized categorical policy, IGP naturally aligns the policy support with the search candidates, eliminating the projection error and reducing the residual approximation to a bounded discretization error. To bypass the combinatorial explosion of high-dimensional discrete action spaces, IGP pairs Gumbel Top-$K$ candidate sampling with an MPPI-style multi-round iterative search to refine the policy at each state. Empirically, IGP achieves state-of-the-art aggregate performance and sample efficiency on DMControl and HumanoidBench. Furthermore, it produces more stable action sequences with lower temporal variance, demonstrating its practical potential for real-world robotic deployment.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Energy-Based Policy Orchestration
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Weirui Ye, Yen-Jen Wang, Elvis Hsieh, Zhiyang Dou, Shibo Zhao
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator that optimizes runtime selection of policy-goal pairs for robust robot behavior in dynamic tasks.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy-goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy's goal and executes the lowest-energy policy-goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision-robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://yewr.github.io/epo

Rajpurkar Lab.title: RCR-Router: Efficient Role-Aware Context Routing for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Structured Memory
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Jun Liu, Zhenglun Kong, Changdi Yang, Fan Yang, Tianqi Li
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The RCR-Router optimizes multi-agent LLM systems by efficiently routing role-relevant context, reducing token usage by 35% and runtime by 38% while enhancing performance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into multi-agent systems for complex reasoning and decision-making tasks. However, scaling such systems can substantially increase inference cost, especially when multiple agents repeatedly process overlapping or role-irrelevant context. Many existing multi-agent frameworks focus on orchestration and role specialization, but still rely on full-context sharing or static context routing, leading to redundant token consumption, increased runtime, and inefficient memory utilization. We present \emph{Role-Conditioned Context Routing (RCR)}, an execution-time layer that allocates role-relevant shared-memory items to agents under token budgets. Given a structured shared memory and a set of role-specialized agents, RCR selectively routes task-relevant memory items to each agent according to its role, optional task-stage metadata, and token budget. RCR integrates role-conditioned relevance scoring, token-budgeted memory selection, and iterative memory updates to reduce redundant context exposure during multi-agent execution. Experiments on multi-hop QA, embodied reasoning (ALFWorld), and web-based decision-making (WebShop) show that RCR reduces token usage by 35\% on average and runtime by 38\% on average relative to Full-Context, while maintaining or improving task performance.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Jun Liu, Dajie Sun, Zhenglun Kong, Zhenjiang Fan, Peiyan Dong
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper audits test-time scaling in world-action models, revealing limited candidate selection benefits and efficiency gains, emphasizing the need for comprehensive evaluation beyond success rates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Samuel Schmidgall, Tim Strother, Alex Bijamov, Min Woo Sun, Anil Palepu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Training language models in simulated environments significantly enhances their performance in psychiatric intake interviews, improving diagnostic accuracy and patient communication while highlighting the need for clinician oversight.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer for Steerable Robot Manipulation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT) enhances robot manipulation by enabling preference adaptation across tasks using self-labeled demonstrations, achieving high accuracy and task success without manual annotations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: UMI-Live is an open-source bimanual robotics system enabling in-the-wild data collection without external calibration, validated through successful task demonstrations and released datasets.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $π_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Effectiveness of Curriculum Learning Depends on Reward Sparsity and Competing Optima
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: John J. Vastola, Ann Huang, Satpreet H. Singh, Samuel J. Gershman, Kanaka Rajan
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This study reveals that curriculum learning enhances reinforcement learning effectiveness primarily in sparse reward scenarios by reducing reward sparsity and guiding agents away from competing optima.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: While animals and people tend to learn a task more quickly and reliably when they first train on simpler versions of it, curriculum learning's effectiveness in artificial settings varies, and appears substantially greater in reinforcement learning than in supervised learning. In this work, we construct and analyze a minimal model of policy learning to better understand why. We consider an open-loop, episodic target interception task whose parameters---especially how close the agent must be to the target to receive an informative reward signal---can be chosen so that the agent either receives informative rewards frequently ('dense' rewards) or rarely ('sparse' rewards). We mathematically and numerically analyze the dynamics of REINFORCE-based policy learning in both cases. In the dense reward case, curricula have only marginal benefits; in the sparse case, curricula can be required for learning to occur at all. We find that this is especially true when the agent has the conflicting goals of minimizing effort and accumulating high reward, since this can produce distinct reward landscape optima which compete with one another. Our characterization of useful curricula in this setting indicates that they address two issues: they (i) make rewards less sparse to speed up learning, and (ii) shape the reward landscape to steer agents away from bad local optima.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Vahid Hosseinzadeh, T. Anderson Keller, Michael Puthawala
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper introduces Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM (MELSTM), enhancing sequence modeling by treating motion as a gauge symmetry, outperforming traditional models in various tasks.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Yuzhen Chen, Hannah Yao, Chonghe Jiang, Rao Fu
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: T-WLA integrates visual memory with tactile feedback to enhance contact-rich manipulation, achieving significant improvements in hand-motion prediction and real-world task success rates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan. Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task. We introduce T-WLA, a world-language-action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction. At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation. The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch. Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction. We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks. Videos and code are available at https://anonymous-submission-20.github.io/T-WLA.github.io/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: AI-driven Prices for Externalities and Sustainability in Production Markets
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Panayiotis Danassis, Aris Filos-Ratsikas, Haipeng Chen, Milind Tambe, Boi Faltings
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This paper presents a deep reinforcement learning agent that optimizes market prices to address negative externalities and enhance sustainability in production markets.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Traditional competitive markets do not account for negative externalities; indirect costs that some participants impose on others, such as the cost of over-appropriating a common-pool resource (which diminishes future stock, and thus harvest, for everyone). Quantifying appropriate interventions to market prices has proven to be quite challenging. We propose a practical approach to computing market prices and allocations via a deep reinforcement learning policymaker agent, operating in an environment of other learning agents. Our policymaker allows us to tune the prices with regard to diverse objectives such as sustainability and resource wastefulness, fairness, buyers' and sellers' welfare, etc. As a highlight of our findings, our policymaker is significantly more successful in maintaining resource sustainability, compared to the market equilibrium outcome, in scarce resource environments.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This paper presents a method for force-aware manipulation using visual force prediction from a compliant gripper, eliminating the need for specialized force sensors during deployment.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Learning to Be Different: Component Specialization for Compositional Diffusion Policies
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Alec Laprevotte, Haonan Chen, Xiaoshen Han, Yilun Du
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This paper introduces a score-decorrelation loss to enhance component specialization in diffusion policies, improving task decomposition and interpretability in multitask robotic learning.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task-wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition. However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory. Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double-counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics-score-decorrelation.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: A latent control model for realistic rodent motion
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Aidan Sirbu, Charles Y. Zhang, Yuanjia Yang, Bence P. Ölveczky, Talmo D. Pereira
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: SCAMPER is a novel system that trains an embodied virtual rat model to exhibit realistic movements during both goal-directed tasks and exploratory behavior using dual priors.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaboration With Uniform Exclusion Using Trust
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Thomas Kaminsky, Áron Vékássy, Hammad Izhar, Angelia Nedić, Stephanie Gil
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents a robust algorithm for safe multi-robot collaboration that selectively incorporates trusted communication links, ensuring performance despite potential malicious data.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Robot swarms coordinate through directed, time-varying local communication links, some of which may be compromised to allow the transmission of arbitrary malicious data. We provide an algorithm that acts as a wrapper around robot communication---when a robot seeks to update its state using data from some incoming links, our wrapper provides a subset of trusted links whose data can be safely incorporated. It selects these links by testing a stream of trust values---data collected from an anomaly detector on each robot---using Safe Anytime-Valid Inference. We require only that the detector be better than chance. This wrapper ensures safe and performant autonomy by providing two powerful statistical guarantees: it uniformly excludes all compromised links for all time with high user-chosen probability, but nevertheless quickly learns to trust legitimate links. Both guarantees are vital to secure generic tasks, but no previous work provides them simultaneously without restrictive assumptions on connectivity structure or the number of compromised links that are not guaranteed in practice. We study our Safe Wrapper's performance in hardware for two contrasting tasks---neural implicit mapping and heading consensus---deploying on 3 LoCoBots and 8 GoPiGos, respectively. We provide simulations using trust values sampled from hardware to validate that our approach scales well to swarms of hundreds of robots.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Composing What Each Teacher Learned: Delta Distillation for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Learning
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yuanda Xu, Hejian Sang, Zhengze Zhou, Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Xiaomin Li
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper introduces $Δ$-MOPD, a novel method for multi-teacher on-policy learning that improves performance by focusing on teacher-minus-base logit shifts rather than endpoint policies.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) is used in two settings. In common-domain composition, several teachers score each student rollout from one prompt domain and their signals form a single target; in routed-domain distillation, prompts from different domains are assigned to the corresponding specialist. Both settings usually transfer each teacher's endpoint policy, which mixes what post-training changed with preferences inherited from the teacher's base. We introduce $Δ$-MOPD, which transfers each teacher's teacher-minus-base logit shift re-anchored at the student's frozen initialization, and compare it with endpoint supervision in both settings while holding teacher selection fixed. We first expose the mechanism that impedes endpoint transfer: inherited base pull can exceed the post-training shift. Removing it reduces the teacher-term norm ratio and target--student KL. Across our experiments, the results suggest that shift targets are particularly useful when teacher signals are combined at a state. With three composed teachers, $Δ$-MOPD exceeds endpoint composition by $4.11$ Math and $1.95$ five-benchmark points; with two, it matches endpoint accuracy. Under phased routing, it achieves higher mean performance in both phase orders and reduces the observed order gap from $10.50$ to $6.42$ points. Under interleaved routing, where each update involves one teacher, the two targets perform comparably. The phased results provide supporting evidence that the benefit may extend to signals accumulated across training phases. Target construction is thus an independent design axis in MOPD, complementary to teacher selection. The experiment repo could be find at https://github.com/HJSang/Delta-MOPD

Rajpurkar Lab.title: ACTS: Learning Visuo-Tactile World Models from Human Physical Interaction
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Yuxiang Ma, Weihan Xu, Pengfei Ye, Anna Mei, Yuxin Ray Song
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: ACTS learns visuo-tactile world models from human interactions, enabling robots to predict contact dynamics more reliably than visual appearances in manipulation tasks.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Abstract Action-conditioned world models for contact-rich manipulation require data that captures how contact forms, slides, and releases under varying force. Such data are slow to collect through robot teleoperation, which often lacks force feedback and is constrained by gripper geometry. We ask whether these dynamics can instead be learned from human physical interaction and transferred to a robot. We present ACTS, a visuo-tactile world model trained only on human interaction data. Operators manipulate handheld GelSight sensors while we record third-person and wrist video, tactile images, 6-DoF sensor motion, and tactile-derived normal force, yielding React, a 4.9-hour bimanual dataset across three objects. We represent actions at the tactile sensor as motion augmented by force change, providing a shared action space for human collection and robot execution. ACTS jointly predicts future scene, wrist, and tactile observations. On held-out human data, ACTS improves scene-view prediction by 0.7-2.0 dB PSNR over the stronger of two visuo-tactile world models trained from scratch on React. Without fine-tuning, in the robot teleoperation rollouts we inspected, predicted tactile imprints still appear and disappear with recorded contact. Visual transfer is less robust: camera predictions exceed frame copying on PushT, are mixed on Rope, and fall below it on Motherboard, while wrist views can blur or hallucinate structure. These results suggest that contact dynamics transfer more reliably than visual appearance from human to robot.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: DreamCan introduces a hierarchical policy for robot manipulation that utilizes sparse visual planning to generate executable subgoals from video models, outperforming existing planning methods.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Shi Feng, Qimin Zhong, Siwei Wang, Yifei Shen, Shang-Hua Teng
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: This study explores error detection in Transformer planning by training models to recognize invalid transitions, enhancing planning reliability through abort mechanisms and retry strategies.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: SteerAct: Unlocking Action Models through Few-Shot Temporal Steering
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Kaichen Zhou, Zhiyan Li, Chongkai Gao, Yuhan Wang, Wenlong Huang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: SteerAct enhances pretrained robot action models by using few-shot temporal steering to optimize feature activations, improving task success by 10% without weight updates.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Improving pretrained robot action models at test time from only a few rollouts remains challenging. Activation steering offers a lightweight approach by modifying feature activations while keeping model weights fixed. However, effective steering requires identifying which features to modify and determining the timing and strength of modification. We introduce SteerAct, a few-shot temporal steering framework that uses a shared temporal descriptor of sparse-feature dynamics for offline feature selection and online control. A pretrained sparse autoencoder provides candidate features, and our temporal descriptor summarizes the distribution of local activation-order patterns for each feature, enabling comparisons across rollouts without requiring timestep alignment. Before steering begins (offline), we use successful and failed reference rollouts to select a single task-specific feature whose temporal descriptors best distinguish the two outcomes and construct its reference banks. During each new execution (online), we compare the feature's evolving temporal descriptor with these references to determine when to intervene and how strongly to increase or decrease its activation via a steering coefficient. Using only 24 outcome-labeled rollouts per task, SteerAct improves task success by approximately 10% relative to unsteered models in evaluations spanning $π_{0.5}$, Fast-WAM, RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and real-world manipulation, without updating action-model weights. Code and demos are available at: https://steeract.github.io/.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: MOIRA: Policy Memory and Belief Revision for Language-Model Agents in Non-Stationary Pair Trading
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Polydoros Giannouris, Yuechen Jiang, Lingfei Qian, Yuyan Wang, Xueqing Peng
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents MOIRA, a language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for pair trading that optimizes high-level and low-level policies using large language models, enhancing decision-making under non-stationarity.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Many sequential decision-making problems exhibit hierarchical structure, where high-level semantic choices constrain downstream actions and feedback is delayed and ambiguous. Learning in such settings is challenging due to credit assignment: performance degradation may arise from flawed abstractions, suboptimal execution, or their interaction. We study this challenge through pair trading, a domain that naturally combines long-horizon semantic reasoning for asset pair selection with short-horizon execution under partial observability. We formulate pair trading as a hierarchical reinforcement learning problem and propose a language-driven optimization framework in which both high-level and low-level policies are parameterized by large language models (LLMs) and optimized exclusively through prompt updates. Our approach leverages pretrained LLMs as hierarchical policies and uses trajectory- and episode-level textual feedback to adapt abstractions and execution without gradient-based fine-tuning. By explicitly separating abstraction selection from execution, the framework reduces non-stationarity across hierarchical levels and enables targeted adaptation under delayed feedback. Experiments on real-world market data show consistent improvements over traditional and LLM-based baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of language-driven hierarchical reinforcement learning.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Parham M. Kebria, Saeid Nahavandi, Mehrdad Saif, Fernando Bello
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: SurGPT is a multi-task foundation model that automates robotic surgical skills assessment and gesture recognition, enhancing training scalability and providing interpretable evaluations.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatiotemporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model's ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Can a Frontier VLM Serve as a Robot Policy for Memory-Dependent Manipulation?
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Jack B. Jedlicki, Amish Sethi, Heng Yang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The frontier vision-language model GPT-6-Astra outperforms previous benchmarks in memory-dependent manipulation tasks, achieving 92.1% success without specific training.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems. Project website: https://embodied-astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied-astra-robomme.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Runhan Huang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yitong Li, Yen-Jen Wang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: RAX is an open-source framework that enhances robot agents' online exploration capabilities, enabling autonomous skill acquisition and improved generalization across diverse tasks without prior demonstration data.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: VISTA: A Multimodal Egocentric Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Perception and Assistance to Blind and Low-Vision Users
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Noé Mosca, Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Muhammad Hamza, Joshua Yeh, Suryodaya Bikram Shahi
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: VISTA is a new multimodal benchmark designed to enhance goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users by evaluating various sensor inputs and task categories.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Momentum: Persistent Dynamics for Video World Models
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Nedko Savov, Stefan Maria Ailuro, Danda Pani Paudel, Yilun Du, Xi Wang
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: Momentum introduces a two-stage pipeline for video world models that enhances dynamic scene consistency by utilizing synchronized videos from multiple camera rigs, outperforming static methods.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Video world models must capture how a scene evolves beyond the current camera view to generate consistent observations when its content reappears. Existing approaches rely on observation history, static point clouds, or image caches constructed from past frames. These representations are often expensive and, more importantly, cannot update dynamic scene content outside the field of view: generated vehicles and pedestrians may be forgotten after leaving the field of view or reappear in physically inaccurate states. We represent an evolving scene through synchronized videos from reference-camera rigs, each comprising eight cameras that jointly cover the surrounding scene. We connect these rigs in a graph and propagate video generation between neighboring rigs to coordinate scene dynamics across locations and time. We introduce Momentum, a two-stage pipeline: WorldUpdate jointly generates reference-camera videos as a shared memory of scene dynamics, and WorldInteract grounds camera-controlled video generation in this evolving memory, allowing moving content to remain represented outside the target view and reappear consistently. To support training and evaluation, we develop a CARLA pipeline that captures synchronized videos from reference camera rigs and a moving target camera, together with an evaluation framework measuring consistency within the generated world state and the target observations.Experiments on generated street scenes show that grounding target videos in scene dynamics generated by Momentum improves dynamic scene consistency by 126.2% in unseen scenes over static image conditioning, while also improving visual fidelity. Our models and source code will be made publicly available.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: AdaLoop: Thinking with the Vision Encoder
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Xinran Nicole Han, Yiyang Lu, Katelyn Gan, Todd Zickler
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: AdaLoop enhances vision-language models by enabling question-conditioned visual recurrence, improving reasoning through iterative visual computation while utilizing frozen pretrained vision encoders.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) treat the vision encoder as a static feature extractor: it encodes an image once, independently of the question, and leaves subsequent reasoning to the language model. Yet different questions may require different visual operations and processing depths. We present AdaLoop, a framework for question-conditioned visual recurrence in VLMs. AdaLoop adapts visual computation to the question and reuses the encoder's transformations across multiple iterations, with the pretrained vision weights frozen. We also introduce VisRO, a procedural dataset and generation pipeline for training and evaluating vision-centric reasoning. On six VisRO tasks, AdaLoop outperforms standard fine-tuning and question-conditioned single-pass baselines with matched training data and optimizer updates. These gains hold across three VLM families on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Our findings suggest that pretrained vision encoders can contribute to reasoning through task-directed, iterative visual computation.

Rajpurkar Lab.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms
Rajpurkar Lab.authors_text: Guowei Xu, Zhenting Qi, Amani Kiruga, Himabindu Lakkaraju, Yilun Du
Rajpurkar Lab.summary: The paper presents a market-based post-training framework for decentralized agent swarms, enabling simultaneous learning of action policies and self-orchestration, enhancing adaptability and performance.
Rajpurkar Lab.debug_abstract: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Amani Kiruga, Zhiyi Li, Ruojin Cai, Hansen Lillemark, Xiaoshan Wu
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: UGG is a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that integrates RGB video and geometric representations, enhancing visual generation and geometric prediction through conditional completion.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Zilin Dai, Lehong Wang, Yi Yang, Xiang Fei
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: WireSeg-32K is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 images for wire instance segmentation, utilizing a co-simulation pipeline for realistic wire deformation and improving model performance in real-world applications.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Shuyue Stella Li, Priyanka Kargupta, Haocheng Wang, Jinu Lee, Dean Light
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: This paper analyzes cognitive elements in reasoning, revealing differences between human and LLM processes, and proposes a framework to enhance model reasoning accuracy through structured guidance.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning and knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and apply it to 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, alongside 1,346 human think-aloud traces on a new, domain-agnostic dataset for human-model comparison. We find that models are able to deploy cognitive elements seen in human reasoning but differ in how they use them. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffolds successful reasoning topologies, improving the accuracy of the strongest models by 9.7 percentage points on ill-structured problems. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements but rarely targets self-awareness, whose use differs between human and model reasoning. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Haoyu Han, Jack Benarroch Jedlicki, Jiahui Lei, Heng Yang
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: XM4D presents a certifiably optimal framework for 4D reconstruction, efficiently estimating camera motion and non-rigid deformation through structured QCQP and SDP relaxations.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.title: Hindsight Relabeling is All You Need for Reach-Avoid Learning
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.authors_text: Kevin Li, Marinka Zitnik
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.summary: RADT introduces a novel decision transformer for offline goal-conditioned reach-avoid learning, utilizing hindsight relabeling to dynamically specify avoid-regions without reward supervision, outperforming existing methods.
Harvard Microrobotics Laboratory.debug_abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning methods have shown promise for reach-avoid tasks, where an agent must reach a target state while avoiding undesirable regions of the state space.
